images.description: Table showing array vals at address 0x7420 with indices [0]-[4] and values 7,4,9,2,3. Code example and info box about Fun Fact 3.

title: Formula for Addressing Array Elements
summary: Shows the concrete formula start_addr + i*data_size for computing element addresses, and warns that C/C++ does NOT perform bounds checking.
main_text: Assume a 5-element int array: int x[5] = {8,5,3,9,6}; starting at address 7400. When you access x[2], the CPU uses x (to know the starting address) and adds the product of the index 2 times the size of the data type (int = 4 bytes). x[2] => int at address 7400 + 2*4 = 7408. x[3] => int at address 7400 + 3*4 = 7412. General formula: x[i] at start address of array + i * (size of int). To access an element in an array, we need 3 pieces of info: 1) Start address of the array, 2) Index/offset, 3) Type of elements (really the size of that type). Formula: start_addr + i*data_size. Recall: C/C++ does NOT perform bounds checking to stop you from attempting to access an element beyond the end of the array. x[6] => int at address 7400 + 6*4 = 7424 -- this is Garbage since the array only has indices 0-4!
notes_text: The memory table shows addresses 7400-7424 with actual hex values. Accessing x[6] goes to address 7424 which contains whatever happens to be in memory there (a184beef feedface) -- this is undefined behavior and a major source of bugs and security vulnerabilities.

images.description: Memory table showing addresses 7400-7424 with array values and beyond-array garbage. Info box listing 3 pieces needed for array access with formula.

title: Recall: Passing Arrays - Address as Link
summary: Reiterates that when passing arrays, only the starting address (pointer) is passed, and the function uses address, type, and index to access elements.
main_text: The 'link' that is passed is just the starting address of (pointer to) the array in memory (e.g. 7420). Once the function has the start address and the type, it will produce its own index values and be able to access the array in the caller's memory. The code shows int sum(int data[], int size) receiving the address 7420 for the vals array. The diagram shows main's vals array at addresses 7420-7816, with data in sum() receiving just the address value 7420 as a disk/pointer icon. The three pieces of info needed to access an element are: 1) Start address, 2) Index/offset, 3) Type of elements (size of that type).
notes_text: This slide revisits the earlier concept but now with the stack and memory address knowledge. The data parameter in sum() holds the value 7420, which is the memory address of vals[0] in main's stack frame. Using this address plus the index and type size, sum can access any element.

images.description: Diagram showing main's vals array with address 7420 being passed as a pointer value to sum's data parameter. Code listing and info box about array access requirements.

title: Stack View of Passing Arrays: init() Function
summary: Shows the stack layout when passing an array to init(), demonstrating how the address 7420 in init's frame points back to main's vals array.
main_text: The function receives the starting address of the array which it can use along with the type (e.g. int) and index to access the appropriate values from main's stack area of memory. The stack diagram shows: init's frame at addresses 7400-7412 with i (iterating 0-99), data=7420 (the address of vals), size=100, and return link. Main's frame at 7416-7820 with mysum=0, vals[0] through vals[99] at addresses 7420-7816, and return link. Step 1: We copy the address as init()'s argument, not the values. Step 2: The address allows init() to access the original data in main(). The init function sets data[i] = 5 for all i, which modifies vals directly since data points to the same memory.
notes_text: This is a starred/important slide showing the complete stack picture. The key insight is that data in init()'s frame holds 7420 -- the same address where vals[0] lives in main's frame. When init writes to data[i], it's writing to address 7420 + i*4, which IS vals[i].

images.description: Detailed stack diagram showing init's frame with data=7420 pointer and main's frame with vals array at address 7420. Arrows show how data[i] in init accesses vals[i] in main.

metadata.topic: Stack View of Array Passing - init

title: Why Empty Brackets in Array Parameters
summary: Explains why array parameters use empty brackets (int data[]) rather than specifying a size, for generality since C/C++ does not bounds check anyway.
main_text: Why don't we just supply the array size in the formal argument? C/C++ doesn't do bounds checking anyway, so what good would writing 100 be? And why would we want to limit this function to only working with arrays of size 100? Let's let it be general. The code contrasts int sum(int data[100], int size) (restrictive) with int sum(int data[], int size) (general). The stack diagram shows sum's frame with i, total=500, data=7420, size=100, and return link. Main's frame has mysum=0, vals[0]-vals[99]. Using empty brackets allows the same function to work with arrays of any size, making the code reusable.
notes_text: The circled 100 in int data[100] highlights this as a bad practice. Since C/C++ ignores the size in brackets for function parameters anyway (it still just passes the address), specifying it adds no safety and reduces generality. The size parameter serves the purpose of communicating array length.

images.description: Stack diagram showing sum's frame accessing main's vals array via address 7420. Code comparison highlighting int data[100] (bad) vs int data[] (good).

title: Array Summary: Key Facts
summary: Summarizes array rules: fixed size declaration, C/C++ only remembers start address and type, no bounds checking, and the address formula.
main_text: Arrays must be declared with a FIXED size (cannot use a variable for its length). GOOD: int data[50]; BAD: int data[n]; After declaring an array, C/C++ only 'remembers' the starting address of the array and the type of data it holds (to know the data size). Which is all it needs to know to access any element using the formula: start_addr + i*data_size. C/C++ do NO bounds checking. They will simply apply the formula above to WHATEVER index you provide or calculate. This is the most common source of a program crash (and also security vulnerabilities). If your program crashes in CS 103, suspect a bad array access.
notes_text: This is a crucial summary slide. The three key takeaways: 1) Arrays have fixed size at compile time, 2) Only address and type are stored (no length!), 3) No bounds checking means out-of-bounds access causes crashes or security vulnerabilities. Students should always validate indices before using them.

title: C-Strings, cout, and cin Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing C-strings and their special relationship with cout and cin for input/output operations.
main_text: This section covers C-strings (character arrays) and how cout and cin have special behavior when working with character arrays compared to other array types. C-strings are fundamental to understanding text processing in C/C++.
notes_text: C-strings are a legacy from C that are still widely used in C++. Understanding them is important because many system APIs and libraries use them, and they reveal how strings actually work at the memory level.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (1): C-String Basics
summary: Explains that C/C++ string constants are character arrays terminated by the null character '\0', and shows how to declare, initialize, modify, and I/O them.
main_text: In C/C++, string constants (text between double quotes) are just character arrays. Each character consumes 1 element in the array. They end with the null character (0 decimal or '\0' ASCII). This approach of using an array of chars to store a string is referred to as a C-String because there was no string type in C (before C++). The code demonstrates: char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'} and char str2[7] = "CS 103" (initializes the array to 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'). cout << str1 prints "CS", cout << str2 prints "CS 103". str2[5] = '4' changes the string to "CS 104". cin >> str2 with input "hello" replaces the contents. The memory layout shows str2 at addresses 520-526 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'.
notes_text: The null terminator '\0' is critical -- it tells functions like cout where the string ends. Without it, cout would keep reading memory past the array boundary. The string literal "CS 103" automatically includes the null terminator, which is why str2 needs 7 characters (6 for text + 1 for null).

images.description: Memory layout showing str2 at addresses 520-526 with characters 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0'. Code example with output showing string operations.

title: Character Arrays and Loops: How cout Handles Strings
summary: Shows that cout internally loops through character arrays until the null terminator, while other arrays require manual loops for printing.
main_text: How many things can a computer do at a time? One. To print out a string/character array, we would have to print one character at a time. But C/C++ treats character arrays specially. cout has a loop inside its code to print strings/character arrays. Similarly, cin has a loop inside to input a string. We say cout and cin have a special relationship with character arrays. The code shows manual printing with a for loop: for(int i=0; str[i] != '\0'; i++) { cout << str[i]; } But you can simply write: cout << str1; and cout will automatically loop through all characters until it hits '\0'. The memory layout shows str1 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','3','\0' and program output shows both approaches produce the same result.
notes_text: This explains the magic behind cout << str working for character arrays. cout checks if it receives a char* (character pointer/array) and if so, loops character by character until hitting null. For other array types like int[], cout just prints the address, which is why you need manual loops.

images.description: Memory layout of str1 with characters and null terminator. Code showing manual loop vs direct cout output producing identical results.

title: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Demonstrates that cout treats character arrays specially by printing all characters, while for other array types it prints the address or requires manual loops.
main_text: To print out all elements of any array type OTHER than a character array (int, double, bool, etc.) you must write your OWN loop because computers can only do 1 thing at a time. But for character arrays, you can just give cout the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to print out all characters for you. So internally it is actually looping over the characters, so you do not have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to print out all the characters. Thus, we say cout treats character arrays specially. The code shows: for int array, you must loop and print each element. cout << data prints the address (0x7fffce40), not the values. But cout << str1 prints "Many chars". Program output: 9 7 8 9 5 / 0x7fffce40 / Many chars.
notes_text: This is a common source of confusion. When students write cout << intArray, they expect to see the values but get a hex address instead. Only character arrays get the special treatment of printing actual content. This behavior is inherited from C's printf with %s format specifier.

images.description: Two array tables: data[5] = {9,7,8,9,5} and str1 = 'Many chars'. Code showing different cout behavior for int vs char arrays. Program output demonstrates the difference.

title: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Shows that cin treats character arrays specially by reading a full word into the array, while other array types require manual element-by-element input.
main_text: To get input for all elements of an array type OTHER than character arrays (int, double, etc.) you must write your OWN loop. But for character arrays, you can just give cin the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to receive all the characters the user types and store them sequentially in the array. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to get a full string (stopping at the next space). cin treats character arrays specially. The code shows: cin >> data won't even compile for int arrays. For int input, use a loop: for(int i=0; i<5; i++) cin >> data[i]. But cin >> str1 reads an entire word at once. When user types 'CS102', cin stores 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' into str1 automatically, including the null terminator.
notes_text: cin stops reading at whitespace for character arrays. It also automatically appends the null terminator. However, cin does NOT check if the input fits in the array, which leads to buffer overflow problems discussed on the next slide.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1 before cin (garbage values) and after cin with 'CS102' input: 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' stored with null terminator.

title: Buffer Overflow: cin and Character Arrays
summary: Warns that cin does not check array bounds, so input longer than the array overwrites adjacent memory, causing crashes or security vulnerabilities.
main_text: What if the user types in TOO much (more characters than our array has room to store)? cin will not stop! It will keep storing the characters the user types, overwriting whatever data and variables came after the array. Warning: cin does not CHECK that the string typed by the user will fit in the array; instead it simply overwrites memory leading to undefined (bad) behavior! The example shows char str1[4] with int sum = 0 after it. If user types 'CS102' (5 chars + null = 6 bytes), cin writes past str1's 4 bytes, overwriting sum's memory. cout << sum will not see 0 because sum was modified by the overflow. C++ strings fix this issue, allocating more space based on what is typed. Memory diagrams show str1 at addresses 520-523 with sum at 524, and after overflow str1 contains 'C','S','1','0' with '3','\0' overwriting sum.
notes_text: Buffer overflow is one of the most dangerous and common security vulnerabilities in C/C++. It is the basis for many hacker exploits. C++ string objects dynamically resize and are immune to this problem, which is why modern C++ prefers std::string over C-strings.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1[4] and sum before and after buffer overflow from cin input 'CS103'. The overflow overwrites sum's memory location.

title: C-Strings (Character Arrays) Operations Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing operations on C-strings (NULL terminated character arrays) including comparison, copying, and concatenation.
main_text: This section covers operations that can be performed on C-strings (NULL terminated character arrays), including the limitations of using standard operators and the library functions provided to work with them.
notes_text: Unlike C++ string objects which support operators like ==, =, and +, C-strings require special library functions for these operations. Understanding why standard operators fail on C-strings requires understanding that arrays are addresses, not values.

title: C-Strings: No Standard Operators
summary: Explains that C-strings do not support comparison (==), assignment (=), or concatenation (+) operators because arrays are addresses, not values.
main_text: In C, strings were not a first-class type (i.e. no string type). Strings were simply character arrays (char[]) terminated by the null character (0 dec. = '\0' ASCII). These were known as C-Strings. No operations/operators other than typical array operations are provided: No comparison (== or !=), No assignment/copy (=), No append/concatenate (+). The code shows attempting these operations: if(str3 == str1) actually compares addresses, not contents. str3 = str1 and str3 += str2 will not compile because array types are not assignable. The memory shows str1 at address 800 containing 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','\0'.
notes_text: This is a key gotcha for students coming from Python or Java. In those languages, == compares string content. In C/C++ with char arrays, == compares memory addresses (pointers), which is almost never what you want. The compiler may warn about this but it is a common mistake.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str1 at address 800 with C-string contents. Code attempting to use ==, =, and += on C-strings.

title: C-String Errors: Compiler Warnings and Errors
summary: Shows actual compiler errors when attempting to use ==, =, and += on C-strings, demonstrating that these operations fail or behave incorrectly.
main_text: The code attempts three operations on C-strings that fail: 1) if(str3 == str1) generates a compiler warning: 'comparison between two arrays is deprecated; array comparison always evaluates to false'. This compares addresses, not string content. 2) str3 = str1 generates error: 'array type char[15] is not assignable'. Arrays cannot be assigned with =. 3) str3 += str2 generates error: 'invalid operands to binary expression (char[15] and char[7])'. The += operator does not work on arrays. Memory diagrams show str1 at address 800 ('CS103 is '), str2 at 820 ('fun'), and str3 at 840 ('cool' from user input via cin). The compiler output explicitly shows these errors.
notes_text: Showing actual compiler error messages helps students understand what goes wrong and learn to interpret error output. The deprecated warning on == is particularly insidious because it compiles (possibly with just a warning) but gives the wrong result, while = and += are hard errors.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing three C-strings in memory. Compiler error output showing warnings and errors for ==, =, and += operations.

title: C String Function Library: strlen, strcmp, strcpy, strcat
summary: Introduces the cstring library functions for C-string operations: strlen (length), strcmp (compare), strcpy (copy), and strcat (concatenate).
main_text: A library of functions was provided to perform operations on character arrays representing strings (<cstring> in C++, <string.h> in C). int strlen(char dest[]): Returns the length of the string (not counting the null character). int strcmp(char str1[], char str2[]): Returns 0 if equal, >0 if str1 is alphanumerically larger than str2, <0 if str1 is less than str2. char* strcpy(char dest[], char src[]): Copies the whole C-string from src to the dest array (overwriting what's in dest). Ignore the return type for now (think of it as a void function). char* strcat(char dest[], char src[]): Concatenates src to the end of dest. Ignore the return type for now (think of it as a void function).
notes_text: These four functions are the C-string equivalents of .length(), ==, =, and + for C++ strings. They all work by iterating through characters until hitting the null terminator. Students should memorize these function signatures and understand that dest must have enough space for the result.

title: Use of the C-String Library: Complete Example
summary: Demonstrates practical use of strcmp, strcpy, and strcat to compare, copy, and concatenate C-strings, replacing the invalid ==, =, and += operators.
main_text: The code includes <cstring> and shows correct C-string operations: str1[] = "CS103 is ", str2[] = "fun", str3[15] is read from cin (user enters 'cool'). Instead of str3 == str1, use: if(0 == strcmp(str1, str3)) { cout << "Match"; }. Instead of str3 = str1, use: strcpy(str3, str1); -- this copies 'CS103 is ' into str3. Memory shows str3 at 840 now contains 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','\0'. Instead of str3 += str2, use: strcat(str3, str2); -- this appends 'fun' to str3. Memory shows str3 at 840 now contains 'C','S','1','0','3',' ','i','s',' ','f','u','n','\0'. The final cout << str3 prints "CS103 is fun".
notes_text: This example shows the correct replacements for all three failed operations from slide 58. Note that strcmp returns 0 for equal strings (counterintuitive), so the comparison is if(0 == strcmp(...)). strcpy and strcat both require the destination to have enough space, or buffer overflow occurs.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing str1, str2, and str3 at addresses 800, 820, 840 through the stages of strcpy and strcat operations. Code listing with correct C-string function calls.

title: Sample Implementations: strlen and strcpy Exercises
summary: Presents exercises for students to implement strlen and strcpy functions themselves to understand how C-string functions work internally.
main_text: This slide presents exercises for students to implement two fundamental C-string functions: strlen (string length) and strcpy (string copy). Implementing these functions helps students understand how C-string library functions work internally by iterating through characters until the null terminator is found. strlen counts characters until '\0' is reached. strcpy copies characters one by one from source to destination until '\0' is copied.
notes_text: These implementation exercises reinforce that C-string functions are essentially loops that process characters until the null terminator. strlen increments a counter while the current character is not '\0'. strcpy copies each character from src to dest and stops after copying '\0'.

title: Cipher Exercise: Array as Lookup Table for Encryption
summary: Exercise using a character array as a lookup table to implement a substitution cipher for encrypting text.
main_text: Cipher: Using an array as a Look-Up Table. Create a cipher code to encrypt text. The standard alphabet abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz maps to the cipher ghijklmaefnzyqbcdrstuopvwx. Given char orig_string[] = "helloworld" and char new_string[11], after encryption new_string should be "akzzbpbrzj". Define another array: char cipher[27] = "ghijklmaefnzyqbcdrstuopvwx". The question is: how could we use the original character to index ('look up' a value in) the cipher array? The key insight is that subtracting 'a' from a lowercase letter gives its 0-based position (e.g., 'h'-'a' = 7), which can be used as an index into the cipher array.
notes_text: This exercise combines multiple concepts: character arrays, ASCII arithmetic (subtracting 'a' to get 0-based index), and arrays as lookup tables. The conversion cipher[orig_string[i] - 'a'] maps each character through the substitution table. This is a practical application of random access.

title: Input Buffer Overflow: Stack Corruption Example
summary: Demonstrates how cin input longer than the array corrupts the stack, overwriting local variables like size and loc, leading to crashes.
main_text: Depending on user input, this program will likely crash. The program finds the location of the first capital letter in text. It declares char str[8], const int size = 8, int loc = 0, then uses cin >> str. If the user types 'abcdefgh0123456' (more than 8 characters), cin writes past str's 8 bytes, corrupting size and loc on the stack. The stack before execution shows str at address 7300 (8 bytes of garbage), size at 7308 (value 8), loc at 7312 (value 0). After cin >> str with the long input, the ASCII values of the input overwrite everything: str gets 61-68, but size and loc are overwritten with 30-36 (ASCII for '0'-'6'). The isupper check on corrupted data produces unpredictable results.
notes_text: This is a concrete demonstration of why buffer overflow is so dangerous. The stack layout shows exactly how local variables after the array get overwritten. In a real attack, a hacker could craft input to overwrite the return link, hijacking program execution (covered in CS 356).

images.description: Two stack diagrams showing memory before and after cin overflow. Before: str has garbage, size=8, loc=0. After: str and subsequent variables overwritten with ASCII input values. Code listing showing the vulnerable program.

title: Solutions and More Function Examples Section Header
summary: Section divider for self-study solutions and additional function examples covering pass-by-value, array passing, and scope.
main_text: This section provides solutions to earlier exercises and additional function examples for self-study. Students are encouraged to work through these examples and ask questions about concepts that are unclear.
notes_text: The remaining slides provide solutions and reinforcement of key concepts from the unit. Students should trace through the code and stack diagrams on their own before checking the solutions.

title: Pass by Value Solution: Using Return to Communicate
summary: Shows the corrected dec function using return value to properly communicate the decremented result back to main.
main_text: Revisiting the motivating example, the original code with void dec(int y) { y--; } does not change main's y because each function is a completely separate sandbox isolated from other functions and their data, and copies of data are passed and returned between them. The only way to communicate back to main is via return. The solution changes dec to: int dec(int y) { y--; return y; } and main to: y = dec(y). Now dec returns the decremented value 2, which main captures and assigns to its own y. This properly communicates the result back through the return value mechanism.
notes_text: This solution reinforces the Main Point of function isolation. The sandbox analogy shows that modifications to the copy inside dec are lost unless explicitly returned. The corrected version makes dec an int function that returns the modified value.

images.description: Two code panels: original void dec version (prints 3) and corrected int dec version with return y (prints 2). Sandbox diagram showing function isolation.

title: Exercise Solution: Array Element Address Formulas
summary: Provides solutions for the train car analogy: i-th car at A + 5*i, i-th integer at A + 4*i, and i-th double at A + 8*i.
main_text: Consider a train with many copies of the same car. The 0th car starts at point A, each car is 5 meters long. The i-th car is located at A + 5*i meters. Suppose a set of integers start at memory address A, the i-th integer starts at A + 4*i (since int is 4 bytes). Suppose a set of doubles start at memory address A, the i-th double starts at A + 8*i (since double is 8 bytes). The train diagram shows 0th car at A, 1st car at A+5, 2nd car at A+10, reinforcing the general formula: start_address + index * element_size.
notes_text: These formulas are what the CPU calculates internally when you use array indexing. Understanding this helps explain why array access is O(1) -- it is just an arithmetic calculation, not a search. The element size (4 for int, 8 for double, 1 for char) determines the spacing between elements.

images.description: Train cars on number line with formulas A + 5*i, A + 4*i, and A + 8*i shown in boxes for cars, integers, and doubles respectively.

title: Parameter Passing (1): max Function Example
summary: Additional example showing formal vs actual parameters with a max function, reinforcing copy semantics and type matching.
main_text: Formal parameters a and b: Type of data the parameter expects. Names that will be used internal to the function to refer to the values passed (like 'CEO' or 'professor' in contracts that will be replaced with real values). Actual parameters: Actual values ('Jeff Bezos', 'Mark') input to the function by the caller. A copy is made and given to the function. The code shows int max(int a, int b) with if(a > b) return a; else return b; In main, int x=6, z; z = max(x, 4) passes x (value 6) and literal 4 as actuals. The formals a and b receive copies 6 and 4. The function returns 6. Each type is a different shape (int = triangle, double = square, char = circle). Only a value of that type can fit as a parameter.
notes_text: This reinforces the formal/actual parameter distinction with a different function example. The max function demonstrates how return communicates results back. The shape analogy for types (triangle=int) helps visualize type safety.

images.description: Diagram showing actuals x=6 and literal 4 being copied into formals a and b in max() sandbox, with return value 6. Code listing shows max function and main.

title: Scope Example: Global vs Local Variables and Shadowing
summary: Comprehensive scope example showing global variables, local variables, block scope, and variable shadowing with the scope resolution operator.
main_text: Globals live as long as the program is running. Variables declared in a block { ... } live as long as the block has not completed, whether that block is a function, a loop, an if statement, etc. When variables share the same name, the closest declaration will be used by default. The code shows: global int x = 5, main declares int a, x = 8, y = 3. Inside a for loop, int j = 1 is local to the loop block. cout << 'x = ' << x prints 8 (local x shadows global). The doit function takes int x, decrements it, and returns it, operating on its own copy. a = doit(y) passes y=3. cout << 'a=' << a prints 2 (doit returned 3-1=2). cout << 'y=' << y prints 3 (unchanged, pass-by-value). cout << 'glob. X' << ::x prints 5 (scope resolution operator accesses global x). Memory shows globals at low addresses (x=5), main's frame at high addresses (a=2, x=8, y=3).
notes_text: This example combines many scope concepts: global vs local, block scope for loop variables, variable shadowing (local x=8 hides global x=5), and the scope resolution operator (::x) to explicitly access the global. Students should trace through this carefully.

images.description: Code listing with scope annotations and memory layout showing Code, Globals (x=5), Heap, and Stack (main: a=2, x=8, y=3)

title: Recall: Passing Arrays As Arguments - Syntax
summary: Reviews the syntax for passing arrays as function arguments: empty brackets in prototype/definition, array name as actual parameter.
main_text: Syntax for passing arrays: Step 1: In the prototype and function definition, put empty square brackets [] after the formal parameter name if it is an array (e.g. int data[]). Alternatively, put an * between the type and formal parameter name (e.g. int* data). We prefer int data[] for now but int* data is JUST AS VALID and we will learn more about it when we cover pointers. Step 2: When you call the function, just provide the name of the array as the actual parameter. The code shows: int init(int data[], int max_size); as the prototype. In main: int vals[100]; int len = init(vals, 100); The init function reads numbers from cin into the array, stopping when the array is full or user enters -1, and returns the count of elements read.
notes_text: This slide provides a practical template for writing functions that take arrays. The init function demonstrates a common pattern: reading input into an array with a maximum size guard, using a sentinel value (-1) to stop, and returning the actual count of elements stored.

images.description: Code listing showing array function prototype with empty brackets, main function calling init with array name, and init implementation reading from cin.

title: Arrays And Pass-by-Reference: Modifications Visible to Caller
summary: Reinforces that arrays are passed by reference via addresses, so modifications in a called function are visible to the caller.
main_text: Arrays are passed-by-reference. Links (addresses) are passed. These links are actually memory addresses where the array starts. Using these addresses, any function can go to those locations and modify the data (array) from another function. It need not be returned since the function is modifying the original. Thus, changes to the array by a function are visible upon return to the caller. The code shows void init(int data[], int size) setting nums[i] = -1 for all elements. In main, int vals[10] at address 7420 is declared and init(vals, 10) is called. After init returns, cout << vals[2] prints -1, confirming that init modified main's array directly. In this example, nums and vals refer to the same array.
notes_text: This is the complete picture: the formal parameter nums in init is just another name for the same memory that vals occupies in main. Any write through nums[i] = -1 directly writes to vals[i] because they share the same starting address 7420.

images.description: Code showing init function setting all elements to -1 and main verifying the changes. Array visualization showing vals with all -1 values at address 7420.

title: Lack of Array Bounds Checking: Security Implications
summary: Warns that C++ does NOT bounds check array accesses, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes that corrupt stack data and enable hacker exploits.
main_text: C++ does NOT bounds check the index used to access an element. It will simply treat all of memory as part of the array (larger positive indices go past the end, negative offsets go before the array start). This means you could potentially read and write data you should not (including variables from your own function or another function since local variables live on the stack). This issue is a common exploit by hackers (more in future courses like CS 356). The example shows int f1() with int dat[4], x=0. The loop for(int i=0; i <= 4; i++) has an off-by-one error (should be i < 4, not i <= 4). When i=4, dat[4] writes to what is actually x's memory location (since x is adjacent on the stack at address 7436). The input values 9,4,3,7,1000 cause dat[4]=1000 which overwrites x, so cout << x prints 1000 instead of 0. Accessing dat[1000] would likely cause a segmentation fault.
notes_text: This is one of the most important security lessons in the course. Off-by-one errors (using <= instead of <) are extremely common and can overwrite critical stack data including return addresses. In CS 356, students learn how attackers exploit this to inject malicious code.

images.description: Stack diagram showing f1's frame with dat[0-3] at addresses 7420-7432, x at 7436, and return link at 7440. dat[4] at 7436 overlaps with x, and writing 1000 there corrupts x.

title: Stack View of Passing Arrays: sum() Function
summary: Complete stack diagram showing sum() accessing main's vals array through the passed starting address, with init having already set all values to 5.
main_text: The function receives the starting address of the array which it can use along with the type (e.g. int) and index to access the appropriate values from main's stack area of memory. The stack diagram shows two stages: sum's frame at addresses 7396-7412 with i (iterating 0-99), total (accumulating to 500), data=7420, size=100, and return link. Main's frame at 7416-7820 with mysum (updated from 0 to 500), vals[0]-vals[99] (all containing 5 from init). The code shows void init(int data[], int size) and int sum(int data[], int size) prototypes. Main calls init(vals, 100) then mysum = sum(vals, 100). sum iterates through the array using the address 7420, accumulating total = 5*100 = 500, which is returned and stored in mysum.
notes_text: This final stack diagram ties together all the concepts: function stack frames, pass-by-value for size (100 is copied), pass-by-reference for arrays (address 7420 points to main's data), and the address formula for accessing elements (7420 + 4*i). The expression 7420+4*i is shown explicitly for the element access.

images.description: Detailed stack diagram showing sum's frame (i, total=500, data=7420, size=100) accessing main's vals array (all 5s). Arrows show data[i] accessing vals[i] through address 7420+4*i. Code listing shows both init and sum functions.

title: Unit 1d - Algorithms and Runtime
summary: Title slide introducing the Algorithms and Runtime unit for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 1d of CS 103, covering Algorithms and Runtime. The unit explores what algorithms are, how they are represented, and how we measure their efficiency using runtime analysis and big-O notation. Topics include algorithm definitions, pseudocode, searching algorithms (sequential and binary search), sorting algorithms (bubble sort), and time complexity classification.
notes_text: This unit is foundational for understanding computational efficiency. Students should pay attention to how different algorithms solve the same problem with vastly different performance characteristics.

title: Algorithms
summary: Defines algorithms informally and formally, emphasizing their key properties: ordered, unambiguous, executable, and terminating steps.
main_text: Algorithms are at the heart of computer systems, both in hardware (HW) and software (SW). They are fundamental to Computer Science and Computer Engineering. Informal definition: An algorithm is a precise way to accomplish a task or solve a problem. A more formal definition: An ordered set of unambiguous, executable steps that defines a terminating process. Key properties of algorithms include: Ordered - the steps of an algorithm have a particular order, not just any order. Unambiguous - each step is completely clear as to what is to be done. Executable - each step can actually be performed. Terminating Process - the algorithm will stop eventually (sometimes this requirement is relaxed). Examples of everyday algorithms include brushing your teeth and calculating your GPA.
notes_text: The distinction between informal and formal definitions is important. The formal definition's four properties (ordered, unambiguous, executable, terminating) serve as criteria for determining whether a set of instructions qualifies as an algorithm. The terminating requirement is sometimes relaxed for processes like operating systems that run indefinitely.

images.description: An inset box listing the four key properties of algorithms: Ordered, Unambiguous, Executable, and Terminating Process, each with a brief explanation.

title: Algorithm Representation
summary: Explains that algorithms are language-independent and can be represented as flow charts, pseudocode, or specific program implementations.
main_text: An algorithm focuses on how to solve a problem regardless of the language or specific implementation. An algorithm is NOT a program NOR tied to one programming language. Just as a story may be represented as a book, movie, or spoken by a story-teller, an algorithm may be represented in many ways. Common representations include: Flow chart - a visual diagram showing the steps and decision points. Pseudocode - English-like syntax using primitives that most programming languages would have. A specific program implementation in a given programming language like C++. The key insight is that the algorithm is the abstract solution method, separate from any particular way of writing it down.
notes_text: Understanding the distinction between an algorithm and a program is crucial. An algorithm is the conceptual solution strategy, while a program is a concrete implementation in a specific language. This distinction allows computer scientists to analyze and compare algorithms independently of hardware or language considerations.

title: Pseudocode Primitives
summary: Introduces the three fundamental pseudocode constructs: assignment, conditionals (selection), and loops (repetition).
main_text: Pseudocode uses three fundamental primitives to express algorithms. Assignment: name <- expression, where name is a descriptive name/variable and expression describes the value to be associated with name. Select one of two possible choices (conditionals): 'if (condition) then (activity) else (activity)' or 'if (condition) then (activity)' for one-way selection. Repeated execution of statements (loops): 'while (condition) do (activity)' executes as long as condition is true. 'repeat (activity) until (condition)' executes at least once then checks condition. 'foreach name in (set / collection) do (activity)' iterates over each element in a set or collection. These three primitives - assignment, selection, and iteration - form the building blocks of all algorithms expressed in pseudocode.
notes_text: These three constructs correspond to the fundamental control structures in virtually all programming languages. The left arrow (<-) notation for assignment distinguishes pseudocode from languages that use the equals sign. Understanding these primitives is essential for reading and writing algorithms throughout the course.

title: Algorithms and Runtime
summary: Introduces runtime analysis and big-O notation for classifying algorithm efficiency from constant O(1) to exponential O(2^n) time.
main_text: There may be many algorithms for solving the same problem. How do we judge which is more efficient? Efficiency may refer to time (speed), amount of memory used, or even how much power is consumed. This unit focuses on time. Typically, we classify algorithms into bins based on how their run-time scales with an input of size n, using something called big-O notation. The common runtime classifications from fastest to slowest are: O(1) - Constant time (independent of n). O(log n) - Logarithmic time. O(n) - Linear time. O(n * log n) - Log-Linear time. O(n^2) - Quadratic time. O(n^3) - Cubic time. O(2^n) - Exponential time. These classifications help us understand how an algorithm's performance will change as the input size grows.
notes_text: The big-O classification spectrum is one of the most important concepts in computer science. As input size n grows, the differences between these classes become dramatic. An O(n) algorithm might handle millions of inputs easily, while an O(2^n) algorithm becomes impractical for even modest input sizes. The diagram shows an algorithm being classified into one of these bins.

images.description: A classification diagram showing an algorithm being sorted into one of seven big-O runtime bins, with arrows from 'an algorithm' pointing down to each category from O(1) through O(2^n).

title: Algorithm Example 1 - Finding Factors
summary: Demonstrates a factor-finding algorithm using pseudocode with a basic O(n) approach and an improved O(sqrt(n)) optimization.
main_text: Problem: List/print all factors of a natural number n. How would you check if a number is a factor of n? Use the remainder (modulo) operation. What is the range of possible factors? From 1 to n. Basic algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This checks every number from 1 to n, making it O(n). An improvement: Since factors come in pairs (if i is a factor, then n/i is also a factor), we only need to check up to the square root of n. Improved algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= ____) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i and ____ as a factor of n, i <- i+1. Examples shown: factors of 8 are 1,2,4,8; factors of 12 are 1,2,3,4,6,12; factors of 24 are 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24; factors of 36 are 1,2,3,4,6,6,9,12,18,36.
notes_text: This example illustrates how understanding mathematical properties (factor pairs) can lead to more efficient algorithms. The blanks are intentionally left for students to fill in: the loop condition should be i <= sqrt(n), and the second factor listed should be n/i. Notice how factors come in pairs that multiply to n.

images.description: A table showing the complete factor lists for numbers 8, 12, 24, and 36, demonstrating how factors come in pairs.

title: Algorithm Time Complexity
summary: Explains how algorithms are judged by runtime for a given input size n, using worst-case analysis independent of hardware.
main_text: We often judge algorithms by how long they take to run for a given input size, n. Algorithms often have different run-times based on the input size. For example, n equals the number of elements in a list to search or sort. Different input patterns can lead to best-case and worst-case times. Average-case times can be helpful. But we usually use worst case times for comparison purposes. We also want to be able to compare the time an algorithm takes in a way that is independent of the computer running it. The same algorithm might run a lot faster on a server than your phone due to the hardware. This motivates the need for an abstract measure of efficiency that focuses on how the number of operations scales with input size, rather than actual wall-clock time.
notes_text: Worst-case analysis provides a guarantee: the algorithm will never perform worse than this bound. This is particularly important in real-time systems or safety-critical applications. Hardware independence is achieved by counting operations rather than measuring time in seconds.

title: Calculating Runtime
summary: Shows how to calculate runtime by counting steps of work in pseudocode, deriving an expression in terms of input size n.
main_text: Given an input to an algorithm of size n, we start by deriving an expression (in terms of n) for the steps of work an algorithm performs, usually for its WORST CASE run time. Just walk the code and count up 'steps' of work. It is fine if what we call a 'step' of work is a bit imprecise because we will usually apply big-O notation (see next slide). Example pseudocode for finding factors: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (n mod i == 0) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. In this algorithm, the initialization takes 1 step, the while loop condition is checked n times, the modulo and comparison inside the loop each execute n times, and the increment executes n times. The total work is proportional to n.
notes_text: The key technique is to identify the loop and determine how many times it executes in the worst case. Each operation inside the loop contributes a constant amount of work per iteration. The total is the number of iterations multiplied by the work per iteration, plus any constant startup/cleanup work.

images.description: A code box showing the factor-finding pseudocode: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do, if (n mod i == 0) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1.
labels: List i as a factor of n

title: Applying Big-O Notation
summary: Explains how to derive big-O by keeping only the dominant term and discarding constants, with a worked example showing O(5n+1) = O(n).
main_text: From the expression, we find the corresponding big-O expression for that runtime by assuming n is LARGE (approaching infinity) and thus we: Only keep the dominant term in the expression. Discard constant coefficients. The result is the big-O (worst-case or upper-bound) run-time. Example: If an algorithm with input size of n runs in 3n^2 + 10n + 1000 steps, we say that it runs in O(n^2) because if n is large, 3n^2 will dominate the other terms. Detailed step count for the factor-finding algorithm: i <- 1 costs 1 step, while(i <= n) do costs 1*n, if (n mod i == 0) then costs 2*n (modulo and compare are 2 ops), List i as a factor of n costs 1*n, i <- i+1 costs 1*n. Total: 5n+1. O(5n+1) = O(n). Big-O notation lets us express the amount of work an algorithm performs in a way that doesn't require exact precision but helps us compare the efficiency of different algorithms.
notes_text: The two rules for simplifying to big-O are essential: drop lower-order terms and drop constant coefficients. This works because for sufficiently large n, the highest-order term dominates. For example, when n = 1000, 3n^2 = 3,000,000 while 10n = 10,000 and 1000 is negligible. The annotation on the code shows how to count 2 ops for the modulo and compare operations.

images.description: An annotated code box showing the factor-finding algorithm with step counts labeled on the right side: 1 for initialization, 1*n for while check, 2*n for modulo and compare, 1*n for listing, 1*n for increment, totaling 5n+1 which simplifies to O(n).

title: Algorithm Example 1 - Runtime Comparison
summary: Compares the basic O(n) factor-finding algorithm with the improved O(sqrt(n)) version that only checks up to the square root.
main_text: List/print all factors of a natural number, n. What is a factor? What is the range of possible factors? Basic algorithm: i <- 1, while(i <= n) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This has runtime O(n) because the loop runs n times. An improvement: i <- 1, while(i <= sqrt(n)) do: if (remainder of n/i is zero) then list i and n/i as a factor of n, i <- i+1. This improved version has runtime O(sqrt(n)) because the loop only runs up to the square root of n. By recognizing that factors come in pairs (i and n/i), we can cut the search space dramatically. For n = 1,000,000, the basic version checks 1,000,000 values while the improved version only checks 1,000.
notes_text: This is an excellent example of algorithmic optimization. The mathematical insight that factors come in pairs allows us to reduce the number of iterations from n to sqrt(n). This demonstrates that understanding the problem domain can lead to significantly better algorithms without changing the fundamental approach.

title: Algorithm Example 2a - Sequential Search
summary: Introduces sequential (linear) search on an ordered list, showing pseudocode and explaining best case (1 step) and worst case (n steps).
main_text: Problem: Searching an ordered list (array) for a specific value, k, and return its index or -1 if it is not in the list. Option 1: Sequential Search. Start at first item, check if it is equal to k, repeat for second, third, fourth item, etc. Best Case: Find it right away (1 step). Worst Case: Not present in the list (n steps). Pseudocode: i <- 0, while (i < length(List)) do: if (List[i] equal to k) then return i, else i <- i+1. return -1. The algorithm starts at index 0 and moves through the list one element at a time. If it finds k, it returns the index. If it reaches the end without finding k, it returns -1 to indicate the value was not found. Example: searching for k=12 in the list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19] at indices 0 through 8.
notes_text: Sequential search is the simplest search algorithm and works on both ordered and unordered lists. Its simplicity is its advantage, but its O(n) worst-case performance makes it inefficient for large datasets. The example shows a sorted list, which sets up the motivation for binary search on the next slide.

images.description: An array diagram showing a list with values [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19] at indices 0 through 8, with k=12 as the search target.

title: Algorithm Example 2b - Binary Search Introduction
summary: Introduces binary search, which exploits sorted order by comparing with the middle element and eliminating half the list each step.
main_text: Sequential search does NOT take advantage of the ordered nature of the list. It would work the same (equally well) on an ordered or unordered list. Binary Search takes advantage of an ordered list by comparing k with the middle element and based on the result, ruling out all numbers greater or smaller, then repeating with the middle element of the remaining list. Example walkthrough searching for k=6 in list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 15, 19]: Step 1 - Start in middle at index 4 (value 9). Compare: 6 < 9, so eliminate the right half. Step 2 - Look at middle of remaining left portion at index 1 (value 3). Compare: 6 > 4 (value at the midpoint of the left subarray). Step 3 - Narrow down further until 6 = 6 is found. Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements.
notes_text: Binary search is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm. The key prerequisite is that the list must be sorted. The visual walkthrough demonstrates how each comparison halves the search space, which is what gives binary search its logarithmic runtime. Students should trace through the example carefully to understand the elimination process.

images.description: A step-by-step visual trace of binary search for k=6 in the array [2,3,4,6,9,10,13,15,19], showing three stages where the search space is halved each time by comparing with the middle element. Highlighted cells show the current middle element being compared.

title: Algorithm Example 2b - Binary Search Implementation
summary: Provides complete binary search pseudocode using start/end pointers and demonstrates a full trace searching for k=11.
main_text: Binary Search implementation: Compare k with middle element of list and if not equal, rule out half of the list and repeat on the other half. Implementation uses a range of searchable elements defined as [start, end) where start is inclusive and end is exclusive. Pseudocode: start <- 0; end <- length(List); while (start != end) do: i <- (start + end) / 2; if (k == List[i]) then return i; else if (k > List[i]) then start <- i+1; else end <- i; return -1. Example trace for k=11 in list [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 19]: Initially start=0, end=9, i=4. Since 11 > 9 (List[4]), set start=5. Now start=5, end=9, i=7. Since 11 < 15 (List[7]), set end=7. Now start=5, end=7, i=6. Since 11 < 13 (List[6]), set end=6. Now start=5, end=6, i=5. 11 == 11 (List[5]), return 5.
notes_text: The half-open interval [start, end) is a common convention in computer science where start is inclusive and end is exclusive. This simplifies boundary conditions. The trace shows four comparisons to find the element in a list of 9 items, compared to potentially 9 comparisons with sequential search. Notice how start and end converge toward the target.

images.description: A detailed step-by-step trace of binary search for k=11, showing four stages of the array [2,3,4,6,9,11,13,15,19] with start, end, and i pointers converging on the target element at index 5.

title: Complexity of Search Algorithms
summary: Analyzes sequential search as O(n) and begins deriving binary search complexity by tracking how the list halves each iteration.
main_text: Sequential Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires searching through the entire list. Time complexity = an + k, where a is some constant for the number of operations performed in the loop as we iterate, and k is some constant representing startup/finish work outside the loop. Sequential Search = O(n) after dropping constants. Binary Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires continually dividing the list in two until we reach a sublist of size 1. After iteration 1, n/2 items remain. After iteration 2, n/4 items remain. After iteration 3, n/8 items remain. After iteration k, n/2^k items remain. We stop when n/2^k = 1. Solving for k gives the number of iterations needed. The blanks are left for students to fill in: Time = a*log_2(n) + k = O(log_2(n)).
notes_text: This slide sets up the derivation of binary search's O(log n) runtime. The table showing remaining items after each iteration is key to understanding why the runtime is logarithmic. Each iteration halves the remaining search space, so after k iterations, n/2^k items remain. Setting n/2^k = 1 and solving for k gives k = log_2(n). Students should work through this derivation.

images.description: A table showing remaining items after each binary search iteration: iteration 1 leaves n/2, iteration 2 leaves n/4, iteration 3 leaves n/8, iteration k leaves n/2^k, and the final iteration leaves 1 item. Below: Solve n/2^k = 1, k = ___ iterations.

title: Complexity of Search Algorithms - Solution
summary: Completes the derivation showing sequential search is O(n) and binary search is O(log_2 n), with a graph comparing their growth rates.
main_text: Sequential Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires searching through entire list. Time complexity = an + k. Sequential Search = O(n). Binary Search on a list of length n: Worst case requires continually dividing the list in two until we reach a sublist of size 1. Time = a*log_2(n) + k = O(log_2 n). The derivation: After iteration 1, n/2 items remain. After iteration 2, n/4 items remain. After iteration 3, n/8 items remain. After iteration k, n/2^k items remain. Solving n/2^k = 1 gives k = log_2(n) iterations. As n gets large, binary search is far more efficient than sequential search. For a list of 1 billion items, sequential search may need 1 billion comparisons while binary search needs only about 30.
notes_text: The graph on this slide dramatically illustrates the difference between O(n) and O(log n). The linear function grows steadily while the logarithmic function flattens out. This visual reinforcement helps students appreciate why algorithm choice matters so much for large inputs. Binary search requires the list to be sorted, which is a tradeoff worth considering.

images.description: A graph comparing the runtime growth of sequential search (linear, steep line) versus binary search (logarithmic, nearly flat curve) as N increases from 0 to 50, with runtime on the y-axis from 0 to 50.
A table showing remaining items after each binary search iteration, with the solution: k = log_2(n) iterations.

title: Sorting Algorithms
summary: Motivates sorting as a prerequisite for binary search and introduces bubble sort as a simple but inefficient sorting algorithm.
main_text: If we have an unordered list, sequential search becomes our only choice since binary search requires a sorted list. If we will perform a lot of searches, it may be beneficial to sort the list (to make it ordered), then use binary search. The one-time cost of sorting can be amortized over many fast binary searches, making the overall process more efficient. Many sorting algorithms exist with varying run-time efficiencies. Bubble sort is a simple, though not terribly efficient algorithm. More advanced sorting algorithms like Quicksort and Mergesort offer better performance. The choice of whether to sort first depends on how many searches will be performed on the data.
notes_text: This slide bridges the searching and sorting topics. The key insight is the tradeoff between sorting cost and search efficiency. If you only search once, sequential search on an unsorted list is fine. But if you search many times, paying the upfront cost to sort enables much faster binary searches. This cost-benefit analysis is a common pattern in algorithm design.

title: Bubble Sort Algorithm
summary: Explains bubble sort mechanics with C++ code and a visual trace showing how adjacent elements are compared and swapped across multiple passes.
main_text: Bubble sort performs several passes over the data. Variable i tracks the stopping point for each pass. Variable j starts at the beginning of the array, moves sequentially and compares its element with its immediate neighbor. C++ implementation: void bsort(int mylist[], int size) { int i, j; for(i=...) { for(j=...) { if(mylist[j] > mylist[j+1]) { // swap mylist[j] & mylist[j+1] } } } }. Visual trace of Pass 1 with n-1 comparisons on array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Compare 7 and 3, swap to get [3, 7, 8, 6, 5, 1]. Compare 7 and 8, no swap. Compare 8 and 6, swap to get [3, 7, 6, 8, 5, 1]. Compare 8 and 5, swap. Compare 8 and 1, swap to get [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. After Pass 1, the largest element (8) has 'bubbled up' to the end. Pass 2 performs n-2 comparisons on the remaining unsorted portion.
notes_text: The name 'bubble sort' comes from the way larger elements 'bubble up' to the end of the array with each pass. Each pass guarantees that the next largest unsorted element reaches its correct position. The visual trace is essential for understanding the algorithm's mechanics. Notice the for loop bounds are left as exercises for students to fill in.

images.description: A step-by-step visual trace of bubble sort Pass 1 and the beginning of Pass 2 on the array [7,3,8,6,5,1], showing j and i pointer positions, swap/no-swap decisions at each step, with the largest element (8) bubbling to the end after Pass 1.

title: Bubble Sort - Work Analysis (Blank)
summary: Presents bubble sort with blank step counts for each pass, asking students to determine the total work and big-O complexity.
main_text: Bubble Sort is simple though not terribly efficient. On each pass through the list, pick up the maximum element and place it at the end of the list. Then repeat using a list of size n-1 (without the newly placed maximum value). How much total work is required? Starting with the array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Pass 1 produces [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 2 produces [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 3 produces [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 4 produces [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 5 produces [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] with ____ steps. Pass 6 with ____ steps. The total complexity is O(____). Students are expected to fill in the step counts and derive the overall big-O.
notes_text: This is the exercise version of the slide where students work through the analysis themselves. Each pass performs a decreasing number of comparisons: Pass 1 does n-1 comparisons, Pass 2 does n-2, and so on down to 1. The total is the sum (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2, which simplifies to O(n^2).

images.description: A visual trace showing the original array [7,3,8,6,5,1] and the state after each of 6 passes, with blank step counts for students to fill in and a blank O(___) for the final complexity.

title: Bubble Sort - Work Analysis (Solution)
summary: Reveals that bubble sort requires n, n-1, n-2, ... steps per pass, totaling n(n+1)/2 operations, giving O(n^2) complexity.
main_text: Bubble Sort is simple though not terribly efficient. On each pass through the list, pick up the maximum element and place it at the end of the list. Then repeat using a list of size n-1. Solution for the work at each pass starting with array [7, 3, 8, 6, 5, 1]: Pass 1 takes n steps (5 comparisons for 6 elements), producing [3, 7, 6, 5, 1, 8]. Pass 2 takes n-1 steps, producing [3, 5, 1, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 3 takes n-2 steps, producing [3, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 4 takes ... steps, producing [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Pass 5 takes 2 steps. Pass 6 takes 1 step. The total work is the sum: (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 2 + 1. The overall runtime complexity is O(n^2).
notes_text: The sum (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 equals n(n-1)/2 using the arithmetic series formula. Applying big-O simplification: n(n-1)/2 = (n^2 - n)/2. Dropping the lower order term and constant gives O(n^2). This quadratic growth makes bubble sort impractical for large datasets.

images.description: A visual trace showing the array state after each pass with filled-in step counts: Pass 1 (n steps), Pass 2 (n-1 steps), Pass 3 (n-2 steps), Pass 4 (... steps), Pass 5 (2 steps), Pass 6 (1 step), with O(n^2) shown as the final answer.

title: Complexity of Sort Algorithms
summary: Compares bubble sort O(n^2) with advanced sorts like Quicksort and Mergesort at O(n*log n), with a graph showing the dramatic difference.
main_text: Bubble Sort uses 2 nested loops. Execute outer loop n-1 times. For each outer loop iteration, inner loop runs i times. Time complexity is proportional to: n-1 + n-2 + n-3 + ... + 3 + 2 + 1 = (n^2 + n)/2 = O(n^2). Other sort algorithms (Quicksort, Mergesort, etc.) can run in O(n*log_2 n). The difference between O(n^2) and O(n*log n) is dramatic for large inputs. For example, with n = 1,000,000: bubble sort requires roughly 10^12 operations while quicksort requires roughly 2 * 10^7 operations, a factor of 50,000 times faster. The graph comparing N, N^2, and N*log_2(N) shows that while N^2 grows rapidly (reaching 400 at N=20), N*log_2(N) grows much more moderately.
notes_text: This slide provides the capstone comparison for the sorting section. The graph visually demonstrates why O(n^2) algorithms are impractical for large datasets. Quicksort and Mergesort achieve O(n log n) through divide-and-conquer strategies that will be studied in more advanced courses. The key takeaway is that algorithm choice has enormous practical impact on performance.

images.description: A graph comparing three growth functions: N (linear, bottom), N*log_2(N) (moderate growth, middle), and N^2 (steep parabolic growth, top) for N from 0 to 20, with runtime values on the y-axis up to 400.

title: Common Algorithm Runtimes
summary: Summarizes all seven big-O runtime classes with example algorithms and code snippets for constant, cubic, and exponential cases.
main_text: Common algorithm runtimes from fastest to slowest: O(1) Constant - Example: Simple conversions. Code example using quadratic formula: cin >> a >> b >> c; double det = b*b - 4*a*c; compute x1 and x2. Uses formula x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a. O(log n) Logarithmic - Example: Binary Search. O(n) Linear - Example: Sequential Search, Neural Network Back-propagation. O(n * log n) Log-Linear - Example: Quicksort, Mergesort, Heapsort. O(n^2) Quadratic - Example: Bubble sort, Image convolution. O(n^3) Cubic - Example: Matrix Multiply. Code: for(int i=0; i<N; i++) for(int j=0; j<N; j++) { C[i][j]=0; for(int k=0; k<N; k++) C[i][j] += A[i][k]*B[k][j]; }. O(2^n) Exponential - Example: Many Combinatoric or Optimization algorithms, Subset Sums. Problem: Does any subset of inputs add or subtract equal to N given 37 192 42 7 3 86 102 91. In general, focus on nested loops to help determine runtime.
notes_text: This is a comprehensive reference slide. The constant time example shows the quadratic formula which requires a fixed number of operations regardless of input. The cubic example demonstrates three nested loops for matrix multiplication. The exponential example (subset sums) shows a problem where every possible combination must potentially be checked. The key heuristic: count the depth of nested loops to estimate runtime.

images.description: A comprehensive table showing seven runtime classes (O(1) through O(2^n)) with their names (Constant through Exponential) and example algorithms, plus three code snippets illustrating constant (quadratic formula), cubic (matrix multiply), and exponential (subset sums) complexity.

title: Importance of Time Complexity
summary: Explains why time complexity matters: it determines whether problems are efficient, possible, or impossible to solve in practice.
main_text: Time complexity makes the difference between efficient, possible, and impossible. Many important problems currently can only be solved with exponential run-time algorithms (e.g. O(2^n) time). No known polynomial-time algorithm exists for these problems. Usually, algorithms are only practical if they run in polynomial time (O(n^k) for some constant k). A comparison table shows how different complexities scale with input size N: For N=2: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=1, O(n)=2, O(n*log_2 n)=2, O(n^2)=4, O(2^n)=4. For N=20: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=4.3, O(n)=20, O(n*log_2 n)=86.4, O(n^2)=400, O(2^n)=1,048,576. For N=200: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=7.6, O(n)=200, O(n*log_2 n)=1528.8, O(n^2)=40,000, O(2^n)=1.60694E+60. For N=2000: O(1)=1, O(log_2 n)=11.0, O(n)=2000, O(n*log_2 n)=21,931.6, O(n^2)=4,000,000, O(2^n)=#NUM! (overflow, too large to compute).
notes_text: The table powerfully illustrates why exponential algorithms are impractical. At N=200, O(2^n) produces a number with 60 digits, and at N=2000 it overflows entirely. Meanwhile O(log n) barely grows at all. This connects to the famous P vs NP problem in computer science: whether problems solvable in exponential time can be solved in polynomial time. This remains one of the greatest open questions in mathematics and computer science.

images.description: A comparison table showing the computed values for six complexity classes (O(1), O(log_2 n), O(n), O(n*log_2 n), O(n^2), O(2^n)) at four input sizes (N=2, 20, 200, 2000), dramatically showing how exponential growth becomes impossibly large while logarithmic growth stays manageable.

title: Unit 1e - Compilation Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing the Compilation unit for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp. Covers the compilation process for C++ programs.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 1e of CS 103, titled Compilation. The unit is presented by Mark Redekopp and covers the process of compiling C++ programs, using the command line, dealing with compiler errors, multifile compilation, header files, and basic debugging techniques.
notes_text: This unit transitions students from using GUI-based compile-and-run buttons to understanding the underlying compilation process using command line tools like g++.

title: Compilation Section Header
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Compilation topic. Introduces the core concept of the unit.
main_text: This is a section header slide with the heading COMPILATION. It marks the beginning of the main content covering how C++ source code is compiled into executable programs using command line tools.
notes_text: This section covers the fundamental compilation workflow: writing source code, invoking the compiler, and running the resulting executable.

title: Compiling and Running
summary: Introduces the need to understand compilation beyond GUI buttons. Students will learn what happens behind the scenes when compiling and running programs.
main_text: Until now, most assignments have allowed you to just click a button to compile AND run your program. But what is happening behind the scenes? What if you did not have these conveniences? This slide motivates learning the manual compilation process by showing that the convenient 'Compile & Run' button and automated check systems (like those showing 'Check 1 passed', 'Check 2 passed', etc.) will no longer always be available. Students need to understand how to compile and run programs from the command line.
notes_text: The slide uses red prohibition symbols over the 'Compile & Run' button and the automated checking interface to emphasize that students must move beyond these conveniences and learn the underlying process.

images.description: A 'Compile & Run' button from an IDE with a red prohibition symbol overlaid, indicating students should not rely on this convenience. Below it, an automated test results panel showing 'Check 1 passed' through 'Check 6 passed' also with a prohibition symbol.

title: Using the Command Line
summary: Introduces the command line interface (terminal) on Linux, explaining its advantages over GUIs and basic capabilities for navigating files and running programs.
main_text: While GUIs are nice, we often have more control when using the command line interface (i.e. the terminal). Linux (the OS used by Codio and in CS 103, 104, etc.) has a rich set of command line utilities. Mac and Windows do too, though Windows uses different names for the utilities. By typing commands, we can: navigate the file system (like you would with Explorer or Finder), start programs (vs. double-clicking an icon), and copy, move, delete, rename files and folders. Documentation often uses the symbols $ or > as a placeholder for the command prompt. Don't type it. If you see: $ ./test, you should just type ./test.
notes_text: The command line provides more precise control over compilation and program execution than GUI tools. Learning to use the terminal is essential for professional software development and is the standard interface used in CS 103 and CS 104 courses via the Codio platform running Linux.

images.description: Three images showing terminal interfaces: a terminal icon with a command prompt symbol, a Linux terminal view showing the prompt 'student@studentVM:~$', and a Codio terminal view showing a welcome message with system information and the prompt.

title: Compilers
summary: Lists available C++ compilers including g++, clang++, XCode, and MS Visual Studio, and introduces the concept of Integrated Development Environments (IDEs).
main_text: Several free and commercial compilers are available for C++ development: g++, clang++, XCode, and MS Visual Studio. Several of these have 'integrated' editors, debuggers and other tools and thus are called IDEs (Integrated Development Environments). An IDE combines a text editor, compiler, debugger, and other tools into a single application, making development more convenient.
notes_text: In CS 103, g++ is the primary compiler used. It is a free, open-source compiler available on Linux systems including the Codio platform. Understanding different compiler options helps students recognize that the compilation concept is universal even if the specific tool varies.

title: Compilation and Execution Process
summary: Illustrates the full compilation and execution pipeline from C++ source code through the g++ compiler to an executable binary that runs on the CPU.
main_text: The compilation and execution process involves three main steps. Step 1: Edit and write code in a C++ source file (e.g., test.cpp) containing code like #include <iostream>, using namespace std, int main() with variable declarations and cout statements. Step 2: Compile and fix compiler errors by running the g++ compiler, which takes the source file along with C++ Standard and other libraries and produces an executable binary image (a file of binary machine code like 1110 0010 0101 1001). The compiler command has three parts: options/flags, input file(s) (source), and output executable name. Common compiler options include: -g to enable debugging, -Wall to show all warnings, and -o <name> to specify the output executable program name. The full command is: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. Step 3: Load and run the executable program by typing ./test. The executable is loaded into memory (RAM) and executed by the CPU.
notes_text: This is a critical slide showing the end-to-end workflow. The dollar sign ($) represents the command prompt and should not be typed. The ./ prefix before the executable name tells the shell to look in the current directory for the program. The compiler translates human-readable C++ into machine-readable binary instructions.

images.description: A flowchart showing the compilation pipeline: C++ source file (test.cpp) flows into the g++ compiler along with C++ Standard Libraries, producing an executable binary image of machine code, which then flows to a CPU/RAM diagram for loading and execution. Below, a detailed breakdown of the g++ command showing options, input files, and output executable name components.

title: Just Know This! - The g++ Command
summary: Emphasizes the essential g++ command students must memorize, breaking down each component: options/flags, input source files, and output executable name.
main_text: This slide highlights the critical g++ command that students must memorize: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. The command is broken into labeled components: the $ is a placeholder from the command prompt (don't actually type this), g++ is the compiler invocation, -g -Wall are options (aka flags) that enable debugging and warnings, test.cpp is the input file(s) (source), -o is the flag to specify output name, and test is the output executable name (can be anything but usually the base name of the .cpp file). Pro tip: Never type this command more than once per session. The terminal saves your commands. Type the Up-Arrow to cycle through previous commands!
notes_text: This is marked with star icons to indicate it is must-know material. Students frequently lose points or waste time by not knowing this command. The up-arrow shortcut for command history is a valuable time-saver during development.

images.description: An annotated diagram of the g++ command with arrows pointing from labels to each part of the command: Options/Flags pointing to '-g -Wall', Input file(s) pointing to 'test.cpp', Output executable name pointing to 'test', and Command prompt pointing to '$'. Star icons frame the title to emphasize importance.

title: Compiling with g++
summary: Details g++ usage including basic invocation, common options (-o, -g, -Wall), default executable naming (a.out), and how to run the compiled program.
main_text: Most basic usage of g++ is simply: g++ cpp_filenames. This creates an executable using the default name a.out. Common options include: -o to specify the output executable name (other than default a.out), -g to include info needed by debuggers like gdb and kdbg, and -Wall to show all warnings. The most common usage form is: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test. Without the -o option, you can run the default executable with: $ ./a.out. To run the program, precede the executable name with ./ which specifies the local directory. Use whatever executable name you gave to g++ via the -o option. Example terminal session: $ g++ test.cpp creates an implicit output with program name a.out, run with $ ./a.out. With options: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test, then run with $ ./test.
notes_text: The ./ prefix is necessary because the current directory is typically not in the system PATH for security reasons. Without -o, the default output name is always a.out regardless of the source file name. The -g flag should always be used during development as it enables debugger support with no runtime cost.

images.description: Two terminal windows showing compilation examples: one showing basic g++ usage producing a.out, and another showing the full command with -g -Wall flags and -o option followed by running the executable with ./test.

title: Dealing with Compile Errors
summary: Explains the difference between compiler errors and runtime errors, and provides practical tips for solving compiler errors using line numbers and error messages.
main_text: Compiler errors are a good kind of error (or at least better than runtime errors). The compiler GIVES you a line number and error message to help you. Runtime errors usually just produce the wrong outputs or crash, leaving no clues as to why (harder to debug). Tips for solving compiler errors: Find the line number, look at your code on that line, and read the error message carefully. Do an Internet search of key words from the error message (leave out any specific names in the error message) to see if there is an explanation online. Deal with the FIRST error by scrolling to the top of the error messages. If there is too much output, use I/O redirection (more to come), for example: $ g++ -g prog.cpp -o ./prog >& errors.txt and then view errors.txt.
notes_text: A common beginner mistake is trying to fix errors from the bottom of the output. Always start with the first error because later errors are often cascading consequences of the first one. Fixing the first error and recompiling often eliminates many subsequent errors.

title: An Example of Compiler Errors
summary: Shows a concrete example of C++ code with multiple errors and the corresponding compiler error output, demonstrating how to read and interpret error messages.
main_text: This slide presents a side-by-side example of buggy C++ code and the resulting compiler error messages. The source code (errors.cpp) contains: #include <iostream>, int main() with declarations int a, b, c and void* ptr, then attempts cout << bc (undeclared), *ptr = a (void pointer dereference), and return "0" (string instead of int). Compiling with g++ -Wall errors.cpp produces several errors: 'cout' was not declared in this scope (missing 'using namespace std'), did you mean 'std::cout'; 'bc' was not declared in this scope, did you mean 'c'; 'void*' is not a pointer-to-object type; invalid conversion from 'const char*' to 'int' for return "0". It also shows warnings: unused variable 'b' and unused variable 'c' from the -Wall flag.
notes_text: This example demonstrates multiple common beginner mistakes: forgetting 'using namespace std', typos in variable names, misusing void pointers, and returning the wrong type. The compiler output shows file name, line number, and column number for each error, making it possible to locate the exact position of each problem.

images.description: Left side shows C++ source code with line numbers 1-9 containing multiple intentional errors. Right side shows the terminal output from compiling with g++ -Wall, displaying multiple error messages with file names, line numbers, and descriptions highlighted in different colors.
labels: error: 'void*' is not a pointer-to-object type
