Example: char s1[20]; cin >> s1; int len = strlen(s1); With input 'TommyTrojan', len = 11. C++ Strings: Remembers its size! Just call the .size() or .length() method. Runs in O(1) because the size is stored as a data member. Example: string s2; cin >> s2; int len = s2.size(); With the same input, len = 11. The string object shows size=11 and data pointing to 'TommyTrojan\0'.
notes_text: The O(n) vs O(1) performance difference is significant in loops that repeatedly check string length. With C strings, calling strlen() in a loop condition like for(int i=0; i < strlen(s1); i++) recalculates the length every iteration, making the loop O(n^2). With C++ strings, s2.size() is constant time, keeping the loop O(n).

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string requiring strlen() (O(n) scan) versus C++ string using .size() (O(1) member lookup), both returning 11 for 'TommyTrojan'.

title: String Assignment: strcpy vs = Operator
summary: C strings cannot use = after declaration; must use strcpy. C++ strings support = which automatically performs deep copy with dynamic resizing.
main_text: C Strings: Assign one string to another. Cannot assign a new string after declaration. Would have to use strcpy(). MUST ensure you don't copy more than the array size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; char s3[6] = "Maria"; s1 = s3; does NOT work. Must use strcpy(s1, s3); and strcpy(s1, "abcde...wxyz"); but if the source exceeds 20 characters, overflow occurs. C++ Strings: Assign one string to another. CAN GROW automatically as you enter text via a DEEP COPY! Example: string s2 = "Jane"; string s4 = "Maria"; s2 = s4; works perfectly. s2 = "abcde...wxyz"; also works. The string internally deallocates old memory, allocates new memory of the right size, and copies the data. The diagram shows size changing from 4 to 5 to 26 and data pointer updating accordingly, with old arrays being freed.
notes_text: This is a critical difference. C strings cannot use the = operator for assignment after declaration because arrays are not assignable in C/C++. The C++ string class overloads the = operator to perform a proper deep copy: it frees the old internal array, calculates the new size, allocates a new array, and copies the data. This eliminates an entire class of bugs.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string assignment requiring strcpy (with overflow risk marked in red) versus C++ string assignment using = operator with automatic deep copy. The C++ side shows the string object updating its size and data pointer, with old allocations being freed.

title: String Concatenation: strcat vs + Operator
summary: C strings require strcat() for concatenation with overflow risk. C++ strings use the + or += operator with automatic memory growth.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT concatenate/append another string. Cannot use '+' to append a new string except through strcat(). MUST ensure you don't copy more than the array size! Example: char s1[20] = "Jane"; char s3[5] = " Doe"; s1 += s3; does NOT work. Must use strcat(s1, s3); resulting in s1 containing 'J','a','n','e',' ','D','o','e','\0'. C++ Strings: Can concatenate/append easily (with + op). Can use '+' to append. CAN GROW automatically via a DEEP COPY! Example: string s2 = "Jane"; string s4 = " Doe"; s2 += s4; The string object updates: size changes from 4 to 8, data is reallocated to point to a new array containing 'Jane Doe\0', and the old 'Jane\0' array is freed.
notes_text: Concatenation highlights another major advantage of C++ strings. With C strings, strcat has no bounds checking and can easily overflow. With C++ strings, += performs the necessary steps automatically: allocate new memory large enough for both strings, copy the combined content, free the old memory. The + operator can also be used to create a new string: string s5 = s2 + s4;

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string concatenation with strcat (fixed array, overflow risk) versus C++ string concatenation with += (automatic reallocation from size 4 to 8, old memory freed).

title: String Comparison: strcmp vs ==, <, > Operators
summary: C strings cannot use ==, <, > directly; must use strcmp(). C++ strings support all comparison operators directly with lexicographic ordering.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT compare C-strings directly. Would have to use strcmp(). Example: char s1[20] = "abc"; char s3[5] = "aba"; if(s1 == s3){} and if(s1 > s3){} do NOT work (they compare pointer addresses, not string content). Must use: if(strcmp(s1,s3) == 0) {} which is false, and if(strcmp(s1,s3) == 1) {} which is true (since 'c' > 'a'). C++ Strings: Can use basic ==, <, > operators to compare! Example: string s2 = "abc"; string s4 = "aba"; if(s2 == s4) {} is false. if(s2 > s4) {} is true. Comparison is lexicographic (dictionary order).
notes_text: When comparing C strings with == or <, you are comparing the pointer addresses, not the string contents, which almost never gives the result you want. C++ string comparison operators perform character-by-character lexicographic comparison automatically. Lexicographic comparison compares characters left to right; the first difference determines the result. If all compared characters match, the shorter string is considered less than the longer one.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing C string comparison attempts that fail (comparing addresses) versus C++ string comparisons that work correctly with ==, <, > operators.

title: Conversion to Numerics: atoi/atof vs stoi/stod
summary: Neither C nor C++ strings can be cast to numeric types. C uses atoi()/atof(), while C++ uses stoi()/stod(). C++ also provides to_string() for reverse conversion.
main_text: C Strings: CANNOT cast to numeric types. Use atoi() and atof(). Example: char s1[20] = "123.67"; char s3[5] = "42"; double x = (double) s1; does NOT work. int y = (int) s3; does NOT work. Must use: double x = atof(s1); and int y = atoi(s3); C++ Strings: Also, CANNOT cast to numeric types! Use stoi() and stod(). Example: string s2 = "abc"; string s4 = "aba"; double x = (double) s2; does NOT work. int y = (int) s4; does NOT work. Must use: double x = stod(s2); int y = stoi(s4); Additionally, string s6 = to_string(y); converts a number back to a string.
notes_text: The conversion functions are important for parsing user input and file data. atoi/atof (ASCII to integer/float) are C functions. stoi/stod (string to integer/double) are C++11 functions that work with std::string objects. to_string() is the reverse operation, available since C++11. Note that stoi/stod will throw exceptions on invalid input, which is safer than atoi/atof which return 0 on failure.

title: String Documentation and Other Functions: size(), substr()
summary: Use the dot operator to call string member functions. Key functions include .size() for length and .substr() for extracting substrings.
main_text: Use the dot operator to call an operation (function) on an object or access a data value. Asking for the string size: call the .size() function on a string to get the number of characters stored in the string. Can generate substrings by calling either of the 2 versions: .substr(start_index) or .substr(start_index, length) function on the string. Many more member functions are available at http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/string/string/. Example: string mystr = "CS 103"; cout << mystr.size() << endl; outputs 6. string s = mystr.substr(2); gives s = "103". mystr = "Computer Science"; cout << mystr.size() << endl; outputs 16. s = mystr.substr(9,2); gives s = "Sc".
notes_text: The .substr() function is very useful for string parsing. With one argument, it returns everything from the start index to the end. With two arguments, it returns 'length' characters starting from start_index. These are member functions called with the dot operator on a string instance, demonstrating the object-oriented pattern of invoking operations on objects.

images.description: Code example showing string member function usage: .size() returning 6 for 'CS 103' and 16 for 'Computer Science', and .substr() extracting '103' and 'Sc' from different strings.

title: Other Member Functions: c_str(), find(), replace, rfind
summary: c_str() converts to C string. find() searches for substrings returning the index or string::npos. Other functions include replace and rfind.
main_text: Get C String (char *) equivalent using .c_str(). Find a substring: Searches for occurrence of a substring. Returns either the index where the substring starts or string::npos. std::npos is a constant meaning 'just beyond the end of the string', a way of saying 'Not found'. Others: replace, rfind, etc. Example: string s1("abcdef"); char my_c_str[80]; strcpy(my_c_str, s1.c_str()); cout << my_c_str << endl; outputs 'abcdef'. size_t idx = s1.find("bcd"); if(idx != string::npos){ cout << "Found bcd starting at pos="; cout << idx << endl; } else { cout << "Not found" << endl; } Output: abcdef, Found bcd starting at pos=1.
notes_text: The .c_str() function is essential for interoperability between C++ strings and C functions that expect char*. The .find() function performs substring search and returns the starting index, or string::npos if not found. Always check against string::npos before using the returned index. rfind() searches from the end of the string backward.

images.description: Code example demonstrating c_str() for C string conversion and find() for substring search, with output showing 'abcdef' and 'Found bcd starting at pos=1'.
labels: Output: Found bcd starting at pos=1

title: String to Number Conversion: to_string, stoi, stod
summary: Casting does NOT work for string-numeric conversion. Use to_string() for number-to-string and stoi()/stod() for string-to-number, available since C++11.
main_text: Recall: Casting does NOT work for string to numeric conversions. Instead, use functions defined in <string>. Conversion from number to string: string to_string(int); and string to_string(double); Conversion from string to number: int stoi(string); unsigned int stoul(string); double stod(string); Example code: double a = 3.6; int b = static_cast<int>(a) / 2; works (b = 1, casts 3.6 to 3). int c = 123; string d = static_cast<string>(c); does NOT compile. string d = to_string(c); works (since C++11). string e = "42"; int f = static_cast<int>(e); does NOT compile. int f = stoi(e); works (string-to-int, since C++11). Use stod() for string-to-double.
notes_text: static_cast works between compatible numeric types (int to double, double to int) but does NOT work between strings and numbers because they are fundamentally different types. The to_string/stoi/stod functions perform the actual parsing and formatting needed for conversion. These functions were added in C++11 and are now standard. stoi throws std::invalid_argument if the string does not contain a valid number.

images.description: Code example demonstrating valid and invalid conversions: static_cast works for numeric types, fails for string-numeric. to_string() and stoi()/stod() are the correct approaches for string-numeric conversion.

title: Exercises (If Time Allows)
summary: Practice exercises on palindrome checking and circular shift string operations for reinforcing string manipulation concepts.
main_text: Two exercises are suggested if time allows: Palindrome (checking if a string reads the same forwards and backwards) and Circular Shift (rotating characters in a string). These exercises provide hands-on practice with the string operations covered in this unit.
notes_text: Palindrome checking exercises .size(), [] indexing, and loop construction. A circular shift involves moving characters: for example, 'abcd' shifted left by 1 becomes 'bcda'. Both exercises reinforce understanding of string indexing, .size(), .substr(), and concatenation.

title: Backup Section Header
summary: Section divider for backup/supplementary slides that provide additional examples and details.
main_text: This is a section header slide for the Backup section containing supplementary slides with additional examples and details on topics covered in the main lecture.
notes_text: Backup slides are provided as additional reference material. They may cover the same concepts with different examples or provide more detailed explanations for students who need extra support.

title: Memory View of Objects: Pixel Array in Memory (Backup)
summary: Each struct instantiation allocates contiguous memory for all members. A pixel array stores red, green, blue bytes sequentially per element.
main_text: Each instantiation allocates memory for all the members/components of the object (struct or class). The code defines: struct pixel { unsigned char red; unsigned char green; unsigned char blue; }; Then instantiates: pixel p1; pixel image[256][256]; The memory layout at address 0x7400 shows: p1 occupies 3 bytes (red=0x00 at 0x7400, green=0xFF at 0x7401, blue=0x00 at 0x7402). Then image[0][0] starts at 0x7403 (red=0xFF, green=0x00, blue=0x00). image[0][1] starts at 0x7406 (red=0x48, green=0xC9, blue=0x17). Each pixel is exactly 3 bytes, and they are stored contiguously in memory.
notes_text: This backup slide provides a more detailed memory view than the earlier pixel example. The hex values help students connect the abstract concept of struct layout to actual byte-level memory representation. Note that p1 is green (R=0, G=255, B=0), image[0][0] is red (R=255, G=0, B=0), and image[0][1] has specific color values (R=72, G=201, B=23).

images.description: Detailed memory map showing pixel p1 at addresses 0x7400-0x7402 and image array elements at subsequent addresses, with hex values for each byte and labels indicating which pixel and color channel each byte represents.

title: C++ Strings: Do's and Don'ts (Backup)
summary: Key rules for C++ strings: include <string>, initialize with = or constructor, use [] for indexing, use cin/cout, and do not worry about input size.
main_text: In C++, the string class provides an easier alternative to working with plain-old character arrays. Do's and Don'ts: Do #include <string> and put using namespace std; Do initialize using = or by giving an initial value in parentheses (aka use the constructor syntax). Don't need to declare the size (i.e. [7]), just assign. Do still use it like an array by using [index] to get individual characters. Do still use cin/cout with strings. Don't worry about how many characters the user types when inputting to a C++ string. Example: char str1[7] = "CS 103"; (initializes C-style). string str2 = "CS 103"; (initializes C++ string). string str3("Hello"); (constructor syntax). str2[5] = '4'; makes str2 = "CS 104". cout << str2 << endl; prints "CS 104". cin >> str1; (if user types more than 6 chars, uh oh!). cin >> str2; (str2 will adjust to hold whatever the user types).
notes_text: This backup slide serves as a quick reference card for C++ string usage. The most important points are: always include <string>, remember that strings auto-resize so you never specify a size, and you can use the same [] indexing and cin/cout operations you are already familiar with from char arrays.

images.description: Code example showing C++ string declaration, initialization with = and constructor syntax, character modification with [], output with cout, and safe input with cin.

title: What Happens Behind the Scenes: String Internal Operations
summary: Strings internally abstract character arrays. Assignment and concatenation trigger deallocation, reallocation, and copy of the underlying char array.
main_text: Strings simply abstract character arrays. Behind the scenes strings are just creating and manipulating character arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Can concatenate (append) to a string with the + operator. Example: string str2 = "CS 102"; (str2 stores 6 chars = "CS 102"). str2 = "Computer Science"; (now str2 stores 16 characters: the old 'CS 102' array is freed, a new 16-character array is allocated, and 'Computer Science' is copied in). str2 = str2 + " is cool"; (now str2 stores 24 characters: the old 16-char array is freed, a new 24-char array is allocated, and 'Computer Science is cool' is copied in). The string object internally contains a data pointer and a size member. Each reassignment or concatenation may trigger deallocation of old storage and allocation of new storage.
notes_text: Understanding the behind-the-scenes behavior is important for performance awareness. Every time a string grows beyond its current capacity, memory reallocation occurs (which involves allocating new memory, copying all characters, and freeing old memory). This is why repeatedly concatenating in a loop can be slow. In practice, string implementations often allocate extra capacity to reduce the frequency of reallocations.

images.description: Diagram showing a string object str2 with data and size members. Three states are shown: initial 'CS 102' (6 chars), reassigned to 'Computer Science' (16 chars), and concatenated to 'Computer Science is cool' (24 chars). Old arrays are crossed out with prohibition symbols to show deallocation.

title: String Comparison: C-Strings vs C++ Strings with Operators
summary: Comparison operators do not work with C-string char arrays (compare addresses). C++ strings perform correct lexicographic comparison with ==, <, > operators.
main_text: Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Quiz examples: "a" < "z" ? True. "a" > "aa" ? False (shorter string that matches prefix is less). "ab" < "ba" ? True (first char difference: 'a' < 'b'). "aab" < "aac" ? True (third char difference: 'b' < 'c'). Code example: char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if(str1 == "abc") does not work (compares pointer addresses). if(str2 == "abc") works, returns true. if(str1 < "aac") does not work. if(str2 < "aac") works, returns false (since "abc" > "aac"). string str3 = "acb"; if(str3 > str2) works, returns true.
notes_text: Lexicographic comparison works character by character from left to right. The first position where characters differ determines the result. If all characters match up to the length of the shorter string, the shorter string is considered less than the longer one. This is the same ordering as a dictionary. Understanding this is essential for sorting strings and for search algorithms.

images.description: Code example showing comparison operators failing with char arrays (comparing addresses) but working correctly with C++ strings, demonstrating lexicographic ordering results.

title: Summary: Objects, Dot Operator, Constructors, and Operators
summary: Key takeaways: iostream, fstream, and string are objects you already use. Initialize with = or constructors. Use dot operator for methods. Some operators are overloaded.
main_text: You have already used objects: iostream (cin and cout), now file streams and strings. There will be many more objects we can use from the C++ library. Can initialize at declaration by passing initial value in parentheses (known as a constructor). Use the dot operator to call an operation (function) on an object or access a data value. Some special operators can be used on certain object types (+, -, [], etc.) but you have to look them up. Example: #include <iostream>, #include <fstream>, Using namespace std; int x; char line[80]; ifstream myfile(argv[1]); if(!myfile.fail()){ myfile >> x; } cin.getline(line, 80); cout << line << endl; cin, cout, ifstreams, and ofstreams are examples of objects.
notes_text: This summary ties everything together by pointing out that students have been using objects all along: cin and cout are objects of the iostream class, ifstream/ofstream are file stream objects. The dot operator is used to call member functions like myfile.fail() and cin.getline(). Understanding that these familiar tools are objects helps solidify the object-oriented concepts introduced in this unit.

images.description: Code example showing familiar objects in use: ifstream with constructor, myfile.fail() and cin.getline() using the dot operator, demonstrating that students have already been using objects.

title: Unit 3b - Classes: Title Slide
summary: Title slide introducing Unit 3b on Classes in C++ for CS 103, presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 3b of CS 103, covering the topic of Classes in C++. The unit is presented by Mark Redekopp. Classes are a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming that allow programmers to define custom data types that bundle data and functions together. This unit will cover the basics of defining and using classes in C++.
notes_text: This unit on classes builds on prior knowledge of structs and functions. Classes are the primary mechanism for implementing object-oriented programming in C++, enabling encapsulation, abstraction, and code reuse.

title: Object-Oriented Approach
summary: Introduces the object-oriented approach: modeling software as interacting objects that fuse data and functions, supporting encapsulation and abstraction.
main_text: The object-oriented approach models an application or software system as a set of objects that interact with each other. Objects fuse data (variables) and functions (also known as methods) that operate on that data into one item (an object). Objects replace global-level functions as the primary method of encapsulation and abstraction. Encapsulation means hiding implementation and controlling access. It involves grouping data and the code that operates on that data together into one unit, and only exposing a well-defined interface to control misuse of the code by other programmers. Abstraction refers to hiding data and implementation details. It is how we decompose the problem and think about our design at a higher level rather than considering everything at the lower level.
notes_text: Encapsulation and abstraction are two of the four pillars of object-oriented programming (along with inheritance and polymorphism, covered later). Encapsulation protects internal state from unintended modification, while abstraction lets users work with simplified interfaces without needing to understand the underlying complexity.

title: Object-Oriented Programming: Data Members and Methods
summary: Explains that objects contain data members for state and methods for behavior, using a Deck of cards as a concrete example.
main_text: Objects contain two main components: data members and methods/functions. Data members are the data needed to model the object and track its state or operation, similar to struct fields. Methods or functions are the code that operates on the object, modifies it, and provides behavior. As an example, consider a Deck of cards object. Its data members include an array of 52 entries (one for each card) indicating their ordering, where integers 0 through 51 represent the 52 cards, and a top index tracking the current position. Its methods or functions include shuffle(), cut(int where), and get_top_card(). The slide shows a table mapping array indices 0 through 6 to values 0 through 6, which correspond to cards like 2 of clubs, 2 of spades, 2 of hearts, 2 of diamonds, 3 of clubs, 3 of spades, and 3 of hearts.
notes_text: This example demonstrates how real-world entities can be modeled as objects. The Deck class encapsulates both the card data and the operations you can perform on a deck. The integer representation of cards (0-51) is an implementation detail hidden from the user of the class.

images.description: A table showing how array indices 0-6 map to integer values 0-6, which in turn represent playing cards (2 of clubs through 3 of hearts), demonstrating the integer-to-card mapping scheme.

title: Visualizing What Objects Do
summary: Visualizes an object as having internal state (data members) and functions (buttons) that update state, perform operations, or retrieve results.
main_text: An object has internal state represented by data members and functions that allow you to update the state, perform operations on the object, and retrieve data or results from the object. The slide shows a visualization of a Deck object named d. After declaring 'Deck d;', calls from main() interact with the object through its interface. Calling d.shuffle() triggers the shuffle() function. Calling d.cut(26) passes the value 26 to the cut(int) function. Calling 'int card = d.get_top_card()' retrieves a value from the object. Inside the object, the internal state includes top_index (initialized to 0) and the int cards[52] array containing values 0, 1, through 51. The visualization shows buttons representing the methods and internal storage representing the data members, with the object acting like a machine that receives inputs and produces outputs.
notes_text: This 'black box' visualization reinforces the concept of encapsulation. External code interacts with the object only through its public methods (the buttons), while the internal data (cards array and top_index) is hidden inside. The get_top_card() method returns a value (0 in the example) to the caller.

images.description: A 3D box diagram representing the Deck object 'd'. The top surface shows three 'buttons' for shuffle(), cut(int), and get_top_card() methods. Inside the box, top_index stores 0 and cards[52] stores values 0 through 51. Arrows show method calls from main() flowing into the object and get_top_card returning value 0.

title: C++ Classes: Step 1 - Define the Class
summary: Introduces classes as the programming construct for defining objects, showing step 1: defining data members and function/method prototypes.
main_text: Classes are the programming construct used to define objects, their data members, and methods/functions. They are similar in idea to structs. The process involves three steps, and this slide shows the first step: define the class's data members and function/method prototypes. The code example shows a file called cardgame.cpp with a class Deck definition. The class has a public section containing method prototypes: void shuffle(), void cut(int where), and int get_top_card(). The private section contains the data members: int cards[52] and int top_index. The class definition ends with a semicolon after the closing brace.
notes_text: Notice that the class definition separates public and private sections. Public members are accessible from outside the class, while private members can only be accessed from within the class's own member functions. The semicolon after the closing brace of the class definition is required and a common source of compiler errors if forgotten.

images.description: A code snippet showing the Deck class definition in cardgame.cpp with public method prototypes (shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data members (cards[52], top_index), labeled as step 1.

title: C++ Classes: Step 2 - Write Member Function Implementations
summary: Shows step 2 of class creation: writing the member function implementations using the scope resolution operator (::).
main_text: This slide continues the three steps for creating C++ classes, now showing step 2: write the function/method implementations. The code example in cardgame.cpp now includes the class definition (step 1) and the member function implementations (step 2). The shuffle function is implemented as 'void Deck::shuffle()' which uses a Fisher-Yates shuffle algorithm: it loops from i=51 down to i>0, generates a random index r = rand() % i, and swaps cards[i] with cards[r]. The get_top_card function is implemented as 'int Deck::get_top_card()' which returns cards[top_index++], returning the current top card and incrementing the index. Key terminology: a Class is the definition or blueprint of an object.
notes_text: The double colon (::) is the scope resolution operator. Writing 'Deck::shuffle()' tells the compiler this function belongs to the Deck class, giving it access to the class's private data members. Without this prefix, the compiler would treat it as a standalone function with no access to cards[] or top_index.

images.description: Code showing the Deck class definition (step 1) and member function implementations (step 2) including Deck::shuffle() with a randomized swap loop and Deck::get_top_card() returning cards[top_index++].

title: C++ Classes: Step 3 - Instantiate and Use Objects
summary: Completes the three-step class process by showing step 3: instantiating objects and calling their methods in main().
main_text: This slide completes the three steps for C++ classes by showing step 3: instantiate/declare object variables and use them by calling their methods. The complete cardgame.cpp now contains: step 1 (class definition with public methods and private data), step 2 (member function implementations), and step 3 (the main application). In main(), a Deck object d is declared, an int array hand[5] is created, then d.shuffle() is called, followed by d.cut(26). A for loop iterates 5 times calling hand[i] = d.get_top_card() to deal 5 cards. Key terminology: a Class is the definition/blueprint of an object. An Object is an instance of the class, representing the actual allocation of memory for that variable.
notes_text: The distinction between class and object is fundamental: the class is like an architectural blueprint, while each object is a house built from that blueprint. Multiple objects can be created from the same class, each with their own independent copy of the data members. When 'Deck d;' executes, memory is allocated for d's cards[52] array and top_index.

images.description: Complete cardgame.cpp code showing all three steps: class definition (1), member function implementations (2), and main() application code (3) that declares a Deck d, shuffles, cuts, and deals 5 cards into a hand array. A small diagram shows the Deck object d with cards and top_index members.

title: Common Class Structure - Split Files
summary: Explains how to split a class across separate header (.h) and source (.cpp) files for reusability and proper compilation.
main_text: It is common to separate a class into separate source code files so it can easily be reused in different applications. The recommended structure involves three files. First, in a header (.h) file (e.g., deck.h), define the class's data members and function/method prototypes, usually in a separate header file. The class must be defined using the syntax: class name { ... };. Second, in a corresponding .cpp file (e.g., deck.cpp), write the member functions/methods. This file includes the header with #include "deck.h". Third, in an application .cpp file (e.g., cardgame.cpp), instantiate/declare object variables and use them by calling their methods. This file also includes #include "deck.h". When compiling at the command line, you must list all .cpp files on the g++ command, for example: g++ deck.cpp cardgame.cpp -o cardgame.
notes_text: Splitting classes into header and implementation files is a best practice in C++. The header file acts as the interface specification, while the .cpp file contains the implementation details. This separation supports the principle of information hiding and allows multiple source files to use the same class without redefining it. The #include directive essentially copies the header file contents into each .cpp file that needs it.

images.description: Three code panels showing the split file structure: deck.h (class definition with public methods and private data, step 1), deck.cpp (includes deck.h, step 2 for method code), and cardgame.cpp (includes deck.h, step 3 for main application using Deck d).

title: Access Specifiers: Public, Private, and Protected
summary: Explains public, private, and protected access specifiers, showing how they enforce encapsulation by controlling what code can access class members.
main_text: Each function or data member can be classified as public, private, or protected. These classifications support encapsulation by ensuring that no other programmer writes code that uses or modifies your object in an unintended way. Private data/method members are INACCESSIBLE to non-member functions of the class, forcing non-members to ONLY utilize the PUBLIC interface. Private members can be called or accessed only by methods/functions that are part of that class. Public members can be called or accessed by any other code. Protected access will be covered later. Everything is private by default in a class, so you must use the public: label to make things visible. The general practice is to make the interface public and the internal workings (the guts) private. The code example shows that attempting to directly access d.cards[0] or d.top_index from main() will not compile because those are private members.
notes_text: Access specifiers are the mechanism that enforces encapsulation in C++. By making data members private, you prevent external code from putting the object into an invalid state. For example, if someone directly set top_index to -1, get_top_card() would access memory out of bounds. The public interface provides controlled, validated access.

images.description: Code showing deck.h with public methods (constructor, destructor, shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data members (cards[52], top_index). Cardgame.cpp shows that d.cards[0] = ACE and d.top_index = 5 won't compile because they access private members.

title: Public/Private and Structs vs. Classes
summary: Explains that the only difference between structs and classes in C++ is default access: structs default to public, classes default to private.
main_text: In C++ the ONLY difference between structs and classes is that structs default to public access while classes default to private access. Thus, other code (non-member functions of the class) cannot access private class members directly. The slide shows two code examples side by side. In student.h, the code shows 'class Student {' versus 'struct Student {' and asks what the difference is between these two declarations. The class contains constructors (Student() and Student(string name, int id, double gpa)), a destructor (~Student()), and data members: string name_, int id_, and double gpa_. In grades.cpp, a Student s1 is declared, and then s1.name_ = myname is attempted. This line would cause a compile error if Student is declared as a class (because name_ would be private by default) but would work if Student is declared as a struct (because name_ would be public by default).
notes_text: This is a commonly tested concept. In practice, the convention is to use struct for simple data holders with no behavior (plain old data types) and class for objects that have methods and enforce invariants through encapsulation. Despite being technically interchangeable except for default access, following this convention communicates intent to other programmers.

images.description: Two side-by-side code panels: student.h showing a Student type with constructors, destructor, and data members (name_, id_, gpa_); grades.cpp showing code that directly accesses s1.name_ which compiles with struct but not with class.

title: Constructors and Destructors: Motivation
summary: Motivates the need for constructors to initialize data members and destructors for cleanup when objects are created or destroyed.
main_text: This slide raises the question: what is the initial value of d.cards and d.top_index when a Deck object is declared? When an object comes alive (is created), we need to have appropriate initial values in our data members so that future calls to member functions will work appropriately. Additionally, when an object dies (goes out of scope or is deleted), we may need to perform some cleanup operations. To help with these tasks, C++ provides Constructor (ctor) and Destructor (dtor) functions. The code example shows deck.h with the Deck class containing public methods (shuffle, cut, get_top_card) and private data (int cards[52], int top_index). In cardgame.cpp, when 'Deck d;' is declared, the cards array and top_index contain unknown/garbage values (shown as question marks), highlighting why initialization through a constructor is necessary.
notes_text: Without a constructor, data members of built-in types (like int) contain whatever garbage values happen to be in memory at the time of allocation. This can lead to undefined behavior when methods try to use these uninitialized values. Constructors solve this by guaranteeing a valid initial state.

images.description: Code showing deck.h class definition and cardgame.cpp where Deck d is created. A small diagram of the Deck object shows cards and top_index filled with question marks, indicating uninitialized/garbage values.

title: Constructors and Destructors: Implementation
summary: Details constructor and destructor syntax, behavior, and implementation, showing how constructors initialize state and destructors perform cleanup.
main_text: A Constructor (ctor) is a function of the same name as the class itself (e.g., Deck()). It is called automatically when the object is created, either when declared or when allocated via new. Constructors are used to initialize the object's data members to some desired or known initial state. Constructors return nothing (not even void). A Destructor (dtor) is a function of the same name as the class with a tilde (~) in front (e.g., ~Deck()). It is called automatically when the object goes out of scope or when it is deallocated by delete or when the scope completes. Destructors are used to free/delete any memory allocated by the object or close any open file streams. Destructors also return nothing. The code example shows deck.h declaring Deck() as constructor and ~Deck() as destructor. In deck.cpp, Deck::Deck() sets top_index = 0 and initializes cards[i] = i in a loop for i from 0 to 51. Deck::~Deck() is empty since this class does not need cleanup. In cardgame.cpp, when 'Deck d;' executes, the constructor Deck() is called automatically. When main() returns, ~Deck() is called automatically.
notes_text: Currently the course does not have occasion to use destructors, but they become essential later when classes dynamically allocate memory (using new). The destructor would then use delete to free that memory, preventing memory leaks. Note that Deck::Deck() is NOT the same as Deck() - the first is the member function implementation, the second is just a call.

images.description: Three code panels: deck.h with constructor/destructor prototypes, deck.cpp showing Deck::Deck() initializing top_index to 0 and filling cards array with 0-51, and Deck::~Deck() empty. Cardgame.cpp shows constructor called at declaration and destructor called at return. A small diagram shows the initialized Deck with cards containing 0,1,2,3,4 and top_index = 0.

title: Multiple Constructors and Default Constructor
summary: Explains how classes can have multiple constructors with different argument lists, and defines the default constructor as the one with no arguments.
main_text: A class can have multiple constructors with different argument lists to provide options to client software for how they would like to initialize the object. A constructor with NO ARGUMENTS is known as the DEFAULT constructor. The Student class example in student.h shows two constructors: Student() as the default constructor, and Student(std::string name, int id, double gpa) as an 'initializing' constructor. The class also has a destructor ~Student(), getter methods (get_name(), get_id(), get_gpa()), and setter methods (set_name(), set_id(), set_gpa()). Private data members use a naming convention with trailing underscores: std::string name_, int id_, and double gpa_. This naming decorator makes it obvious to other programmers that the variable is a data member. In student.cpp, Student::Student() sets default values: name_ = 'Jane Doe', id_ = 0, gpa_ = 2.0. Student::Student(string name, int id, double gpa) sets name_ = name, id_ = id, gpa_ = gpa. In the main code, 'Student s1;' calls the default constructor, then uses setter methods to configure values. 'Student s2(myname, 32421, 4.0);' calls the initializing constructor directly.
notes_text: Multiple constructors are an example of function overloading in C++. The compiler determines which constructor to call based on the arguments provided. The trailing underscore convention for member variables (name_, id_, gpa_) is widely used to distinguish data members from local variables and function parameters, preventing naming conflicts.

images.description: Code showing student.h with two constructors, destructor, getters, setters, and private members with underscore naming. Student.cpp shows both constructor implementations. Main code demonstrates calling each constructor type.

title: Writing Member Functions and the Scope Resolution Operator
summary: Explains why the scope resolution operator (::) is needed when implementing member functions and how member functions can call each other.
main_text: The slide asks what is wrong with writing a function 'void f1() { top_index = 0; }' versus 'Deck::Deck() { top_index = 0; }'. The compiler needs to know that a function is a member of a class. To indicate this, include the name of the class followed by '::' (the scope resolution operator) just before the function name. This allows the compiler to check access to private/public variables. Without the scope operator, writing 'int get_top_card()' rather than 'int Deck::get_top_card()' would make the compiler think it is some outside function (not a member of Deck) and thus generate an error when it tries to access data members like cards and top_index. The code example shows deck.cpp with Deck::Deck() initializing top_index and cards, Deck::~Deck() as an empty destructor, and Deck::shuffle() which calls cut() directly. Within shuffle(), cut() is called without the Deck:: prefix because one member function can call another member function directly. Deck::get_top_card() increments top_index and returns cards[top_index-1].
notes_text: The scope resolution operator :: is critical in C++ class implementations. Inside a member function body, you have implicit access to all other members (both data and functions) of the same object. That is why shuffle() can call cut() without any prefix - the compiler already knows it is operating within the context of a Deck object.

images.description: Code comparison showing a non-member function f1() that cannot access top_index versus Deck::Deck() that can. Deck.h and deck.cpp code show proper use of scope resolution operator in all member function implementations. Deck::shuffle() demonstrates calling cut() directly from within a member function.

title: Accessor and Mutator Methods
summary: Introduces accessor (get) and mutator (set) methods for controlled access to private data, and the use of const for read-only methods.
main_text: Define public 'get' (accessor) and 'set' (mutator) functions to let other code access desired private data members in a controlled way. A good practice is to use 'const' after the argument list for functions that DO NOT modify data members. This ensures data members are not altered by the function. The Student class in student.h shows accessor methods declared as const: std::string get_name() const, int get_id() const, and double get_gpa() const. Mutator methods are: void set_name(string s) and void set_gpa(double g). In student.cpp, the implementations are: Student::get_name() const returns name_, Student::get_id() const returns id_, Student::set_name(string s) sets name_ = s, and Student::set_gpa(double g) sets gpa_ = g. In the main application, s1.set_name(myname) sets the name, and name_copy = s1.get_name() retrieves it.
notes_text: The const keyword on accessor methods is more than a convention - it provides a compiler-enforced guarantee that the method will not modify the object's state. This enables the method to be called on const objects and const references, which is important for passing objects by const reference to functions. If you accidentally try to modify a data member in a const method, the compiler will generate an error.

images.description: Code panels showing student.h with const accessor methods (get_name, get_id, get_gpa) and non-const mutator methods (set_name, set_gpa). Student.cpp shows their implementations. Main code demonstrates calling set_name and get_name on a Student object.

title: Calling Member Functions from Outside the Class (1)
summary: Explains how to call member functions from outside the class using the dot operator with the specific object name.
main_text: When outside the class scope (in main() or some outside function), you must precede the member function call with the object name of the specific object that it should operate on, using the dot operator (e.g., d1.shuffle()). The slide shows two Deck objects, d1 and d2, each with their own independent cards[52] array and top_index. Initially both have cards containing 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 and top_index = 0. The code in main() declares 'Deck d1, d2;' and 'int hand[5];'. When d1.shuffle() is called, it is not Deck.shuffle() or shuffle(d1) - it must be d1.shuffle(). The call d1.shuffle() indicates the code of shuffle() should be operating implicitly on d1's data members versus d2 or any other Deck object. After shuffling d1, its cards become 41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17 and its top_index becomes 1 after calling get_top_card(). Meanwhile d2 remains unchanged with its original ordered values.
notes_text: Each object is an independent instance with its own copy of all data members. Calling d1.shuffle() only affects d1's cards array and has no effect on d2. This is a key aspect of object-oriented programming: objects maintain their own independent state. The dot operator is how you specify which object's methods and data you want to access.

images.description: Diagram showing two Deck objects d1 and d2 with independent memory. Before shuffle: both have cards 0-7 and top_index 0. After d1.shuffle() and get_top_card(): d1 has shuffled cards (41,27,8,...) with top_index 1, while d2 remains unchanged. Code shows proper dot-operator syntax.

title: Calling Member Functions from Inside the Class
summary: Shows that within a member function, you can call other member functions directly without a preceding object name, as the object is implicit.
main_text: When inside the class scope (within a member function), no preceding object is necessary. Within a member function, you can just call other member functions directly. The example shows poker.cpp with main() declaring 'Deck d1, d2;' and calling d1.shuffle(). In deck.cpp, the Deck::shuffle() function calls cut(26) directly without any object prefix. Since shuffle() was implicitly working on d1's data (because main called d1.shuffle()), the call to cut() inside shuffle() also implicitly operates on d1's data. The annotation explains that d1 is implicitly passed to shuffle(), and since shuffle was implicitly working on d1's data, d1 is again implicitly passed to cut(). After execution, d1's cards show shuffled values (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) while d2 remains unchanged with ordered values (0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7). The shuffle implementation includes a Fisher-Yates algorithm using rand() % (52-i) for random indices, swapping cards using a temp variable.
notes_text: Behind the scenes, C++ passes a hidden 'this' pointer to every member function call. When you call d1.shuffle(), the compiler effectively passes &d1 as the 'this' pointer. Inside shuffle(), when cut(26) is called, it is equivalent to this->cut(26), meaning the same object (d1) is used. This implicit passing of the object is what makes member function chaining work.

images.description: Code showing poker.cpp calling d1.shuffle(), with an arrow to deck.cpp where Deck::shuffle() calls cut(26) directly. Annotations explain d1 is implicitly passed to both functions. Memory diagrams show d1 with shuffled cards and d2 unchanged.

title: Big Picture: Data Members as State and Member Functions as Behavior
summary: Summarizes that data members represent persistent object state while member functions modify or compute on that state, with guidelines for design.
main_text: Data members represent the 'state' of the object. State consists of values that need to be remembered or retained across various function calls for the lifetime of the object, enabling it to perform appropriate tasks. Data members should be the information needed by or across multiple member functions (e.g., set then get, add_score then avg_scores()). Member functions modify or perform computation on that state. Input arguments of member functions should be values needed only DURING or FOR that particular function call timeline. The Student class example shows: Student() default constructor, Student(string name, int id) as an initializing constructor, void set_name(std::string n), void add_score(int id, double score), and double avg_scores() const. Private members include std::string name_, int id_, and double scores_[10]. In main(), a Student s1 is created with 'Tommy Trojan' and id 12345, then s1.set_name('CS Sandy') changes the name, s1.add_score(0, 82.5) adds a score, and cout << s1.avg_scores() outputs 82.5.
notes_text: The distinction between what should be a data member versus a function parameter is an important design consideration. If a value needs to persist between method calls (like a student's name or accumulated scores), it belongs as a data member. If a value is only needed for the duration of one method call (like which index to store a score at), it should be a parameter. This principle guides good class design.

images.description: A 3D box diagram representing a Student object s1. The box shows data members: name ('Tommy' then changed to 'CS Sandy'), id (12345), and scores (82.5, -, -). Method calls s1.set_name(), s1.add_score(0, 82.5), and s1.avg_scores() are shown interacting with the box. avg_scores() outputs 82.5.

title: Class Pointers: Declaring and Using with new
summary: Introduces declaring pointers to class types, using the arrow operator (->) to access members, and allocating objects on the heap with new.
main_text: You can declare pointers to class types just like pointers to any other type. Use the -> (arrow) operator to access member functions or data through a pointer. The code example shows a makeDeck() function that returns a Deck pointer. Inside, 'Deck* d1 = new Deck;' allocates a new Deck object on the heap, and the constructor is called. Then d1->shuffle() and d1->cut(26) are called using the arrow operator. The function returns the pointer d1. In main(), 'Deck* myd = makeDeck();' receives the pointer. The for loop calls hand[i] = myd->get_top_card() to deal cards. The diagram shows d1 as a pointer on the stack of makeDeck() containing the address 55512a8, which points to a Deck object on the heap with cards[52] containing {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7} and top_index = 0.
notes_text: When using new to allocate objects, the constructor is automatically called just as with stack-allocated objects. The key difference is that heap-allocated objects persist beyond the scope in which they were created, so makeDeck() can return a pointer that remains valid. The arrow operator (->) is syntactic sugar for (*ptr).member - it dereferences the pointer and accesses the member in one step.

images.description: A memory diagram showing the stack frame of makeDeck() containing pointer d1 with value 55512a8. An arrow points from d1 to a Deck object on the heap at address 55512a8, containing cards[52] with values 0-7 and top_index = 0.

title: Class Pointers: Using and Deleting Heap Objects
summary: Shows the complete lifecycle of heap-allocated class objects, including using the pointer in main() and calling delete to invoke the destructor.
main_text: This slide continues the class pointers example, showing the state after the Deck has been used. In makeDeck(), 'Deck* d1 = new Deck;' calls the constructor (Ctor called), then d1->shuffle() and d1->cut(26) are called, and the pointer is returned. In main(), 'Deck* myd = makeDeck();' stores the returned pointer. The code calls myd->shuffle() and uses a loop with hand[i] = myd->get_top_card() to deal 5 cards. After use, 'delete myd;' deallocates the heap memory and the destructor (Dtor) is called automatically. The memory diagram shows the stack of main() with myd holding address 55512a8, pointing to the Deck on the heap. After dealing 5 cards, the heap object shows cards with shuffled values (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) and top_index = 5. The delete statement frees this heap memory and triggers ~Deck().
notes_text: Failing to call delete on heap-allocated objects causes a memory leak - the memory remains allocated but inaccessible after the pointer goes out of scope. This is one of the primary reasons destructors exist: to ensure proper cleanup when delete is called. Modern C++ recommends using smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) to automate this cleanup, but understanding raw pointers and manual memory management is foundational.

images.description: Memory diagram showing main()'s stack with myd pointer (55512a8) pointing to a Deck object on the heap. The heap Deck shows shuffled cards (41,27,8,39,25,4,11,17) and top_index = 5 after dealing cards. Code annotations show Ctor called at new and Dtor called at delete.

title: Exercises
summary: Closing slide directing students to complete in-class exercises to practice the concepts covered in this unit on classes.
main_text: This slide directs students to work on in-class exercises related to the material covered in Unit 3b on Classes. These exercises provide hands-on practice with defining classes, implementing constructors and destructors, using access specifiers, writing member functions with the scope resolution operator, and working with class pointers.
notes_text: In-class exercises are an important opportunity to apply the concepts of class definition, object instantiation, access control, constructors, destructors, and pointer-based object usage covered in this lecture.

title: Unit 4a - Linked List Title Slide
summary: Title slide for Unit 4a on Linked Lists in CS 103, authored by Mark Redekopp. Introduces the linked list topic within the Managing Data unit.
main_text: Unit 4a - Linked List. This lecture is part of CS 103 and covers the topic of linked lists. The instructor is Mark Redekopp. This unit falls under the Managing Data section of the course.
notes_text: This is the opening slide for the linked list module. Linked lists are a fundamental data structure that will be contrasted with arrays and built step by step throughout this lecture.

title: Course Structure Overview
summary: CS 103 is divided into six units each with lectures, labs, homework, and projects. Unit 4 covers Managing Data and is the current focus.
main_text: The course is broken into 6 units each consisting of: Lectures, Labs (Tools + Practice + small group Help), Homework(s) (Formative programming problems), and Project(s) (Cumulative programming problems). The six units are: 1. C++ Bootcamp, 2. Pointers and Memory, 3. Objects 1, 4. Managing Data (current unit, highlighted), 5. Objects 2, 6. Recursion.
notes_text: Unit 4 on Managing Data is where linked lists are introduced. This builds on prior knowledge of pointers and memory (Unit 2) and objects (Unit 3), both of which are essential for implementing linked data structures.

images.description: Diagram showing the course structure with a rounded rectangle containing four components (Lectures, Labs, Homework, Projects) and six numbered circular icons representing the six units, with Unit 4 (Managing Data) highlighted in red.

title: NULL Summary
summary: NULL and nullptr both represent 0 and indicate an invalid address. Always check that a pointer is not NULL before dereferencing it.
main_text: NULL and nullptr both evaluate to 0. They are used to indicate an INVALID address. Before dereferencing a pointer, check that it is NOT NULL using a conditional check: if(ptr != NULL) { /* safe to dereference */ }. Three example pointer declarations are shown: int* ptr1, char* word, and double* ptr2, each containing the value 0 when set to NULL.
notes_text: NULL checking is critical for linked list operations because the end of a linked list is marked by a NULL next pointer. Forgetting to check for NULL before dereferencing leads to segmentation faults, one of the most common errors when working with linked lists.

images.description: Three memory boxes showing pointer variables (int* ptr1, char* word, double* ptr2) each containing the value 0, illustrating that NULL pointers hold the value zero regardless of the pointer type.

title: Arrays Review
summary: Arrays provide fast O(1) access using contiguous memory and address arithmetic, but cannot grow or resize once declared on the stack or heap.
main_text: Fast access: Because arrays are contiguous in memory, we can jump straight to element i with only the start address and data type. Recall the formula: start_addr + i*data_size. If we know integer element i is at location 7304, we know where element i+1 is (at 7308, since integers are 4 bytes). Can't grow (resize): Once we declare the array (either statically on the stack or dynamically on the heap) we cannot increase its size. To add one more value when the array is full, we must allocate a new larger array, copy over all existing items, then add the new value. Example code shows declaring int data[25] and accessing data[i]. Another example shows dynamically allocating with int *ptr = new int[size] and the problem of needing more than the allocated size.
notes_text: The inability of arrays to resize is the key motivation for introducing linked lists. The copy-and-reallocate approach for growing arrays is expensive at O(n) for each resize. Linked lists solve this by allowing element-by-element allocation.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing addresses 7300-7308 with dat[0]=103, dat[1]=104, dat[2]=170 in contiguous locations, demonstrating how array elements are stored sequentially in memory.
Diagram showing the process of growing an array: old full array of 6 elements, allocating a new array of 12 slots, and copying items over then adding the new value 21.
labels: Copy over items then add value

title: Linked Lists Overview Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Linked Lists Overview portion of the lecture.
main_text: LINKED LISTS OVERVIEW. This section begins the core discussion of linked lists as a data structure.
notes_text: This divider separates the review material (arrays, NULL) from the new linked list content that follows.

title: Analogy - Lists
summary: Lists are a natural strategy for ordered items where you can add, remove, and reorder entries. Arrays require knowing max size ahead of time.
main_text: Natural strategy when we have a set of items that require specific ordering is to create a list. Write down what you know now. Can add more items later (usually to the end of the list). Remove (cross off) others when done with them. Can only do this with an array if you know max size of list ahead of time (which is sometimes fine). We could track the start and end (aka head and tail) but only a portion would be used at a time (wasteful!). Example shows a to-do list: 1. Do CS 103 HW, 2. Join ACM or IEEE, 3. Play Video Games, 4. Watch a movie. Items can be crossed off (completed) and new items like Exercise and Eat dinner can be added. The list can also be represented as separate cards/slots rather than a numbered sequential list.
notes_text: This analogy connects the abstract concept of a list to everyday experience. The key insight is that real-world lists grow and shrink dynamically, which motivates the need for a data structure that can do the same without pre-allocating a fixed size.

images.description: Two representations of a to-do list side by side: a numbered list on the left showing items being crossed off and added, and a card/slot representation on the right where each item occupies its own box with empty slots available for growth.

title: Linked Lists Introduction
summary: A linked list stores values in separate dynamically allocated objects, each containing a pointer to the next. Only the head pointer is needed to access the list.
main_text: A linked list stores values in separate chunks of memory (i.e. a dynamically allocated object). To know where the next one is, each one stores an explicit pointer to the next. Then, all we need to do is track where the first object is (i.e. the head pointer). We can allocate more or delete old ones as needed so we only use memory as needed, changing pointers as we go. The Item struct contains two fields: int val and Item* next. The struct definition is: struct Item { int val; Item* next; };. An example linked list is shown with head pointer at 0x148 pointing to an Item with val=3 and next=0x1c0, which points to an Item with val=9 and next=0x164, which points to an Item with val=2 and next=0x0 (NULL).
notes_text: This is the fundamental definition of a singly linked list. Each node (Item) contains data and a pointer to the next node. The last node's next pointer is NULL, marking the end of the list. Unlike arrays, linked list elements can be scattered anywhere in memory -- they are connected only through pointers.

images.description: Diagram showing the Item struct blueprint as a box with two fields (int val and Item* next), and a concrete linked list with three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164 connected by next pointers, with the head pointer (Item* head) storing 0x148.

title: Linked List Traversal and Modification Exercise
summary: Interactive exercise asking students to determine the order of values, how to insert at the front, and how to remove a value from a linked list.
main_text: What is the order of values in this linked list? How would you insert 6 at the front of the list? How would you remove the value 4? The diagram shows a linked list with head pointer at 0x360, pointing to an Item with val=5 at address 0x360 with next=0x240. The node at 0x240 has val=4 and next=0x3e0. The node at 0x3e0 has val=1 and next=0x200. The node at 0x200 has val=8 and next=0x0 (NULL). So the order of values following the pointers from head is: 5, 4, 1, 8.
notes_text: This exercise reinforces understanding of pointer traversal. The order is determined by following next pointers from head, not by memory addresses. To insert 6 at front: create a new node with val=6, set its next to current head (0x360), update head to point to the new node. To remove 4: find the node before it (val=5), update its next to skip over 4 (point to 0x3e0), then delete the node with val=4.

images.description: Memory diagram showing four linked list nodes scattered in memory at addresses 0x200, 0x240, 0x360, and 0x3e0 with the head pointer at 0x360, demonstrating that list order follows pointers not memory addresses.

title: Arrays vs. Linked List
summary: Arrays allow O(1) random access via address arithmetic but linked lists require sequential traversal. Linked lists trade access speed for the ability to dynamically resize.
main_text: Recall: if we have the start address of an array, we can get the i-th element quickly using: start_addr + i*data_size. Question: If we have the start (head) pointer to a linked list, can we find the i-th element quickly? No! Have to walk the linked list. Items are NOT CONTIGUOUS. Linked lists trade offs: Pro: the ability to resize (grow/shrink). Con: sacrifice speed of access when attempting to get the element at an arbitrary location. Example code shows array access with int data[25] and data[20] = 7. Memory diagram shows data starting at address 100 with contiguous elements. Linked list diagram shows head pointer at 0x148 pointing to nodes at scattered addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, 0x164 with values 3, 9, 2.
notes_text: This is the core tradeoff between arrays and linked lists. Arrays give O(1) random access because elements are stored contiguously and the address can be computed directly. Linked lists require O(n) traversal in the worst case because each node could be anywhere in memory. However, linked lists can grow and shrink without costly reallocation.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing an array with contiguous memory addresses (100, 104, 108...) enabling direct access, versus a linked list with nodes at scattered addresses connected by pointers requiring sequential traversal.

title: In Class Coding Exercise
summary: Directs students to an EdStem/Codio exercise for hands-on practice writing a linked list implementation.
main_text: EdStem/Codio Exercise - Writing a linked list. Students are directed to complete an in-class coding exercise to practice implementing linked list operations.
notes_text: Hands-on coding is essential for understanding linked lists. This exercise likely involves implementing basic operations like push_back, which will be explained in detail in the following slides.

title: Linked List Class Overview
summary: A linked list class uses an Item struct with val and next pointer, a List class with head pointer, and supports operations like push_back, push_front, pop_back, pop_front, and find.
main_text: Use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures including linked lists, trees, graphs, etc. List: Arbitrarily sized collection of values. Can add or remove any number of new values. Only REQUIRED data member: head pointer (though we can add a few other members to increase efficiency). Usually supports following set of operations: Append (push_back), Prepend (push_front), Remove back item (pop_back), Remove front item (pop_front), Find (look for particular value). The Item struct is defined as: struct Item { int val; Item* next; };. The List class is defined as: class List { public: List(); ~List(); void push_back(int v); ... private: Item* head; };. An empty list has head pointing to 0x0 (NULL). Note: Use 'struct' for objects that are purely collections of data without associated operations. Use 'class' when data does have associated functions/methods.
notes_text: This slide establishes the class-based design for a linked list. The separation of Item (struct for data) and List (class for operations) follows good object-oriented design principles. The head pointer initialized to NULL represents an empty list. The destructor ~List() is needed because dynamically allocated Items must be freed.

images.description: Diagram showing the Item struct blueprint with two fields (int val and Item* next) and an empty List object with head pointer set to 0x0 (NULL).

title: Building A Linked List (1) - Constructor Initialization
summary: The List constructor should initialize the head pointer. Students are asked to determine the correct initial value for head in an empty list.
main_text: How should we initialize our list object? The constructor List::List() sets head equal to a blank (to be filled in by students). The code shows #include<iostream>, using namespace std, and the constructor with head = _____________; (blank for students to fill). In main(), a List mylist is declared, which calls the constructor. The diagram shows the head pointer box with an empty value, representing the state after construction.
notes_text: The answer is head = NULL (or nullptr). An empty linked list has no nodes, so the head pointer should be NULL to indicate there are no items. This is the starting state before any elements are added. Always initialize pointers to NULL to avoid dangling pointer issues.

images.description: Diagram showing a List object after construction with the head pointer box containing an empty/unset value, prompting students to determine the correct initialization.

title: Building A Linked List (2) - Adding an Element
summary: When adding elements to a linked list, always handle two cases: when the list is EMPTY (head is NULL) and when the list is NON-EMPTY. Items should be allocated on the heap.
main_text: How do we add an element? Anytime we code for a linked data structure we should always account for 2 cases: When the structure is EMPTY (and thus head is NULL), and when the structure is NON-EMPTY. How should we allocate our Item? On the stack or on the heap? The push_back function checks if(head == NULL) for the empty case. In the empty case, an Item newItem is created as a local variable and head is set to &newItem. The code shows: List::List() { head = NULL; } and void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL) { // list is empty -- Item newItem; head = &newItem; } else { ... } }.
notes_text: This slide introduces the critical two-case pattern for linked list operations. The stack allocation shown here (Item newItem) is intentionally problematic -- it will be corrected in the next slide. Stack-allocated items are destroyed when the function returns, leaving a dangling pointer. This sets up the lesson about heap allocation.

images.description: Diagram showing head pointer at 0x0 and a separate Item struct with val and next fields, illustrating the initial state before adding the first element to an empty list.

title: Building A Linked List (3) - Dynamic Heap Allocation
summary: ALL linked list node allocations SHOULD be dynamic allocations on the heap using new, so they persist beyond the scope of the function call.
main_text: ALL allocations SHOULD be dynamic allocations on the heap so they persist beyond the scope of the push_back call. Two side-by-side examples are shown. WRONG approach (left, marked with prohibition sign): Item myitem; myitem.val = v; myitem.next = NULL; head = &myitem; -- This allocates on the stack and the item is destroyed when push_back returns, leaving a dangling pointer. CORRECT approach (right): head = new Item; head->val = v; head->next = NULL; -- This allocates on the heap using new, so the item persists after the function returns. Both show the result of mylist.push_back(3) with head at 0x148 pointing to an Item with val=3 and next=NULL.
notes_text: This is a critical lesson. Stack-allocated variables are destroyed when their scope ends. Since push_back is a function, any local Item variables die when it returns. Using 'new' allocates on the heap, where memory persists until explicitly deleted. The arrow operator (->) is used to access members through a pointer: head->val is equivalent to (*head).val.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of wrong (stack) and correct (heap) allocation approaches for linked list nodes, both showing head at 0x148 pointing to a node with val=3 and next=NULL, but the left approach is marked as incorrect with a prohibition sign.

title: Always Handle 2 Cases
summary: When coding linked list operations, always handle the EMPTY case (head is NULL) and the NON-EMPTY case (head is NOT NULL) separately.
main_text: Handle the EMPTY case (when head is NULL): The head pointer contains 0x0, meaning no items exist in the list. Handle the NON-EMPTY case (when head is NOT NULL): The head pointer contains a valid address (e.g., 0x148) pointing to the first item. In the non-empty example, head points to a chain of three items: at 0x148 with val=3 and next=0x1c0, at 0x1c0 with val=9 and next=0x0 (NULL), and at 0x164 with val=2 and next=0x0 (NULL). The last item shown separately with its own NULL next pointer.
notes_text: This is a starred/important concept. The two-case pattern (empty vs non-empty) applies to virtually every linked list operation: push_back, push_front, pop_back, pop_front, find, print, destructor, etc. Forgetting to handle the empty case is one of the most common sources of segmentation faults in linked list code.

images.description: Two diagrams showing the empty case (head pointer containing 0x0) and the non-empty case (head at 0x148 pointing to a chain of three nodes with values 3, 9, and 2).

title: Building A Linked List (4) - Inserting a Second Item
summary: To insert a second item using push_back, we need to walk to the last element in the list and append the new item there.
main_text: To insert a second item, what would need to change in our current list? The push_back function handles the empty case with if(head == NULL){ ... } and the non-empty case in the else block where we need to walk to the last element. The code shows: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { // Walk to the last element } }. After push_back(3) and push_back(9), head at 0x148 points to the node with val=3 whose next pointer (previously NULL) now needs to point to the new node with val=9.
notes_text: The key insight is that for push_back on a non-empty list, we cannot simply use the head pointer to add the new item. We must traverse the entire list to find the last element (the one whose next is NULL), then set that element's next pointer to the newly allocated item.

images.description: Diagram showing head at 0x148 pointing to node with val=3 and next=(NULL), with a new node containing val=9 that needs to be linked, illustrating the need to walk to the last element.

title: Building A Linked List (5) - Iterating to the Last Element
summary: For push_back on a non-empty list, we must iterate to the last element using the head pointer since that is our only entry point into the list.
main_text: To insert a second item, what would need to change in our current list? Answer: The last element in the list. When the list is NON-EMPTY with ONE or MANY elements already in the list, we must iterate to the last element in the list to insert our new Item. Given that we only have the head pointer, how do we step through the list? The code shows three push_back calls: mylist.push_back(3), mylist.push_back(9), mylist.push_back(2). The resulting list has head at 0x148 pointing to val=3 (next=0x1c0), then val=9 (next=0x0 NULL), then val=2 (next=0x0 NULL) as a separate node to be linked.
notes_text: This slide emphasizes that the only way to access elements in a singly linked list is through the head pointer and then following next pointers. There is no random access. To reach the last element, you must visit every element before it. This is fundamentally different from arrays where you can jump to any index.

images.description: Diagram showing a linked list with head at 0x148, nodes with values 3, 9, and 2 at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164, with the last node needing to be reached for push_back.

title: Building A Linked List (6) - Why Not Use Head to Traverse
summary: Do NOT use the head pointer to step through the list because moving head causes us to lose track of the beginning of the list permanently.
main_text: Given that we only have the head pointer, how do we step through the list? Would we even WANT TO use head to step through the list? No!!! The code shows a while loop: while( /* TBD */ ) { head = _____________; }. BEFORE: head at 0x148, pointing to nodes 3->9. AFTER (incorrectly using head to traverse): head moves to 0x1c0, now pointing to the second node (val=9). The first node (val=3 at 0x148) is now orphaned -- we have lost access to it. The head pointer has been overwritten and we can no longer find the start of the list.
notes_text: This is Common Linked List Mistake 1. If you use head = head->next to step through the list, you permanently lose the address of the first node. Since head is the only way to access the list, this effectively destroys part of the list. The solution is to use a temporary pointer variable instead.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing how using head to traverse causes head to move from 0x148 to 0x1c0, losing access to the first node (val=3). Before shows head at 0x148, after shows head at 0x1c0 with the first node orphaned.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 - Losing the Head
summary: Changing head to traverse the list causes amnesia -- we forget where the list starts. Solution: do NOT change head, use a temp pointer instead.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. BEFORE: head at 0x148, pointing to nodes with val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=NULL). AFTER using temp: head stays at 0x148 (unchanged), and a new Item* temp pointer at 0x148 is used to traverse. The temp pointer can be moved without affecting head.
notes_text: The lesson 'Don't lose your head' is a memorable mnemonic. The temp pointer is a local variable that copies the value of head, then can be safely advanced through the list using temp = temp->next. Head remains pointing to the first element throughout the traversal.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing the correct approach: head stays at 0x148 while a separate temp pointer (also starting at 0x148) is used for traversal, preserving access to the start of the list.

title: Building a Linked List (7) - Using a Temp Pointer
summary: When the list is not empty, initialize a temp pointer to head and step through the list. Two key questions: what code takes a step, and when to stop.
main_text: When the list is NOT EMPTY use a temp pointer (initialized with head) and then stepping through the list to the last element. Questions: What code would we use to 'take a step'? When would we want to stop (and thus what condition would we use in our while loop)? The code shows: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { // Iterate to last element Item* temp = head; while( /* when to stop? */ ) { temp = _____________ // take a step } } }. The diagram shows head at 0x148, temp also at 0x148, and three nodes with values 3, 9, 2 at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, 0x164.
notes_text: The two key questions here are answered in the next slides: taking a step means temp = temp->next, and the stopping condition is when temp->next == NULL (meaning temp is at the last element). Using temp != NULL as the stop condition would go one step too far -- temp would be NULL and we couldn't modify the last node's next pointer.

images.description: Diagram showing head and temp both pointing to 0x148, with three linked nodes at 0x148 (val=3), 0x1c0 (val=9), and 0x164 (val=2), illustrating the starting position for traversal.

title: Common LL Task: Taking a Step
summary: To move from one item to the next in a linked list, use temp = temp->next. This advances the pointer to follow the next link.
main_text: What is the C++ code to take a step from one item to the next? Answer: temp = temp->next. Lesson: To move a pointer to the next item use: temp = temp->next. The code context shows the push_back function with Item* temp = head; and while loop with temp = temp->next as the step. BEFORE: temp at 0x148 pointing to node with val=3. AFTER: temp at 0x1c0 pointing to node with val=9. The head pointer remains at 0x148 unchanged.
notes_text: The expression temp = temp->next reads the next pointer from the current node and stores it in temp, effectively advancing temp to point to the next node. This is the fundamental operation for linked list traversal. Note that head is never modified during this process.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing temp moving from 0x148 (pointing to val=3) to 0x1c0 (pointing to val=9) after executing temp = temp->next, while head stays at 0x148.

title: When Should We Stop Iterating
summary: Stop when temp->next is NULL (Option 1), not when temp is NULL (Option 2), because we need to modify the last element's next pointer to link the new node.
main_text: Option 1: When temp->next is NULL? Option 2: When temp is NULL? We need to modify the LAST element's next pointer, so we must stop when temp->next is NULL.
