If we stop when temp is NULL, we have gone one step past the last element and lost access to it. The code shows: while(temp->next != NULL) { temp = temp->next // take a step }. Option 1 stops temp at 0x1c0 (the last node with val=9, whose next is NULL). Option 2 would advance temp to 0x0 (NULL), which is one step too far and we can no longer access the last node.
notes_text: This distinction is critical. For push_back, we need to modify the last node's next pointer to point to the new node. If temp is NULL, we have no node to modify. By checking temp->next != NULL, we stop when temp IS the last node, allowing us to set temp->next = newNode. This is a common source of bugs for beginners.

images.description: Diagram showing two options for where temp stops. Option 1 has temp at 0x1c0 (pointing to the last node with val=9). Option 2 has temp at 0x0 (NULL), having gone past the end. Option 1 is correct.

title: Building a Linked List (8) - Complete Push Back Solution
summary: Complete push_back implementation for non-empty list: use temp to iterate to last element, allocate new node with new, set its fields, and link it via temp->next.
main_text: When the list is NOT EMPTY use a temp pointer (initialized with head) and then stepping through the list to the last element. Solution shown: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { Item* temp = head; while(temp->next != NULL) { temp = temp->next // take a step } Item* newp = new Item; newp->val = v; newp->next = NULL; temp->next = newp; } }. After calling mylist.push_back(3), mylist.push_back(9), mylist.push_back(2): temp ends at 0x1c0 (node with val=9), newp is at 0x164. The node at 0x1c0 has its next changed from NULL to 0x164, linking the new node with val=2.
notes_text: This is the complete push_back solution. The steps are: (1) initialize temp = head, (2) walk temp to the last node using while(temp->next != NULL), (3) allocate a new Item on the heap, (4) set its val and next=NULL, (5) link it by setting temp->next = newp. The entire push_back operation is O(n) because we must traverse the entire list to find the end.

images.description: Diagram showing the final state after push_back(2): head at 0x148, temp at 0x1c0, newp at 0x164. Three nodes linked: 3->9->2->NULL. The temp pointer found the last node (val=9) and linked newp (val=2) to it.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [1]
summary: Introduction to removal operations. Students are asked to determine what code is needed to remove the front item using pop_front.
main_text: Now let's look at removal. What code is necessary to remove the FRONT item? Modify the diagram below to show what we would WANT to happen. The code shows: void List::pop_front() { // What code goes here }. In main(): List mylist; mylist.push_back(3); mylist.push_back(9); mylist.push_back(2); mylist.pop_front();. The current state shows head at 0x148, nodes: 3 (0x148, next=0x1c0) -> 9 (0x1c0, next=0x164) -> 2 (0x164, next=NULL). The desired outcome is to remove the first node (val=3) and have head point to the second node (val=9).
notes_text: Removal from the front is simpler than from the back because we do not need to traverse the list. However, there are subtle issues with order of operations: we need to save the address of the first node before moving head, then delete the old first node. These issues are explored in the following slides.

images.description: Linked list diagram showing head at 0x148 pointing to three nodes with values 3, 9, 2. Students need to determine what the list should look like after removing the front item.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [2] - Simply Updating Head
summary: Simply updating head to head->next skips the first node but causes a memory leak because the old first node is never freed.
main_text: Could we simply update head? Unfortunately, that causes a problem. The code shows: void List::pop_front() { // What code goes here head = head->next; }. After execution, head moves from 0x148 to 0x1c0, now pointing to the node with val=9. However, the node at 0x148 (val=3) is still allocated on the heap but is no longer accessible. This is a memory leak -- the old first node cannot be freed because we no longer have a pointer to it. The prohibition sign indicates this approach is wrong.
notes_text: Memory leaks occur when dynamically allocated memory is no longer reachable by any pointer. In this case, the node with val=3 still occupies heap memory but has no pointer referring to it. Over time, repeated memory leaks can consume all available memory. We need to delete the old node before or after updating head.

images.description: Diagram showing head moved to 0x1c0 after head = head->next, with the node at 0x148 (val=3) now orphaned and marked with a prohibition sign, indicating a memory leak.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [3] - Delete Before Update Problem
summary: Deleting head first then updating head->next fails because after delete, head points to freed memory and accessing head->next is undefined behavior.
main_text: To avoid a memory leak, we CANNOT just change head. We need to free/delete the old first item! But what is wrong with the given code? The code shows: void List::pop_front() { delete head; head = head->next; }. The problem is that after delete head, the memory at 0x148 is freed. Then head = head->next tries to access the next pointer of the deleted node, which is undefined behavior -- the memory has been returned to the system. The diagram shows head being crossed out at 0x148, with the node at 0x148 being deleted but then trying to read its next field.
notes_text: This is the chicken-and-egg problem: we need head->next to know where the second item is, but we also need to delete the first item to avoid a leak. We cannot do both with just the head pointer -- we need a temporary pointer to save the address of the first item (or the second item) before performing the delete.

images.description: Diagram showing the problem of deleting head first: the node at 0x148 is freed (marked with prohibition sign), then head = head->next tries to access freed memory, which is invalid.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [4] - Correct Solution with Temp Pointer
summary: Correct pop_front: save head in a temp pointer, update head to temp->next, then delete temp. This avoids both memory leaks and use-after-free.
main_text: To avoid the chicken vs. egg problem about deleting the first item vs. using it to get the second item's address, let's introduce a temp pointer. Three steps: 1. Introduce a temp pointer that is a copy of head. 2. Get the next pointer from the first item to update head. 3. Delete the old first item. The correct code: void List::pop_front() { Item* temp = head; head = temp->next; delete temp; }. Step 1: temp = head (both point to 0x148). Step 2: head = temp->next (head moves to 0x1c0). Step 3: delete temp (frees the node at 0x148). The diagram shows numbered steps with temp at 0x148, head moving to 0x1c0, and the old first node being deleted.
notes_text: This is the correct pattern for removing the front item. The temp pointer preserves access to the node being removed, allowing us to both update head and free the memory. This pattern (save, redirect, delete) is used frequently in linked list operations. Note that this does not handle the edge case of an empty list -- in production code you would check if head is NULL first.

images.description: Numbered step diagram showing: (1) temp copies head at 0x148, (2) head updates to 0x1c0 via temp->next, (3) delete temp frees the node at 0x148. Prohibition signs mark the deleted node.

title: Final Result After Remove
summary: After executing pop_front, the list correctly has head pointing to the second node (val=9) with the first node (val=3) properly deleted.
main_text: After execution of pop_front(): The correct code is: Item* temp = head; head = temp->next; delete temp;. The final state shows head at 0x1c0 pointing to the node with val=9 (next=0x164), which points to val=2 (next=NULL). The node that previously held val=3 at 0x148 has been properly freed. In main(): List mylist; mylist.push_back(3); mylist.push_back(9); mylist.push_back(2); mylist.pop_front();
notes_text: The final list after pop_front contains only two elements: 9 and 2. The memory for the removed node (val=3) has been properly returned to the heap via delete. No memory leak occurs and no undefined behavior is triggered because we used the temp pointer pattern.

images.description: Final linked list state showing head at 0x1c0 pointing to node with val=9 (next=0x164), then node with val=2 (next=NULL). The deleted node at 0x148 is no longer shown.

title: Recall: Destructors
summary: A destructor (~ClassName) is called automatically when an object goes out of scope or is deleted. Data members are cleaned up automatically but pointed-to resources are not.
main_text: Destructor (dtor for short) is a function of the same name as class itself with a ~ in front (e.g. ~Deck()). Called automatically when object goes out of scope (i.e. when it is deallocated by 'delete' or when scope completes). Returns nothing. Important: Data members of an object are cleaned up / destroyed automatically by the destructor (without you adding any code). Note: The Deck class did not require a destructor. Example shows class Deck with constructor Deck(), destructor ~Deck(), private members int cards[52] and int top_index. The Deck destructor body is empty: { /* not needed for this class */ }. In main, Deck d is created (Deck() called), and ~Deck() is called automatically at return 0.
notes_text: This review of destructors sets up the need for a List destructor. The Deck class only has stack-allocated members (an array and an int), so they are automatically cleaned up. But the List class has a head pointer to heap-allocated nodes -- those nodes will NOT be automatically freed, causing memory leaks unless the destructor explicitly deletes them.

images.description: Code files deck.h, deck.cpp, and cardgame.cpp showing the Deck class definition, empty destructor implementation, and main function where Deck constructor and destructor are called automatically.

title: Need for Destructor in Linked List
summary: The List destructor must explicitly delete all heap-allocated nodes because the automatic cleanup only destroys the head pointer itself, not the nodes it points to.
main_text: Important: Data members of an object are cleaned up / destroyed automatically by the destructor (without you adding any code). Implication: Your destructor does NOT need to worry about deallocation or cleaning up your data members. Your destructor NEEDS to clean up things that your data members POINT TO or REFERENCE that won't be cleaned up if your data member(s) die. So, we'd need to deallocate each item remaining in the list. The List destructor must walk the list and delete each Item. Code shows: List::~List() { // Do we need code to clean up what our members refer to? }. After pop_front, the remaining list has head at 0x1c0 pointing to val=9 (next=0x164) and val=2 (next=NULL). When ~List() is called, head (the pointer variable) is automatically destroyed, but the nodes it points to remain on the heap -- a memory leak without explicit cleanup.
notes_text: The destructor must iterate through the list and delete each node, similar to calling pop_front repeatedly until the list is empty. A common implementation uses a while loop: while(head != NULL) { Item* temp = head; head = head->next; delete temp; }. This ensures all heap memory is reclaimed.

images.description: Diagram showing head pointer at 0x1c0 with a prohibition sign, pointing to two heap-allocated nodes (val=9 and val=2). When head is destroyed, the nodes remain as leaked memory.

title: Destructors: Another Example - Memory Leak Without Destructor
summary: When a LinkedList object on the stack goes out of scope without a destructor, its head pointer is destroyed but heap-allocated nodes remain, causing a memory leak.
main_text: The LinkedList object is allocated as a static/local variable, but each element is allocated on the heap. When y goes out of scope only the data members are deallocated. You may have a memory leak. The struct Item has int val and Item* next. The class LinkedList has void push_back(int v) and private Item* head. In doTask(), LinkedList y is created, then y.push_back(3) and y.push_back(5) are called. When doTask returns, the stack frame for doTask is destroyed, including the LinkedList object y and its head pointer. But the two heap-allocated nodes (val=3 at 0x93c and val=5 at 0x748) remain in memory with no pointer to them. The label 'MEMORY LEAK: When y is deallocated we have no pointer to the data' is shown.
notes_text: This example concretely shows the stack vs heap distinction. The LinkedList object y lives on the stack within doTask's stack frame. When doTask returns, y's stack memory (including the head pointer) is reclaimed. But the Items were allocated with 'new' on the heap, and without a destructor to delete them, they leak.

images.description: Memory diagram showing stack area with doTask and main frames, and heap area with two nodes (val=3, val=5). When doTask's frame is popped, the head pointer in y is destroyed but heap nodes persist as leaked memory.

title: Destructors: Another Example - Solution with Destructor
summary: An appropriate destructor will solve the memory leak problem by walking the list and deleting each node before the object is destroyed.
main_text: The LinkedList object is allocated as a static/local variable, but each element is allocated on the heap. When y goes out of scope only the data members are deallocated. You may have a memory leak. An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This. The same struct Item and class LinkedList are shown. In main, doTask() is called, which creates LinkedList y, calls y.push_back(3) and y.push_back(5). The stack/heap diagram shows the same layout but now with the message 'An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This' highlighted. When doTask returns, the destructor ~LinkedList() is called automatically before y's memory is reclaimed, giving it a chance to delete all heap-allocated nodes.
notes_text: The destructor is the C++ mechanism for deterministic cleanup. It is called automatically at the right time (when the object goes out of scope or is deleted), making it the ideal place to free heap-allocated resources. This is the RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) pattern: the constructor acquires resources and the destructor releases them.

images.description: Same stack/heap diagram as slide 31, but with a prominent label 'An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This' indicating that adding a destructor prevents the memory leak.
labels: An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This

title: Comparing Performance - Arrays vs Linked Lists (Exercise)
summary: Exercise comparing Big-O complexity for common operations on arrays vs linked lists: element access, adding to tail, and adding to front.
main_text: Arrays: Go to element at index i: O(__). Add something to the tail (assume you have a tail index): O(__). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(__). Linked Lists: Go to element at index i: O(__). Add something to the tail (assume you have only head pointer and n elements in the list): O(__). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(__). The blanks are left for students to fill in as an exercise.
notes_text: The answers are provided on slide 44. For arrays: O(1) for index access, O(1) for tail add with tail index, O(n) for front add (must shift all elements). For linked lists: O(i) or O(n) for index access (must traverse), O(n) for tail add with only head (must traverse), O(1) for front add (just update head). This comparison highlights the complementary strengths of each data structure.

title: Odds and Ends Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Odds and Ends section covering additional linked list topics and common mistakes.
main_text: ODDS AND ENDS. This section covers additional topics, common mistakes, and useful patterns for working with linked lists.
notes_text: This section revisits common mistakes and tasks as a review and reference, reinforcing the key lessons from the main lecture content.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 (Repeated) - Don't Lose Your Head
summary: Review: changing head to traverse loses the list's starting address. Always use a temp pointer to preserve head.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. The code shows push_back with a while loop where head = _____________ would incorrectly modify head. BEFORE: head at 0x148, nodes 3->9. AFTER (correct): head stays at 0x148, temp pointer at 0x148 is used instead for traversal. Head remains unchanged while temp advances through the list.
notes_text: This is a repeated slide from the main content (same as slide 19), included in the Odds and Ends section for review and reference. The key takeaway remains: never modify head during traversal operations.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing head preserved at 0x148 while temp pointer is used for traversal, with nodes containing values 3 and 9.

title: Common Linked Task/Mistake 2 - Head is Not an Item
summary: Head is just a pointer, not an Item struct. Use head (not head->next) to get a pointer to the first item. Many students mistakenly think head->next points to the first item.
main_text: What code will give us a pointer to the beginning item in the list? Mistake: Many students think head->next is how you get a pointer to the first item: Item* temp = head->next; (WRONG). Just use head to get the pointer to the beginning item. head is special. It is NOT an actual ITEM struct. head is just a pointer that points to the beginning (data-filled) item struct. head->next actually points to the 2nd item, not the 1st because head already points to the 1st item. Lesson: To get a pointer to the FIRST item, just use head. A train analogy is shown: the engine represents head (not a data car), and each train car represents an Item. Students mistakenly think head is an Item with val and next fields, or that head->next gives the first item.
notes_text: This mistake stems from confusing the head pointer with a node. Head is an Item* (a pointer TO an Item), not an Item itself. It does not have val or next fields. Only the Items (nodes) have those fields. Item* temp = head correctly gives a pointer to the first node. Item* temp = head->next gives a pointer to the SECOND node.

images.description: Train analogy showing engine (head) pulling data cars (Items). Diagrams show the correct understanding (head points to first Item) vs mistakes (thinking head->next is the first item, or thinking head itself is an Item with val/next fields).
labels: Mistake: Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item
Mistake: Students think head is an Item

title: Common Linked Task/Mistake 3 - Unnecessary Allocation
summary: Do not use 'new' when creating a temporary pointer for traversal. Just declare the pointer and assign it. Using new allocates an unnecessary Item that causes a memory leak.
main_text: Common errors we see is that to create a temporary pointer students also dynamically allocate an item and then immediately point it at something else causing a memory leak. Item* temp = new Item; then temp = head; or temp = head->next; (WRONG -- the allocated Item is leaked). You may declare pointers without having to allocate anything: Item* temp; (uninitialized), Item* temp = NULL; (initialized to null), Item* temp = head; (initialized to head's value). Lesson: Only use 'new' when you really want a new Item to come alive (i.e. in functions that are supposed to add an Item to the list). The diagram shows: Item* temp=NULL stores 0x00, Item* temp=head stores 0x148, Item* temp stores ??? (uninitialized). The mistake diagram shows temp allocated at 0x240 pointing to a new Item, then immediately overwritten to point to head, leaving the allocated Item leaked.
notes_text: This is a very common beginner mistake. Students associate pointer declaration with allocation, but pointers are just variables that hold addresses. Declaring Item* temp = head simply copies head's address into temp -- no new memory is allocated. Using 'new' creates a real Item on the heap, and if you immediately overwrite the pointer, that Item becomes unreachable (leaked).

images.description: Diagram showing the mistake of allocating with new Item then overwriting with head, causing a memory leak at address 0x240. Also shows correct pointer declarations without allocation: temp=NULL (0x00), temp=head (0x148), temp uninitialized (???).
labels: Mistake: Allocating an item when you declare a temporary pointer

title: Other Functions - Print, Find, Remove by Value
summary: Overview of additional linked list operations: printing all items, finding an item by value, and removing an item by value (which requires updating the previous node's next pointer).
main_text: Write a function to print all items in list: Copy head to a temp pointer then use it to iterate over the items until the next pointer is NULL. Print each item as you iterate. Find if an item in the list (return address of struct if present or NULL): Copy head to a temp pointer then use it to iterate over the items until you find an item with the desired value or until next pointer is NULL. Remove item with given value (i.e. find and remove): If found, need to change the next link of the previous item to point at the item after the item found. Example shows removing VAL=9 from list: head at 0x148, nodes 3 (next=0x168) -> 9 (next=0x168) -> 2 (next=NULL). To remove 9, the node with val=3 has its next changed from 0x1c0 to 0x168, bypassing the node with val=9.
notes_text: For remove-by-value, you need to track the previous node so you can update its next pointer. This can be done with two pointers (prev and curr) or by looking ahead (checking temp->next->val). The edge case where the item to remove is the first item (head) must be handled separately since there is no previous node -- you update head directly.

images.description: Diagram showing removal of node with val=9: the node with val=3 has its next pointer changed to skip over val=9 and point directly to val=2, with the removed node's links crossed out.

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Solutions section, which provides answers to exercises and fill-in-the-blank questions from earlier slides.
main_text: SOLUTIONS. This section provides the solutions and answers to the exercises and questions posed earlier in the lecture.
notes_text: The solutions section includes completed versions of the common mistakes and common tasks slides, with all blanks filled in and all answers revealed.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 Solution - Use Temp Pointer
summary: Solution: if we change head we lose access to the first item. Use a temp pointer initialized to head for traversal instead of modifying head directly.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. The push_back code shows the else branch with a while loop for iterating to the last element. Using head = _____________ to step would destroy the list. BEFORE: head at 0x148. AFTER (correct solution): head remains at 0x148, temp at 0x148 is used for traversal. Two linked nodes shown: val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=NULL).
notes_text: This is the solution version of Common Mistake 1, confirming the temp pointer approach. The pattern Item* temp = head; while(...) { temp = temp->next; } is the standard traversal idiom for singly linked lists.

images.description: Before and after diagrams confirming the solution: head stays at 0x148 while temp pointer handles traversal through nodes with values 3 and 9.

title: Common Mistake 2 Solution - Use Head for First Item
summary: Solution: head is just a pointer, not an Item. To get a pointer to the first item, use head directly. head->next points to the second item, not the first.
main_text: What code will give us a pointer to the beginning item in the list? Mistake: Many students think head->next is how you get a pointer to the first item: Item* temp = head->next; (WRONG). Just use head to get the pointer to the beginning item. head is special. It is NOT an actual ITEM struct. head is just a pointer that points to the beginning (data-filled) item struct. head->next actually points to the 2nd item, not the 1st because head already points to the 1st item. Lesson: To get a pointer to the FIRST item, just use head. Train analogy: Engine = head, Each car = Item. Mistake diagrams show: (1) Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item (temp = head->next gives 0x1c0, the second node). (2) Students thinking head is an Item with a question mark for val.
notes_text: This solution slide confirms that Item* temp = head is the correct way to get a pointer to the first item. The train analogy is helpful: the engine (head) pulls the first car (first Item), so the engine IS the reference to the first car. You don't need to go to the next car to find the first one.

images.description: Train analogy and diagrams showing correct usage (head points to first item) vs common mistakes (thinking head->next gives the first item, or thinking head is an Item struct).
labels: Mistake: Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item
Mistake: Students think head is an Item

title: Common Mistake 3 Solution - Don't Allocate for Temp Pointers
summary: Solution: only use new when adding a node to the list. Declaring a temporary pointer requires no allocation -- just assign it to head or NULL.
main_text: Common errors we see is when creating a temporary pointer, students also dynamically allocate an item and then immediately point it at something else causing a memory leak. Item* temp = new Item; then temp = head; or temp = head->next; (the new Item is leaked). You may declare pointers without having to allocate anything: Item* temp; (uninitialized), Item* temp = NULL; (safe default), Item* temp = head; (pointing to first node). Lesson: Only use 'new' when you really want a new Item to come alive (i.e. in functions that are supposed to add an Item to the list). Correct: Item* temp=NULL stores 0x00, Item* temp=head stores 0x148, Item* temp stores ??? (uninitialized, assign with temp = head to get 0x148).
notes_text: The rule is simple: use 'new' only in push_back, push_front, or insert operations where you actually want to create a new node. For traversal, searching, or removal operations, just declare a pointer variable and point it at an existing node. No allocation needed.

images.description: Diagram showing correct pointer declarations without allocation and the mistake of allocating then overwriting, with before/after traversal states.
labels: Mistake: Allocating an item when you declare a temporary pointer

title: Common Task 1 Solution - Taking a Step
summary: Solution: to move a pointer to the next item in a linked list, use temp = temp->next. This follows the next pointer to advance to the subsequent node.
main_text: What is the C++ code to take a step from one item to the next? Answer: temp = temp->next. Lesson: To move a pointer to the next item use: ptr = ptr->next. The diagram shows head at 0x148, two nodes: val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=0x0 NULL). Before taking step: temp = 0x148 (pointing to first node). After taking step: temp = 0x1c0 (pointing to second node). The operation temp = temp->next reads the next field of the current node (0x1c0) and stores it in temp, advancing the pointer.
notes_text: This is the fundamental linked list traversal operation. The expression temp->next accesses the next pointer stored in the node that temp currently points to. Assigning this value back to temp makes temp point to the next node. This is equivalent to incrementing an array index (i++) but for linked structures.

images.description: Diagram showing temp pointer advancing from 0x148 to 0x1c0 after executing temp = temp->next, with two linked nodes (val=3 and val=9) and before/after labels.

title: Comparing Performance - Arrays vs Linked Lists (Answers)
summary: Performance answers: Arrays have O(1) access and tail add, O(n) front add. Linked lists have O(i) access, O(n) tail add (head only), O(1) front add.
main_text: Arrays: Go to element at index i: O(1). Add something to the tail (assume you have a tail index): O(1). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(n). Linked Lists: Go to element at index i: O(i). Add something to the tail (assume you have only head pointer and n elements in the list): O(n). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(1). Arrays excel at random access (O(1)) and tail operations with a tail index. Linked lists excel at front insertion/deletion (O(1)) and dynamic resizing. Arrays struggle with front insertion (O(n) shifts required). Linked lists struggle with random access (O(i) traversal) and tail operations without a tail pointer (O(n) traversal).
notes_text: This comparison is fundamental to choosing the right data structure. If your use case involves frequent random access, use an array. If your use case involves frequent insertions/deletions at the front, use a linked list. A tail pointer can improve linked list tail operations to O(1). The O(i) notation for linked list access emphasizes that accessing the first element is O(1) but accessing the last is O(n).

title: Unit 4b - Doubly-Linked Lists
summary: Title slide introducing the doubly-linked lists unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 4b - Doubly-Linked Lists. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This unit covers doubly-linked lists, a fundamental data structure that extends singly-linked lists by adding a previous pointer to each node, enabling bidirectional traversal.
notes_text: Opening title slide establishing the unit. Doubly-linked lists build on the singly-linked list concepts covered in prior units.

title: Doubly-Linked Lists Section Header
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the doubly-linked lists topic.
main_text: Doubly-Linked Lists. This section header introduces the main content area of the unit, which will cover the structure, operations, and implementation of doubly-linked lists in C++.
notes_text: Transitional slide separating the title from the core instructional content that follows.

title: Singly-Linked List Review
summary: Reviews singly-linked list structure, dynamic allocation, forward-only traversal, and the inability to recover a previous node's address.
main_text: Singly-Linked List Review. Singly-linked lists use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures. They dynamically allocate each item when the user decides to add it. Each item includes a next pointer to the following item. Traversal and iteration is only easily achieved in one direction (the forward direction). The Item struct contains an int val and an Item* next pointer. The List class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private head pointer. A key question is posed: given a temp pointer to a node, could you ever recover the address of the previous item? The answer is no, because singly-linked lists only store forward pointers. This limitation motivates the need for doubly-linked lists.
notes_text: This review establishes the critical limitation of singly-linked lists: no backward traversal. The code shown uses struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; and class List with Item* head. The memory diagram shows three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164 with values 3, 9, and 2 respectively, each pointing forward via next pointers, with the last node's next set to NULL (0x0).

images.description: Code snippet showing the Item struct with int val and Item* next fields, and the List class declaration with constructor, destructor, push_back, and private head pointer. A struct blueprint diagram shows the layout of the Item struct with val and next fields.

Memory diagram showing three linked nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164. The head pointer (at address 0x1c0) points to the first node containing value 3. Each node has int val and Item* next fields. A temp pointer points to the middle node (value 9). A Q&A box asks whether you can recover the previous item's address given temp, answering 'No!!!' to emphasize the forward-only limitation.
labels: Q: Given temp...could you ever recover the address of the previous item?

title: Doubly-Linked Lists Structure and Definition
summary: Introduces the doubly-linked list structure with prev and next pointers in each node, enabling bidirectional traversal.
main_text: Doubly-Linked Lists. A doubly-linked list includes a previous pointer in each item so that we can traverse/iterate backwards or forward. The first item's previous field should be NULL. The last item's next field should be NULL. The DLItem struct contains three fields: int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next. The DLList class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private DLItem* head pointer. Each node in the list maintains two pointers: prev pointing to the preceding node and next pointing to the following node. This enables traversal in both directions from any given node, solving the limitation of singly-linked lists.
notes_text: The code defines struct DLItem { int val; DLItem* prev; DLItem* next; }; and class DLList with DLItem* head. The memory diagram shows three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x210 with values 3, 9, and 5. The first node's prev is 0x0 (NULL), and the last node's next is 0x0 (NULL). Each interior node has both prev and next pointing to its neighbors. The struct blueprint shows the DLItem layout with three fields: DLItem* prev, int val, DLItem* next.

images.description: Code snippet showing the DLItem struct with int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next fields, and the DLList class declaration. A struct blueprint diagram shows the DLItem layout with prev, val, and next fields side by side.

Memory diagram showing three doubly-linked nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x210 with values 3, 9, and 5. The head pointer points to address 0x148. Each node shows DLItem* prev, int val, and DLItem* next fields. Arrows show both forward (next) and backward (prev) connections between nodes. The first node's prev is NULL and the last node's next is NULL.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Front (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of adding a new node to the front of a doubly-linked list, emphasizing pointer update order to avoid losing information.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Front. Adding to the front requires you to update which pointers? Take care of the ORDER in which you update the pointers not to lose information you need. Tip: Fill in the blank fields/pointers first before changing existing ones. This slide presents the problem setup: a new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 needs to be inserted at the front of the existing list. The existing list has head pointing to address 0x148 (value 3), followed by nodes with values 9 and 5. The code area shows 'head = p; // ??' suggesting that simply setting head to p is not sufficient and more pointer updates are needed. Students must determine the correct sequence of pointer assignments.
notes_text: This is the 'before' state of the add-front operation. The key pedagogical point is that pointer update order matters critically. If you update head first, you lose the reference to the old front node. The tip to fill in blank fields first (the new node's prev and next) before modifying existing pointers (head, old front's prev) is a general strategy for linked list operations.

images.description: Diagram showing the state before insertion. A new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 has blank prev and next fields. The head pointer currently points to address 0x148. The existing list contains three nodes (3, 9, 5) with full prev/next linkage. A gray code box shows 'head = p; // ??' indicating the operation is incomplete.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Front (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for adding a node to the front, identifying the three pointers to update and their correct order in code.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Front. Adding to the front requires you to update which pointers? The answer is three pointers must be updated: Head, New front's next and previous, and Old front's previous. The correct code sequence is: p->prev = NULL; p->next = head; head->prev = p; (or equivalently p->next->prev = p;) head = p; The new node's prev is set to NULL since it will be the new first node. The new node's next points to the current head. The old head's prev pointer is updated to point back to the new node. Finally, head is updated to point to the new node. The order matters: head must be updated last, after using it to access the old front node.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows the new node (value 12) at address 0x190 is now the front of the list. Its prev is NULL (0x0), its next points to 0x148 (old front, value 3). The old front's prev now points to 0x190 instead of NULL. Head is updated from 0x148 to 0x190. The key insight is that we use head to set up the old front's prev pointer before reassigning head itself. The comment 'or p->next->prev = p' shows an alternative way to access the old front through p's next pointer after it has been set.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing node p (value 12) at 0x190 inserted at the front. Dashed arrows show the new linkages: p->prev is NULL, p->next points to 0x148, the old front node's prev now points to 0x190, and head has been updated to 0x190. A code box shows the four assignment statements in order.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of inserting a new node into the middle of a doubly-linked list, showing the initial state before insertion.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle. Adding to the middle requires you to update which pointers? This slide presents the problem setup for middle insertion. A new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 needs to be inserted after the node pointed to by curr (which points to head at 0x148, the node with value 3). The existing list has three nodes: value 3 at 0x148, value 9 at 0x1c0, and value 5 at 0x210. Students must identify which pointers need updating and determine the correct order of operations to insert the new node between the first and second nodes.
notes_text: The curr pointer represents the node after which we want to insert. In this example, curr points to the first node (value 3). The new node will be placed between nodes with values 3 and 9. The diagram shows p pointing to a new node with blank prev and next fields, emphasizing that these must be filled in as part of the insertion.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the state before middle insertion. Head and curr both point to 0x148 (value 3). A new node p at 0x190 with value 12 has blank prev and next fields. The existing three-node list (3, 9, 5) is fully linked with prev and next pointers. An arrow from curr to p indicates where the insertion should occur.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for middle insertion, identifying four pointers to update and providing the correct code sequence.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle. Adding to the middle requires you to update which pointers? Four pointers must be updated: Previous item's next field, Next item's previous field, New item's next field, and New item's previous field. The correct code sequence is: p->prev = curr; p->next = curr->next; curr->next->prev = p; (or equivalently p->next->prev = p;) curr->next = p; (or equivalently p->prev->next = p;) The new node's prev points to curr (the node after which we insert). The new node's next points to curr's current next. The node that was after curr has its prev updated to point to p. Finally, curr's next is updated to point to p. The order matters: curr->next must be used before it is overwritten in the last step.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows node p (value 12) at 0x190 successfully inserted between nodes at 0x148 (value 3) and 0x1c0 (value 9). The final list order is 3 -> 12 -> 9 -> 5. The alternative forms using p->next->prev and p->prev->next work because p's prev and next have already been set in the first two lines. The key ordering constraint is that curr->next->prev must be set before curr->next is reassigned, since we need curr->next to still point to the old next node.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing node p (value 12) at 0x190 inserted between nodes at 0x148 (value 3) and 0x1c0 (value 9). All four pointer updates are shown with arrows: p->prev to 0x148, p->next to 0x1c0, node at 0x1c0 prev updated to 0x190, node at 0x148 next updated to 0x190. A code box shows the four assignment statements.

title: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of removing a node from the middle of a doubly-linked list, showing the initial state before removal.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle. Removing from the middle requires you to update which pointers? This slide presents the problem setup for middle removal. The curr pointer at address 0x1c0 points to the middle node (value 9) which is the node to be removed. The existing list has three nodes: value 3 at 0x148, value 9 at 0x1c0, and value 5 at 0x210. A prohibition symbol (red circle with slash) is drawn over the middle node to indicate it should be removed. Students must identify which pointers need updating to bypass the removed node and properly link the remaining nodes.
notes_text: The curr pointer identifies the node to delete. Unlike singly-linked lists where you need a pointer to the node BEFORE the one to delete, doubly-linked lists allow deletion given only a pointer to the target node itself, since you can access both neighbors through curr->prev and curr->next. This is a major advantage of doubly-linked lists.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the state before middle removal. Head points to 0x148 (value 3). Curr points to 0x1c0 (value 9), the node to be removed, which has a red prohibition symbol overlaid. The three-node list (3, 9, 5) is fully linked. The prohibition symbol indicates this node will be deleted.

title: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for middle removal, identifying three operations: update previous node's next, update next node's prev, and delete the node.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle. Removing from the middle requires you to update which pointers? Three operations are needed: Previous item's next field must be updated, Next item's previous field must be updated, and the item object must be deleted. The correct code is: curr->next->prev = curr->prev; curr->prev->next = curr->next; delete curr; The first line sets the next node's prev pointer to skip over curr and point to curr's predecessor. The second line sets the previous node's next pointer to skip over curr and point to curr's successor. After both bypass pointers are set, the node is safely deleted with delete curr. The order of the first two statements does not matter relative to each other, but both must occur before the delete.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows the middle node (value 9) at 0x1c0 removed with a prohibition symbol. The remaining two nodes (value 3 at 0x148 and value 5 at 0x210) are now directly linked: node 3's next points to 0x210, and node 5's prev points to 0x148. Head remains at 0x148. Unlike the add operations where order was critical, here the two pointer updates can happen in either order since we are only reading from curr (not modifying it) until the final delete. Memory for the removed node is freed with delete.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing the middle node (value 9) at 0x1c0 deleted with a prohibition symbol. The remaining list has two nodes: value 3 at 0x148 with next pointing to 0x210, and value 5 at 0x210 with prev pointing to 0x148. A code box shows the three statements: curr->next->prev = curr->prev, curr->prev->next = curr->next, and delete curr.

title: Unit 4c - Vectors Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the Vectors unit in CS 103, covering the C++ vector container class. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4c on Vectors in the CS 103 course. The unit covers the C++ vector class, which is a key data structure in the Standard Template Library (STL). Vectors provide a managed, resizable array implementation that is widely used in C++ programming. This unit will cover how vectors work, their member functions, performance characteristics, and practical usage tips.
notes_text: Vectors are one of the most commonly used containers in C++ and understanding them is essential for effective C++ programming.

title: Vector Class Overview
summary: Introduces the vector class as a full-featured managed array that grows automatically, performs deep copies, tracks size, and supports random access indexing.
main_text: The vector class is a full-featured, managed array implementation with several key capabilities. It will grow the array as needed, meaning you do not have to worry about running out of space. It will perform deep copies, so assigning one vector to another creates an independent copy of all elements. It tracks its size automatically, so you always know how many elements are stored. It still allows array-like indexing (also known as random-access) such as data[i], making it familiar to use. It also provides several other capabilities beyond basic arrays. The vector class is similar to Java's ArrayList or Python's list objects, providing dynamic array functionality. More details can be found in the online documentation for the C++ standard library.
notes_text: The vector class solves the key limitations of raw C++ arrays: fixed size, no built-in size tracking, and shallow copy behavior. Understanding these advantages helps explain why vectors are preferred over raw arrays in most C++ code.

title: C++ Standard Template Library (STL)
summary: Introduces the C++ STL as a collection of templatized container classes including vector, list, deque, set, priority_queue, and map.
main_text: C++ has defined a whole set of templatized classes for you to use out of the box, known as the Standard Template Library (STL). The STL includes several important container classes: vector<T> for dynamic arrays, list<T> for linked lists, deque<T> for double-ended queues, set<T> for ordered unique collections, priority_queue<T> for heap-based priority queues, and map<K,V> for key-value associative containers. The T in angle brackets represents a template parameter that specifies the type of data the container will hold. These containers and their implementation are the focus of CS 104, the follow-up course. In CS 103, the focus is on learning how to use these containers, particularly vectors.
notes_text: The STL is a fundamental part of modern C++ programming. Each container has different performance characteristics suited for different use cases. Vectors are covered here, while the full details of all these containers are explored in CS 104.

title: Templates and C++ STL Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide transitioning to the topic of Templates and the C++ Standard Template Library.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the topic of Templates and the C++ Standard Template Library. Templates are the mechanism that allows STL containers like vector to work with any data type. Understanding templates is important for understanding how containers in the STL are designed and used.
notes_text: Templates are a core C++ feature that enables generic programming, allowing code to be written once and used with many different types.

title: Templates - The Problem of Code Duplication
summary: Motivates C++ templates by showing the problem of duplicating linked list code for different data types like int and double.
main_text: Previously, a linked list was built to store integers. But what if we want a list of doubles or chars or other objects? Without templates, we would have to define the same code but with different types, which is wasteful duplication. For example, an IntItem struct contains an int val and IntItem* next pointer, and its ListInt class has push_back(int newval). Similarly, a DoubleItem struct contains a double val and DoubleItem* next pointer, and its ListDouble class has push_back(double newval). The code is essentially identical except for the types used. Enter C++ Templates, which allow one set of code to work for any type the programmer wants, eliminating this code duplication problem.
notes_text: This slide motivates why templates exist. Without them, every new data type would require writing a separate version of the same data structure, leading to maintenance nightmares and code bloat. Templates solve this by parameterizing the type.

images.description: Two code blocks showing duplicate struct and class definitions: IntItem/ListInt for integers and DoubleItem/ListDouble for doubles, illustrating the code duplication problem that templates solve.

title: Templates - Declaring and Using Templatized Code
summary: Shows how C++ templates allow type parameterization so one class definition works for int, double, or any custom type like Quad.
main_text: C++ Templates allow the type of variable to be a parameter (variable) specified by the programmer. The compiler will generate separate class/struct code versions for any type desired when instantiated as an object. To declare templatized code, use the syntax 'template <typename T>' before the struct or class definition. For example, a generic Item struct uses 'T val' and 'Item<T>* next', and a generic List class uses 'void push_back(T newval)' with 'Item<T>* head' as a private member. To use templatized code, specify the type in angle brackets when creating objects: List<int> ilist causes an int version of the code to be generated by the compiler, List<double> dlist causes a double version, and List<Quad> qlist causes a Quad version. Usage is then straightforward: ilist.push_back(5), dlist.push_back(5.5125), double x = dlist.pop_front(), int y = ilist.pop_front().
notes_text: The 'template <typename T>' syntax tells the compiler that T is a placeholder for a real type. The compiler generates concrete code for each type used, a process called template instantiation. This is a compile-time mechanism with no runtime overhead.

images.description: Code block showing template declaration with 'template <typename T>' for a generic Item struct and List class, followed by usage in main() creating List<int> and List<double> objects with push_back and pop_front operations.

title: Vector Class Usage and Operations
summary: Demonstrates vector as a resizable container with code showing initialization, push_back, indexing, front/back access, erase, and insert operations.
main_text: The vector is a container class where what it contains is determined by the programmer via a template. It implements an array-based list that can be used like (and gives the benefits of) an array but can resize automatically. A complete code example demonstrates key operations: (0) vector<int> my_vec(5) creates a vector with initial size of 5. (1) Elements can be set using array-style indexing: my_vec[i] = i+50 fills with values 50-54. (1) push_back adds elements to the end: my_vec.push_back(10) and my_vec.push_back(8) append values. (2) Elements can be modified by index: my_vec[0] = 30. Iteration uses my_vec.size() to get the count and my_vec[i] to access elements. (3) back() and front() return the last and first elements respectively. pop_back() removes the last element. (4) erase(my_vec.begin() + 2) removes the element at index 2. insert(my_vec.begin() + 1, 43) inserts 43 at index 1. The diagrams show the array state after each operation, demonstrating how the vector contents change.
notes_text: The numbered steps trace through the code showing the vector state at each point. Notice how push_back grows the vector, erase shifts elements left to fill the gap, and insert shifts elements right to make room. The begin() function returns an iterator to the first element, and adding an offset gives access to other positions.

images.description: Five sequential diagrams showing the vector my_vec state at each step: (0) empty with unknown values, (1) filled with 50-54, (2) after push_back and modification showing [30,51,52,53,54,10,8], (3) after pop_back showing [30,51,52,53,54,10], (4) after erase and insert showing [30,43,51,53,54,10].

title: What Happens Behind the Scenes
summary: Explains vector internals: vectors store a pointer to a dynamically allocated array, track capacity and size, perform deep copies, and resize when needed.
main_text: Vectors abstract arrays. Behind the scenes, vectors are just creating and manipulating arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Vectors store a pointer to the array (which must be dynamically allocated since it is of variable size), the capacity of the array, and the size of used/occupied elements. For example, a vector v1 created with initial size 5 and filled with values 50-54 has data pointer, cap=5, and size=5. When push_back(10) is called, the vector must resize because the array is full. It allocates a new larger array (capacity doubles to 10), copies the old elements over, adds the new element, and updates cap=10, size=6. A shallow copy would have both v1 and v2 pointing to the same underlying array, which is dangerous. Instead, vector assignment (v2 = v1) causes a deep copy where v2 gets its own separate copy of the entire array with its own data pointer, cap, and size values. When the destructor is called on v2 and v1, each safely deallocates its own array.
notes_text: Understanding the internal representation of vectors (data pointer, capacity, size) is crucial for understanding their performance. The capacity is often larger than the size to allow push_back to be fast most of the time. Deep copy on assignment prevents the dangling pointer problem that would occur with shallow copies.

images.description: Diagram showing vector v1 and v2 internal structure with data pointer, cap, and size fields. Shows the resize process when push_back overflows, and contrasts shallow copy (both pointing to same array, marked with prohibition sign) versus deep copy (v2 gets its own array). Arrows show pointer relationships.

title: Vector Class Member Functions Reference
summary: Comprehensive reference of vector member functions including constructor, operator[], push_back, pop_back, size, empty, front, back, erase, and insert.
main_text: The vector class provides the following member functions: The constructor can take an initial number of items or be left blank to create an empty vector. operator[] allows array-style indexed access such as myvec[i]. push_back(T new_val) adds a copy of new_val to the end of the array, allocating more memory if necessary. pop_back() removes the item at the back of the vector but does not return it. size() returns the current number of items stored as an unsigned int. empty() returns true if no items are in the vector. front() and back() return the item at the front or back respectively. erase(index) removes the item at the specified index, where the index is specified using begin() plus an offset. insert(index, T new_val) adds new_val at the specified index, also using begin() plus an offset. The accompanying code example demonstrates all of these operations in a complete program.
notes_text: Note that pop_back does not return the removed value, unlike pop operations in some other languages. To get the last value before removing it, call back() first, then pop_back(). The erase and insert functions use iterator-style indexing with begin() + offset rather than plain integer indices.

title: Understanding Vector Performance
summary: Analyzes vector performance trade-offs: O(1) random access and fast back operations are strengths, while front/middle insert/delete and resizing are weaknesses.
main_text: Vectors are good at some things and worse at others in terms of performance. The Good: Fast access for random access (accessing any index i is O(1) constant time). Allows for fast addition or removal of items at the back of the vector. The Bad: Inserting or removing an item at the front or in the middle requires shifting all items up or down to add or remove the item, making these operations O(n). Adding an item when the underlying array is full will trigger an O(n) resize operation where the vector will allocate a whole new block of memory and copy over every item. However, if implemented wisely, resize is not as bad as it sounds (more details in CS 104). The diagrams illustrate: when deleting from the middle (index 2), elements at indices 3-5 must shift left to fill the gap. When inserting beyond capacity, a completely new larger array must be allocated and all elements copied to the new location, with the new elements appended.
notes_text: The amortized cost of push_back is actually O(1) because resize operations happen increasingly rarely as the vector grows (capacity typically doubles). This amortized analysis is covered in CS 104. The key takeaway is: use vectors when you need fast random access and primarily add/remove from the back.

images.description: Two diagrams showing vector performance issues. Left diagram shows deleting element at index 2 from array [30,51,52,53,54,10] requiring elements to shift left, resulting in [30,51,53,54,10]. Right diagram shows array [30,51,53,54,10] needing to grow when adding 12 and 18, requiring allocation of a new larger array and copying all elements.
labels: After deleting we have to move everyone up

title: Vector Tips and Odds and Ends
summary: Covers important vector usage tips: use push_back for empty vectors, use unsigned int or size_t for loop indices, and vectors make copies when adding items.
main_text: Important: If you don't provide an initial size to the vector, you must add items using push_back(). Creating an empty vector with vector<int> myvec gives cap=0, size=0, and data pointer=0. Attempting to use myvec[i] = i+50 on an empty vector would cause a segfault because no memory has been allocated. Instead, use myvec.push_back(i+50) to add elements. When iterating over the items with a for loop, use 'unsigned int' or 'size_t' type to match the return type of size(). The correct loop syntax is: for(size_t i=0; i < myvec.size(); i++). When adding an item, a copy will be made to add to the vector. For example, with vector<string> v1 and string s1="abc", calling v1.push_back(s1) copies the string into the vector. If s1 is later changed to "xyz", v1[0] still prints "abc" because the vector stored an independent copy.
notes_text: The segfault when indexing an empty vector is a very common beginner mistake. The size() function returns size_t (unsigned integer type), so comparing with a signed int can cause compiler warnings or unexpected behavior with negative values. The copy semantics mean vectors are safe but may be slow for large objects.

images.description: Diagrams showing: an empty vector with cap=0, size=0, data=0; a populated vector with cap=5, size=5 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54]; and a string vector showing s1 containing 'abc' being pushed into v1, where v1 stores its own copy so changing s1 to 'xyz' does not affect v1[0].

title: Vector Pass-By-Value
summary: Demonstrates that passing a vector by value to a function creates a deep copy, so modifications inside the function do not affect the original vector.
main_text: When passing a vector by value to a function, a deep copy is made. In the example, myvec is a vector<int> filled with values 50-54 using push_back (cap=5, size=5, data pointer at address 240). When do_it(myvec) is called, the function void do_it(vector<int> v) receives a complete deep copy of myvec. Inside do_it, v has its own separate data pointer (at address 760), cap=10, size=6 after v.push_back(60) adds 60 to the copy. The push_back(60) only adds to v (the copy), not to myvec. After do_it returns, iterating over myvec shows it is unchanged with its original 5 elements: 50, 51, 52, 53, 54. This is consistent with how other types work with pass-by-value in C++, but can be surprising and expensive for large vectors since every element must be copied.
notes_text: To avoid the cost of deep copying, pass vectors by reference (vector<int>& v) when you want to modify the original, or by const reference (const vector<int>& v) when you only need to read it. Pass-by-value copies can be very expensive for large vectors.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing myvec with data pointer at 240, cap=5, size=5 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54], and the copy v inside do_it with data pointer at 760, cap=10, size=6 pointing to array [50,51,52,53,54,60,?,?,?,?]. Demonstrates that modifications to v do not affect myvec.

title: Your Turn - In-class Exercises
summary: Closing slide directing students to practice with in-class exercises on vectors.
main_text: This slide directs students to complete in-class exercises to practice using vectors. The exercises reinforce the concepts covered in this unit including vector creation, using push_back, pop_back, front, back, erase, insert, and understanding performance characteristics of vector operations.
notes_text: Hands-on practice is essential for mastering vector operations. Students should practice creating vectors, adding and removing elements, and understanding when different operations are efficient or inefficient.

title: Unit 4d - Double-Ended Queues (Deques) Introduction
summary: Title slide introducing the Deques unit in CS 103, covering double-ended queue data structures and their implementations. Presented by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the title slide for Unit 4d on Double-Ended Queues (Deques) in the CS 103 course. A deque is a data structure that supports fast insertion and removal from both the front and back. This unit covers the motivation for deques, explores different possible implementations using singly-linked lists, doubly-linked lists, and arrays, and introduces the C++ deque class from the Standard Template Library.
notes_text: Deques are pronounced like 'deck' and the name comes from 'double-ended queue'. They are an important abstract data type that bridges the gap between stacks and queues.

title: Singly-Linked List Review
summary: Reviews singly-linked lists: each node has a value and next pointer, traversal is only forward, and you cannot recover the previous item from a given node.
main_text: Singly-linked lists use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures. They dynamically allocate each item when the user decides to add it. Each item includes a next pointer to the following item. Traversal and iteration is only easily achieved in one direction (the forward direction). The Item struct contains an int val and an Item* next pointer. The List class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private Item* head member. In the diagram, head points to the first node (value 3 at address 0x148), which points to the next node (value 9 at address 0x1c0), which points to the last node (value 2 at address 0x164) with next=NULL. An important question is posed: given a temp pointer to the middle node, could you ever recover the address of the previous item? The answer is No, because singly-linked lists only have forward pointers.
notes_text: The inability to go backwards in a singly-linked list is the key limitation that motivates doubly-linked lists. This becomes critical when trying to implement a deque, where we need to remove from the back efficiently.

images.description: Diagram showing a singly-linked list with three nodes: node at 0x148 (val=3, next=0x1c0), node at 0x1c0 (val=9, next=0x164), and node at 0x164 (val=2, next=NULL). Head pointer and temp pointer are shown, with a question about recovering the previous node answered with 'No!!!'.

title: Doubly-Linked Lists
summary: Introduces doubly-linked lists where each node has both a previous and next pointer, enabling bidirectional traversal.
main_text: A doubly-linked list includes a previous pointer in each item so that we can traverse/iterate backwards or forward. The DLItem struct contains int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next. The first item's previous field should be NULL, and the last item's next field should be NULL. The DLList class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private DLItem* head member. In the diagram, head points to address 0x148. The first node (val=3) has prev=NULL and next=0x1c0. The second node (val=9, at 0x1c0) has prev=0x148 and next=0x210. The third node (val=5, at 0x210) has prev=0x1c0 and next=NULL. Each node's blueprint shows three fields: DLItem* prev, int val, and DLItem* next, making each node larger than a singly-linked list node but enabling bidirectional traversal.
notes_text: Doubly-linked lists trade memory (extra pointer per node) for the ability to traverse in both directions. This is essential for efficient removal from the back of the list, which is needed for deque implementation.

images.description: Diagram showing a doubly-linked list with three nodes connected by forward and backward pointers. Each node has prev, val, and next fields. Node at 0x148 (val=3, prev=NULL), node at 0x1c0 (val=9), and node at 0x210 (val=5, next=NULL). A blueprint shows the DLItem structure with three fields.

title: Deques and Their Implementation Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to the topic of using a doubly-linked list to implement a deque.
main_text: This is a section divider slide marking the transition to the topic of Deques and Their Implementation. The subtitle indicates the focus will be on using a doubly-linked list to implement a deque. This section explores different linked list configurations and analyzes which ones can achieve the O(1) insertion and removal from both ends that defines a deque.
notes_text: The exploration of different implementation strategies (singly-linked with/without tail, doubly-linked with tail) builds understanding of why certain design choices are necessary.

title: Deques Definition and Operations
summary: Defines a deque as a data structure allowing O(1) insertion and removal from both front and back, with push_front, pop_front, push_back, and pop_back operations.
main_text: A Double-ended queue (deque, like the name sounds: 'D-que') is the name given to any data structure that allows fast (O(1)) insertion and removal from BOTH SIDES (front and back) of the list. The four core operations are: push_front() at O(1), push_back() at O(1), pop_front() at O(1), and pop_back() at O(1). There are several possible implementations of such a data structure. The key requirement is that all four operations must be constant time O(1). The diagram shows a deque as a box with arrows indicating push_front and pop_front on the left side, and push_back and pop_back on the right side, all labeled O(1). The text notes that many possible implementations exist for this abstract data type.
notes_text: A deque is an abstract data type defined by its interface (the four O(1) operations), not by its implementation. This means any data structure that achieves these time complexities qualifies as a deque implementation. The name is a portmanteau of 'double-ended queue'.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque as an orange box labeled 'Deque (Many possible implementations exist)' with arrows on the left for push_front O(1) entering and pop_front O(1) exiting, and arrows on the right for push_back O(1) entering and pop_back O(1) exiting.

title: Can A Vector Be a Deque
summary: Asks whether a vector (array) can serve as a deque implementation by achieving O(1) add/remove from both front and back. The answer is no.
main_text: This slide poses the question: can an array add/remove from the front and back in O(1)? The operations are listed with blank complexities for students to fill in: push_front() O(?), push_back() O(?), pop_front() O(?), pop_back() O(?). While push_back and pop_back can be O(1) for a vector, push_front and pop_front require shifting all elements, making them O(n). Therefore, a vector cannot serve as a deque. The diagram shows a deque box containing array elements [51, 71, 28, 10] with arrows for all four operations labeled O(1), but this is the target behavior that a plain vector cannot achieve.
notes_text: This is a key conceptual question. Vectors are fast at the back (O(1) amortized for push_back, O(1) for pop_back) but slow at the front (O(n) for both push_front and pop_front due to element shifting). This motivates looking at linked-list-based implementations.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque box with array elements [51, 71, 28, 10] inside, with arrows for push_front O(1), pop_front O(1), push_back O(1), and pop_back O(1) representing the ideal deque interface.

title: Deque Implementations Overview
summary: States that while a vector cannot be a deque, several implementations exist including linked-list based and C++ array-based deque implementations.
main_text: While a vector cannot be a deque, there are several possible implementations of such a data structure. The course will first explore a linked-list implementation for a deque, then note that C++ also provides an array-based deque implementation. The diagram shows a deque with push_front and pop_front arrows on the left, and push_back and pop_back arrows on the right, with linked list nodes visible inside the deque container, suggesting the linked-list implementation approach. The nodes are connected with bidirectional arrows indicating a doubly-linked structure.
notes_text: The two main approaches to implementing a deque are: (1) linked-list based, which is explored in detail in this unit, and (2) array-based using a circular buffer, which the C++ STL deque class uses internally.

images.description: Diagram showing a deque container with linked list nodes inside, connected by bidirectional arrows. Push_front and pop_front arrows on the left, push_back and pop_back arrows on the right.

title: Deque Implementation - Exploration Question
summary: Poses the question of whether a singly-linked list can achieve O(1) insertion/removal from both front and back, and sets up analysis of different implementations.
main_text: This slide sets up the exploration of deque implementation. The key question for exploration is: could we use a singly-linked list and still get fast (O(1)) insertion/removal from both front and back? For various implementations, students should analyze the runtime for each operation: push_front(), pop_front(), push_back(), and pop_back(). This systematic analysis will reveal which linked list configurations can and cannot serve as deques, building understanding of why certain design choices are necessary.
notes_text: The approach of analyzing each operation's complexity for different data structure configurations is a fundamental technique in computer science. It helps students understand the trade-offs between different implementations.

title: Singly-Linked List Deque Analysis
summary: Analyzes singly-linked list operations for deque suitability, asking students to determine O(1) vs O(n) complexity for push_front, pop_front, push_back, and pop_back.
main_text: With a singly-linked list (head pointer only), which operations are O(1) vs O(n)? The four operations are listed with blank complexities for students to fill in: push_front() O(?), pop_front() O(?), push_back() O(?), pop_back() O(?). With only a head pointer, push_front is O(1) because we just create a new node and point it to the current head. pop_front is O(1) because we just move head to head->next and delete the old head. However, push_back is O(n) because we must traverse to the end to add a node, and pop_back is O(n) because we must traverse to find the second-to-last node. The diagram shows the linked list: head at 0x148 pointing to node (val=3) -> node (val=9) -> node (val=2, next=NULL).
notes_text: A basic singly-linked list with only a head pointer fails the deque requirements because back operations require traversing the entire list. This motivates adding a tail pointer to speed up back operations.

images.description: Singly-linked list diagram with head pointer at 0x148, three nodes: (3, 0x1c0), (9, 0x164), (2, NULL). Shows the basic structure being analyzed for deque operation complexities.

title: Singly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Push Back Analysis
summary: Adding a tail pointer to a singly-linked list makes push_front O(1), pop_front O(1), and push_back O(1), but leaves push_back's complexity as a question.
main_text: Suppose we keep a second pointer (a tail pointer) to always point at the LAST element. The head points at the FIRST element and tail points at the LAST element. With this configuration, which operations are O(1) vs O(n)? push_front() is O(1) and pop_front() is O(1), same as before since we still have the head pointer. push_back() complexity is left as a question for students. With a tail pointer, push_back becomes O(1) because we can directly access the last node through the tail pointer, create a new node, set the old tail's next to the new node, and update tail to the new node. The diagram shows head at 0x148 and tail at 0x164, with the linked list: node (val=3) -> node (val=9) -> node (val=2, next=NULL).
notes_text: The tail pointer solves the push_back problem by giving direct access to the end of the list. However, pop_back still requires finding the second-to-last node, which the tail pointer alone cannot provide in a singly-linked list.

images.description: Singly-linked list with both head (0x148) and tail (0x164) pointers. Three nodes: (3) -> (9) -> (2, NULL). Tail pointer points directly to the last node, enabling O(1) push_back.

title: Singly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Pop Back Analysis
summary: Shows that even with a tail pointer, pop_back remains a question because removing the last element requires finding the second-to-last node.
main_text: Continuing the analysis of a singly-linked list with tail pointer: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1) thanks to the tail pointer. But pop_back() complexity is left as a question. The diagram now shows four nodes: head at 0x148 pointing to node (val=3) -> node (val=9, at 0x290) -> node (val=9, at 0x1c0) -> node (val=2 at 0x164, next=NULL), with tail pointing to the last node. The challenge with pop_back is that after removing the last node, we need to update the tail to point to the second-to-last node, and in a singly-linked list we have no way to find that node without traversing from the head.
notes_text: Even though we know where the tail is, we cannot move backwards in a singly-linked list. To pop_back, we must traverse from head to find the node whose next pointer equals tail, making it O(n). This is the fundamental limitation.

images.description: Singly-linked list with head and tail pointers, showing four nodes connected by next pointers. The challenge of pop_back is implied: after removing the tail node, how do we update the tail pointer?

title: Singly-Linked List Cannot Remove From Back in O(1)
summary: Concludes that even with a tail pointer, a singly-linked list CANNOT pop_back in O(1) because finding the second-to-last node requires traversal.
main_text: The complete analysis of singly-linked lists with tail pointer shows: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1), but pop_back() is O(n). So even with a tail pointer, a singly-linked list CANNOT remove from the back in O(1). The reason is that we have to update the second-to-last item (make it the new tail and set its next to NULL), and we cannot find that item quickly without walking the entire list from the head. Since pop_back is O(n), a singly-linked list with tail pointer does not meet the deque requirement of all four operations being O(1).
notes_text: This is a critical insight: the singly-linked list's inability to move backwards means pop_back will always be O(n) regardless of what additional pointers we maintain. The solution requires each node to store a pointer to its predecessor, which leads to the doubly-linked list.

images.description: Singly-linked list with head and tail pointers showing four nodes. Pop_back is highlighted as O(n) in red/pink, demonstrating the fundamental limitation of singly-linked lists for deque implementation.

title: Doubly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Setup
summary: Proposes using a doubly-linked list with tail pointer to achieve O(1) for all deque operations, since the prev pointer allows moving backwards.
main_text: Since removal from the back needs to move the tail BACK 1 step to the previous item, the solution is to use a doubly-linked list. With a doubly-linked list and tail pointer: push_front() is O(1), pop_front() is O(1), push_back() is O(1), and pop_back() complexity is left as a question. The diagram shows head at 0x148 and tail at 0x210, with four doubly-linked nodes: node at 0x148 (val=3, prev=NULL, next=0x190), node at 0x190 (val=12, prev=0x148, next=0x1c0), node at 0x1c0 (val=9, prev=0x190, next=0x210), node at 0x210 (val=5, prev=0x1c0, next=NULL). Each node has prev, val, and next fields connected bidirectionally.
notes_text: The doubly-linked list with tail pointer is the key insight. Because each node has a prev pointer, we can access the second-to-last node in O(1) via tail->prev, which is exactly what we need for efficient pop_back.

images.description: Doubly-linked list with head and tail pointers, showing four nodes with prev, val, and next fields. Bidirectional arrows connect consecutive nodes. Head points to first node (val=3) and tail points to last node (val=5).

title: Doubly-Linked List With Tail Pointer - Pop Back is O(1)
summary: Shows that pop_back is O(1) with a doubly-linked list because tail = tail->prev gives direct access to the second-to-last node.
main_text: With a doubly-linked list and tail pointer, all four operations are O(1): push_front() O(1), pop_front() O(1), push_back() O(1), and pop_back() O(1). We can update the tail pointer with the tail item's previous pointer before we delete the tail item, using the expression: tail = tail->prev. The diagram shows the pop_back process: the tail pointer (originally at 0x210 pointing to node val=5) is updated to 0x1c0 (the node with val=9). The node at 0x1c0 has its next pointer set to NULL (shown as 0x0), and the old tail node (val=5) is crossed out with a prohibition sign indicating it will be deleted. The key operation is that tail->prev gives us the second-to-last node in O(1), which was impossible with a singly-linked list.
notes_text: The complete pop_back algorithm is: (1) save tail->prev as the new tail, (2) set the new tail's next to NULL, (3) delete the old tail node, (4) update the tail pointer. All of these are O(1) operations because we have direct pointer access.
