Position 3: At the end of the prototype of a member function - ensures THAT OBJECT's (the calling object's) data members are NOT modified by the function.
notes_text: Position 3 (const at the end) is unique to member functions and is part of the function signature. A const object can only call const member functions, making this declaration critical for const-correctness.

title: The const Keyword - Practical Example
summary: Demonstrates all three uses of const in a Roster class with getGrade function, showing how const protects arguments, data members, and return values.
main_text: The const keyword can be used with: 1. Input arguments to ensure they aren't modified. 2. After a member function to ensure data members of the calling object aren't modified. 3. Return values to ensure they aren't modified. Example: class Roster with private vector<string> names and vector<string> grades ("A+", "B-", etc.), and public const string& getGrade(const string& name) const; The function signature shows all three const positions. In usage: Roster rost; string n = "Jill"; const string& grade = rost.getGrade(n); grade = "A+"; // won't compile (const-ref). The diagram shows the getGrade stack with const string& name pointing to n, and main's stack with const string& grade pointing into the rost.grades vector, with lock icons representing const protection.
notes_text: The const reference return type prevents callers from modifying the internal data of the Roster through the returned reference. This is essential for maintaining encapsulation when returning references to internal data.

images.description: Stack diagram showing getGrade and main frames with arrows indicating const references pointing to Roster data members, with lock icons representing const protection

title: Exercises - Const Exercises
summary: Exercise slide prompting students to practice const keyword concepts covered in the lecture.
main_text: This slide contains a const exercises prompt for students to practice applying the const keyword in various positions of member function prototypes. Students should practice identifying where const should be placed and what each placement protects.
notes_text: Hands-on practice with const placement is essential for developing const-correctness habits in C++ programming.

title: Review Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing review exercises covering const arguments, const member functions, initialization lists, construction order, and friend functions.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Review section. The following slides contain review exercises on const function arguments, const member functions, constructor initialization lists, construction order, friend functions, and friend classes.
notes_text: These review exercises test comprehension of the major topics covered in this unit.

title: Review [1] - Const Arguments and Const Member Functions
summary: Review exercise with two problems: one on const function arguments (will code compile?) and one on const member functions (what does trailing const imply?).
main_text: Const function arguments exercise: Will this code compile? void f1(const vector<int>& x) { x.push_back(103); x.push_back(104); } - this modifies x which is const, so it won't compile. void f2(string& y) { y = "Bye"; } In main(): vector<int> a; string b = "Hi"; f1(a); f2(b); cout << b.size() << endl; - Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles). Const member functions exercise: What does the highlighted const keyword imply in the code below? class Item with int val, public void foo() and int bar() const. void Item::foo() { val = 5; } - modifies val. int Item::bar() const { return val+1; } - does not modify val. void f1(const Item& arg) { int x = arg.bar(); // fine. arg.foo(); // Compiler Error! } - const reference cannot call non-const member function.
notes_text: The f1 function won't compile because push_back modifies the vector, violating the const promise. The f2 function modifies b to "Bye" which has size 3. The const member function bar() cannot modify data members.

images.description: Two side-by-side code exercises: left showing const function argument problems, right showing const member function usage with Item class

title: Review [2] - Initialization Lists and Construction Order
summary: Review exercise on initialization lists (most efficient way to initialize members) and construction order (what gets printed when constructing composite objects).
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists exercise: What is the most efficient means to initialize the vals member to an initial array size of 20 and s to a user-defined string? class Thing with public Thing(const std::string& s_init), private vector<int> vals and string s. The constructor Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) currently has: // is this the most efficient way? vals.resize(20); s = s_init; in the body. Construction Order exercise: What is printed by the code below? class ABC with ABC() { cout << "ABC" << endl; }. class DEF with DEF() { cout << "DEF" << endl; }. class XYZ with ABC m1; DEF m2; and XYZ() { cout << "XYZ" << endl; }. int main() { XYZ x1; return 0; } - Students must determine the output order.
notes_text: For the initialization list question, using : vals(20), s(s_init) in the initialization list is more efficient than default-constructing then reassigning. For construction order, members are constructed in declaration order (ABC then DEF) before the XYZ constructor body runs.

images.description: Two code exercises side by side: left asking about efficient initialization of Thing class members, right asking about construction order output of XYZ with ABC and DEF members

title: Review [3] - Friend Functions and Friend Classes
summary: Review exercise on friend functions (what does the friend keyword imply for operator+?) and friend classes (can DEF access ABC's private member x?).
main_text: Friend Functions exercise: What does the highlighted friend keyword imply in the code below? class Complex with public Complex(), Complex(double r, double i), friend Complex operator+(const int&, const Complex&), and private double real, imag. The operator+ implementation accesses rhs.real and rhs.imag directly. What would break if we remove the friend keyword? Friend Classes exercise: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? class ABC with private int x and public members. class DEF with public void clear(ABC& obj) { obj.x = 0; }. If not, how can class ABC grant access to DEF? Students must determine if friend declaration is needed and where to place it.
notes_text: The friend keyword grants a non-member function access to private members of the class. Without it, operator+ could not access Complex's private real and imag members. For the friend class question, DEF cannot access ABC's private x without ABC declaring DEF as a friend.

images.description: Two code exercises: left showing Complex class with friend operator+ and asking about the friend keyword, right showing ABC and DEF classes asking about private member access

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the solutions to the review exercises from the previous slides.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Solutions section, providing answers to the review exercises on constructor identification, const correctness, initialization lists, construction order, and friend functions/classes.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review exercises before looking at the solutions.

title: Identify that Constructor - Solution
summary: Provides the solutions: s1 uses Student::Student() default constructor, s2 uses Student::Student(string, int) or Student::Student(const char*, int), vals uses vector<int>::vector<int>(int).
main_text: Prototype what constructors are being called here. Given the Student class with default constructor Student() and initializing constructor Student(const string& name), with private members string name_, int id_, vector<int> grades_. In main(): s1 (Student s1;) uses Student::Student() - the default constructor. s2 (Student s2("Tommy", 12345);) uses Student::Student(string, int) or Student::Student(const char*, int). dat (vector<int> vals(10);) uses vector<int>::vector<int>(int) - the vector constructor that takes a size argument.
notes_text: The s2 answer notes both (string, int) and (const char*, int) because the string literal "Tommy" could be implicitly converted to std::string or matched as const char*.

images.description: Code showing Student class with constructors and main() with highlighted declarations, alongside the solutions listing which constructor each call invokes

title: Review [1] Solution - Const Answers
summary: Solutions: f1 won't compile (modifying const vector), b.size() prints 3, trailing const means no data members can be modified nor non-const member functions called.
main_text: Const function arguments solution: Will this code compile? No, modification of x in f1() because x is const vector<int>&. Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles): b.size() will be 3 (f2 changes b to "Bye" which has 3 characters). Const member functions solution: What does the highlighted const keyword imply? No data members can be modified nor non-const member functions called. In void f1(const Item& arg): int x = arg.bar(); is fine because bar() is const. arg.foo(); causes a Compiler Error because foo() is not const and cannot be called on a const reference.
notes_text: The key insight is that a const reference can only call const member functions. This ensures the promise of not modifying the object is maintained throughout the call chain.

images.description: Same code layout as slide 51 with answers filled in: No for compilation, 3 for output, and explanation of const member function implications
labels: No, modification of x in f1()
No data members can be modified nor non-const member functions

title: Review [2] Solution - Initialization Lists and Construction Order
summary: Solutions: use : vals(20) initialization list for efficiency; construction order prints ABC, DEF, XYZ (members first in declaration order, then object).
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists solution: The most efficient way to initialize vals to size 20 is to use the initialization list: Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) : vals(20) { s = s_init; }. The vals(20) in the initialization list calls vector's constructor directly with size 20, avoiding the two-step default-construct-then-resize approach. Construction Order solution: The code prints ABC, DEF, XYZ. When XYZ x1 is constructed: first ABC m1's constructor runs (prints "ABC"), then DEF m2's constructor runs (prints "DEF"), finally XYZ's constructor body runs (prints "XYZ"). Members are constructed in the order they are declared in the class, before the object's own constructor body executes.
notes_text: Note that s could also be initialized in the initialization list as : vals(20), s(s_init) for maximum efficiency. The construction order is always determined by declaration order, not initialization list order.

images.description: Same layout as slide 52 with solutions: initialization list : vals(20) shown in code, and ABC/DEF/XYZ output order shown

title: Review [3] Solution - Friend Functions and Classes
summary: Solutions: friend grants operator+ access to Complex's private members; removing it breaks rhs.real/rhs.imag access; DEF can access ABC.x only with friend declaration.
main_text: Friend Functions solution: What does the highlighted friend keyword imply? That function can access Complex private members. What would break if we remove it? Could not access rhs.real / rhs.imag because they are private members of Complex. The operator+ function needs to access temp.real, temp.imag, and rhs.real, rhs.imag directly. Friend Classes solution: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? Yes (this implies ABC has declared DEF as a friend). If not, how can class ABC grant access to DEF? Add friend definition - specifically, class ABC would add 'friend class DEF;' inside its class body to grant DEF access to its private members.
notes_text: Friend declarations break encapsulation intentionally and should be used sparingly. They are most commonly used for operator overloading where the operator needs access to private data of the class it operates on.

images.description: Same layout as slide 53 with answers: friend grants private access, removing it breaks real/imag access, ABC must add friend class DEF declaration
labels: That function can access Complex private members

title: Not Responsible for Material Past This Point
summary: Divider slide indicating that material after this point is supplementary and not required for exams or assignments.
main_text: YOU ARE NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR MATERIAL PAST THIS POINT. This indicates that the following slides cover advanced or supplementary topics (nested types, static members) that are not required material for the current course assessments.
notes_text: While not required, the supplementary material on nested types and static members is useful for understanding more advanced C++ patterns.

title: Nested Types Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the supplementary topic of nested types (structs/classes defined inside other classes).
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Nested Types section, a supplementary topic. Nested types allow defining structs or classes inside other classes, which is useful for helper types like linked list nodes and iterators that exist solely to support the outer class.
notes_text: Nested types are common in standard library implementations (e.g., iterators) and in data structure implementations.

title: Duplicate Types - The Problem
summary: Shows how using the same struct name (Item) for both integer and double linked lists causes a duplicate type name error.
main_text: Recall linked lists use a helper struct to model each item in the list. It stores a value (of a certain type) and a pointer to the next item. If we want to use a different type list, we would need a different Item struct, but would need to name it differently. For an integer linked list: struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; used by class ListInt. For a double linked list: struct Item { double val; Item* next; }; - this causes an ERROR because of a duplicate type name. Solutions include: Different names (IntItem vs DoubleItem), Templates (more later), or Nested Types.
notes_text: This motivates the need for nested types. Without them, you would need unique names for every helper struct, which becomes unwieldy in large projects.

images.description: Code showing integer linked list Item struct and ListInt class, then a duplicate double linked list Item struct that causes an error

title: Nested Types - Definition and Usage
summary: Explains how nested types (structs/classes defined inside another class) can share names across different classes and be accessed with scope resolution.
main_text: A struct or class can be defined inside another and is known as a nested type. Good practice to nest 'helper' types (i.e. structs/classes that exist SOLELY in support of the outer class). Nested types can share the same name but have different implementations when defined inside of different objects. Examples include linked list Item structs and Iterators (later in the class). Code shows class ListInt with a nested struct Item { int val; Item* next; } and class ListDbl with a nested struct Item { double val; Item* next; }. Both use the name Item without conflict because they are scoped to their respective classes. In main(): ListInt::Item x; x.val = 3; accesses the integer version. ListDbl::Item* p; p = ld.find(2.5); accesses the double version.
notes_text: Nested types are scoped to their enclosing class, so ListInt::Item and ListDbl::Item are distinct types despite sharing the same simple name. This is a form of namespace-like scoping within classes.

images.description: Code showing ListInt and ListDbl classes each with their own nested Item struct, and main() using scoped type names ListInt::Item and ListDbl::Item

title: Declaring and Using Nested Types
summary: Explains scoping rules for nested types: non-members must scope with classname::typename, but member functions can use the type directly.
main_text: Non-members must scope the type name: classname::typename. Member function code does not have to scope the type once inside the member function scope. However, notice the return type of a function is not inside the member function scope. Code shows class ListInt with nested struct Item { int val; Item* next; }, ListInt() constructor, void append(int v), and Item* find(int v) const. In the implementation: void ListInt::append(int v) { Item* x = new Item; // no scoping needed inside member function }. But for the return type: ListInt::Item* ListInt::find(int v) const { ... } - the return type requires scoping because it appears before the function scope begins. In main(): ListInt mylist; ListInt::Item* p = mylist.find(2); // requires scoping the type.
notes_text: The scoping rule for return types is a common gotcha. C++11's trailing return type syntax (auto find(int v) const -> Item*) can avoid this issue.

images.description: Code showing ListInt class with nested Item, member function implementations demonstrating when scoping is and isn't needed

title: Static Members Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the supplementary topic of static data members and static member functions.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Static Members section, a supplementary topic. Static members are variables or functions that belong to the class itself rather than to any particular instance. The following slides cover the motivation for static members, their declaration and initialization, and practical examples like unique ID generation and the singleton pattern.
notes_text: Static members are an important concept for understanding class-level behavior versus instance-level behavior.

title: One For All - Unique ID Problem
summary: Poses the problem of assigning unique IDs to USCStudent objects as they are created, asking how this can be accomplished.
main_text: As USCStudent objects are created we want them to have unique IDs. How can we accomplish this? The class USCStudent has a constructor USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = ________; // ???? } with private string name and int id. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); and USCStudent s2("Jill"); should each have unique IDs. The question is: what value should id be assigned, and how can we ensure each new student gets a different ID?
notes_text: This motivates the need for a shared counter that persists across all instances. A regular data member would give each instance its own counter, which doesn't solve the problem.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent class with blank ID assignment in constructor and main() creating two students

title: One For All - Counter as Data Member (Wrong Approach)
summary: Shows that making a counter a regular data member doesn't work because each instance gets its own separate counter.
main_text: Can we just make a counter data member of the USCStudent class? What's wrong with this? The class USCStudent has a constructor USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = id_cntr++; } with private int id_cntr, string name, and int id. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2. The problem is that id_cntr is an instance member, meaning each USCStudent object has its own id_cntr. When s1 is created, s1.id_cntr is uninitialized. When s2 is created, s2.id_cntr is also uninitialized. The counters are not shared between objects.
notes_text: Each instance having its own counter defeats the purpose. We need a single counter shared by all instances, which is exactly what static members provide.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent with id_cntr as regular member, demonstrating the problem of separate counters per instance

title: One For All - Static Members Solution
summary: Introduces the static keyword to create a shared counter variable that belongs to the class rather than any specific instance.
main_text: It's not something that we can do from within an instance. A student doesn't assign themselves an ID, they are told their ID. Sometimes there are functions or data members that make sense to be part of a class but are shared (only 1 exists) amongst all instances. The variable or function doesn't depend on the instance of the object, but just the general class (family of objects). We can make these 'static' members which means one definition shared by all instances. The class USCStudent has USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = id_cntr++; } with private static int id_cntr, string name, and int id. The static member must be initialized outside the class: int USCStudent::id_cntr = 1;. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2.
notes_text: The static keyword changes the storage class of the member from per-instance to per-class. There is exactly one copy of id_cntr shared by all USCStudent objects.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent with static int id_cntr and its initialization outside the class, demonstrating shared counter

title: Static Data Members - Declaration and Initialization
summary: Details how to declare static members with the static keyword, initialize them outside the class in a .cpp file with class scope, and how they are shared.
main_text: A static data member is a single variable that all instances of the class share. Can think of it as belonging to the class and not each instance. Declare with keyword static. Initialize outside the class in a .cpp (can't be in a header). Must be scoped with class name. Code shows class USCStudent with static int id_cntr declared in the class, and int USCStudent::id_cntr = 1; initialization outside the class. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2. A diagram shows USCStudent::id_cntr as a single box with value 3 (after two increments), with s1 (Tommy, id 1) and s2 (Jill, id 2) as separate instance boxes, illustrating that id_cntr is shared while name and id are per-instance.
notes_text: Static data members must be defined (initialized) outside the class in exactly one .cpp file. Putting the initialization in a header would cause multiple definition errors across translation units.

images.description: Diagram showing USCStudent::id_cntr as single shared box with value 3, and two separate instance boxes for s1 (Tommy, 1) and s2 (Jill, 2)

title: Example: Class Constants (string::npos)
summary: Uses std::string::npos as a real-world example of a static class constant, explaining its use with find() to indicate no match.
main_text: Sometimes there are constants that are useful to define for a class but the same value for all instances. std::string::npos is such a constant. It is used as an input value for a length parameter that means 'until the end of the string'. It is returned by a call to string::find() or string::rfind() to indicate 'no match'. Code example: string s1 = "cs104"; if(s1.find("103") == string::npos) { cout << "We're not in 103 anymore" << endl; }. The find function searches for "103" in s1 and returns string::npos if not found.
notes_text: string::npos demonstrates a practical use of static const members. It is a sentinel value that all string objects share, defined once at the class level.

images.description: Code example showing string::npos usage with find() to check if a substring exists in a string

title: Example: Class Constants (string::npos) - Implementation
summary: Shows that string::npos is implemented as static const size_t npos = (size_t)-1, which is the largest unsigned value (all 1s in binary).
main_text: std::string::npos is set to the largest unsigned value supported by the system (all 1s in binary) which can be achieved by casting -1 (which is all 1s in signed binary) to an unsigned value. A simplified string class shows: class string { public: static const size_t npos; ... };. The initialization outside the class: const size_t string::npos = (size_t)-1;. Casting -1 to size_t produces the maximum unsigned value because -1 in two's complement is all 1 bits, and reinterpreting those bits as unsigned gives the maximum value.
notes_text: This is a clever use of two's complement representation. Since size_t is unsigned, casting -1 to size_t gives the maximum possible value, which serves as an ideal 'not found' sentinel.

images.description: Code showing simplified string class with static const size_t npos declaration and its initialization to (size_t)-1

title: Another Example: Singleton Pattern
summary: Demonstrates static member functions and the singleton design pattern using a President class that allows only one instance.
main_text: In addition to static data members, static member functions are also allowed. Static member functions do NOT take a 'this' pointer (not executing on an instance). They are called by preceding with 'className::'. They can access private members of the class. Code shows class President with public static President* makePresident(string name) and void printName() const, private string name_, President(string name) : name_(name) {} (private constructor to disallow other instances), and static President* thePres. Initialization: President* President::thePres = nullptr;. The makePresident function checks if(nullptr == thePres) then creates thePres = new President(name); and returns thePres. In main(): President* p = President::makePresident("Carol"); President* p2 = President::makePresident("Mark"); p->printName(); // prints "Carol", p2->printName(); // still "Carol" because only one instance is ever created.
notes_text: The singleton pattern ensures exactly one instance of a class exists. The private constructor prevents external creation, and the static factory method controls instantiation. This is a common design pattern in C++.

images.description: Code showing President class implementing singleton pattern with private constructor, static member function makePresident, and static pointer thePres

title: A Related Example - Static Members for Shared State
summary: Shows how static members can represent shared state (all US citizens share one president) and why private static members need accessor functions.
main_text: All US Citizens share the same president, though it changes over time. Rather than wasting memory for each citizen to store a pointer to the president, we can make it static. However, private static members can't be accessed from outside functions. For this we can use a static member function. Code shows class USCitizen with USCitizen() constructor, private static President* pres, string name, and int ssn. In main(): USCitizen c1; USCitizen c2; President* curr = new President; USCitizen::pres = curr; // won't compile because pres is private. The solution is to provide a static setter function.
notes_text: This example motivates static member functions as accessors for private static data. The next slide shows the complete solution with a setPresident static function.

images.description: Code showing USCitizen class with private static President pointer that cannot be accessed directly from main()

title: Static Member Functions
summary: Explains static member functions: they operate at class level, cannot access instance data, are called with className::, and serve as accessors for static data.
main_text: Static member functions do tasks at a class level and can't access data members (since they don't belong to an instance). Call them by preceding with 'className::'. Use them to do common tasks for the class that don't require access to an instance's data members. Static functions could really just be globally scoped functions but if they are really serving a class' needs it makes sense to group them with the class. Code shows class USCitizen with public USCitizen() and static void setPresident(President* p) { pres = p; }, private static President* pres, string name, and int ssn. In main(): USCitizen c1; USCitizen c2; President* curr = new President; USCitizen::setPresident(curr); ... President* next = new President; USCitizen::setPresident(next);.
notes_text: Static member functions are essentially namespaced free functions that have access to private static members. They are called with the class name, not an instance, reinforcing that they operate at the class level.

images.description: Code showing USCitizen class with static setPresident function and main() calling it via USCitizen::setPresident()

title: Old Material Section Divider
summary: Section divider indicating older material follows, likely from a previous version of the course.
main_text: This slide contains just the word OLD, indicating that the following slide contains older or archived material that may have been part of a previous iteration of the course.
notes_text: This appears to be legacy content retained for reference purposes.

title: Review: Parts of a C++ Class
summary: Summarizes the four main parts of a C++ class: data members, constructors, member functions, and destructors, with a LListInt example.
main_text: What are the main parts of a class? Data members: What data is needed to represent the object? Constructor(s): How do you build an instance? Member functions: How does the user need to interact with the stored data? Destructor: How do you clean up after an instance? Example shows class LListInt (a linked list of integers) with public: LListInt() (default constructor), LListInt(int n) (initializing constructor), ~LListInt() (destructor), void push_front(int n), void pop_front(), void printList() const. Private: Item* get(size_t loc) helper function and Item* head pointer. This example demonstrates all four parts: head is the data member, two constructors handle creation, push_front/pop_front/printList are member functions for interaction, and ~LListInt handles cleanup of dynamically allocated nodes.
notes_text: This summary slide ties together all the major concepts from the unit. Every well-designed class should carefully consider each of these four aspects: what data it holds, how it is constructed, what operations it supports, and how it cleans up.

images.description: Code showing LListInt class with all four parts labeled: data members (head), constructors (default and initializing), member functions (push_front, pop_front, printList), and destructor (~LListInt)

title: Unit 5d - Inheritance
summary: Title slide introducing the Inheritance unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5d - Inheritance. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the inheritance unit in CS103.
notes_text: First slide of the deck; establishes unit identity for inheritance concepts in object-oriented programming.

title: Recall: Constructor Initialization
summary: Reviews constructor initialization lists versus assigning values in the constructor body, emphasizing best practices for non-scalar members.
main_text: When writing a constructor, you can assign values to data members inside the constructor body using statements like name = "Tommy Trojan"; id = 12313; scores.resize(10);. However, any member not listed in the initialization list will have its default constructor invoked before the constructor body executes. You can still assign values in the constructor body, but realize that the default constructors will have been called already. So, if you know what value you want to assign a data member, it is good practice to do it in the initialization list. Example: Student::Student() : name("Tommy"), id(12313), scores(10) { }. This would be the preferred approach especially for any non-scalar members (i.e. an object).
notes_text: This slide is a review from earlier material. The key insight is that initialization lists avoid double-initialization: once by the default constructor and again by assignment in the body. For primitive types the cost is negligible, but for objects like strings and vectors, using the initialization list is more efficient.

images.description: Two code boxes showing a Student constructor: the left assigns values in the body, and the right shows the equivalent with an implicit initialization list calling default constructors first. An arrow connects them to show the transformation.

title: Object Oriented Design Concepts
summary: Introduces four pillars of OOP: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism with brief definitions.
main_text: Encapsulation: Combine data and operations on that data into a single unit. Expose a desired public interface and prevent modification or alteration of the implementation. Abstraction: The public interface should simplify use for third parties, handling details internally. Inheritance: Creating new objects (classes) from existing ones to specify functional relationships and extend behavior. Polymorphism: Using the same expression to support different types with different behavior for each type.
notes_text: This slide provides the conceptual framework for the rest of the unit. Inheritance and polymorphism are the focus of this and the next unit, while encapsulation and abstraction were covered earlier. Understanding these four pillars is essential for designing well-structured object-oriented software.

title: Composition - Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide introducing composition as building complex objects from simpler objects used as data members.
main_text: Composition: Building more complex objects by using simpler objects as data members. This section introduces the concept of composition as a way to reuse and combine objects in object-oriented programming.
notes_text: Composition is presented before inheritance to establish the contrast between has-a and is-a relationships, which is a central theme of this unit.

title: Composition
summary: Defines composition as reusing simpler objects as data members to create larger, more complex objects, establishing a has-a relationship.
main_text: A goal of OOP (via encapsulation and abstraction) is to make it easy to reuse objects and build more complex objects from simpler ones. The most obvious way to do that is through composition. Composition (definition): Reusing smaller, simpler objects as data members to create a larger, more complex object. Composition is said to define a 'has-a' relationship. For example, a Connect4Game class has-a Board, has-a HumanPlayer, and has-a AIPlayer. Similarly, a WebServer class has-a Request, has-a Response, and has-a NetSocket.
notes_text: The has-a relationship is key to understanding composition. Each component object exists independently and is contained within the larger object. This contrasts with inheritance's is-a relationship introduced later.

images.description: Two class hierarchy diagrams showing composition. The top diagram shows class Connect4Game containing class Board, class HumanPlayer, and class AIPlayer. The bottom shows class WebServer containing class Request, class Response, and class NetSocket. Each component class is shown as a box nested inside the container class.

title: Composition - Example 1: Connect4 Game
summary: Demonstrates composition with a Connect4 game using Board, HumanPlayer, and AIPlayer classes as data members of Connect4Game.
main_text: This example shows composition with a Connect4 game. The Board class has public methods like Board(int nr, int nc), ~Board(), isFree(), setColor(), getColor(), removePiece(), and hasWon(), with private members int nr_, nc_, and int** boardData_. The HumanPlayer class has public methods HumanPlayer(int color), getUserInput(const Board& b, int& row, int& col), and getColor() const, with private member int color_. The Connect4Game class composes these: it has private members Board b_, HumanPlayer hp_, AIPlayer aip_, int n_, and winner_. Its methods like hasWon() delegate to b_.hasWon(n_, winner_), and nextPlayerTurn() calls hp_.getUserInput(b_, r, c) and then b_.setColor(r, c, hp_.getColor()). This shows how the game object delegates work to its component objects.
notes_text: Notice how Connect4Game does not reimplement board logic or player input. It delegates to the composed objects. This is the power of composition: each class has a single responsibility and the container orchestrates their interactions.

images.description: A small Connect4 board image showing colored pieces (red, yellow, black circles) arranged in a grid, illustrating the game the classes model.

title: (De-)Composition
summary: Introduces decomposition by considering how to break a CSStudent class into smaller, more general, reusable components.
main_text: Consider a class to model a CSStudent and the data members it would have: name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_ (vector<double>), and hoursInSAL_. Especially in larger software designs, consider decomposing large objects into multiple, smaller objects that can be reused and/or coded separately. Consider what aspects of the object might fit with a more general object, and what is truly specific to this object. The CSStudent class has members like name and id that could belong to a more general Student or Person class, while hoursInSAL_ is specific to a CS student.
notes_text: This slide motivates the decomposition process that leads to inheritance. By identifying which members are general (name, id) versus specific (hoursInSAL), we can factor out a base class. This is the analytical step that precedes choosing between composition and inheritance.

images.description: A class definition for CSStudent showing all data members (name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_, hoursInSAL_) alongside a memory layout diagram showing the same members stacked vertically.

title: Student (De-)composition [1]
summary: Shows first decomposition step: extracting a Student class from CSStudent and using composition with a Student data member.
main_text: The first decomposition step extracts a Student class with members name_, id_, major_, gpa_, and grades_. The CSStudent class then contains a Student stu_ as a data member (composition) plus its own hoursInSAL_ member. The CSStudent constructor uses the initialization list to construct the Student: CSStudent::CSStudent(string n, int id, int mjr, int hr) : stu_(n, id, mjr) { hoursInSAL_ = 0; }. Alternatively, without the initialization list, you could call stu_.set_name(n) and stu_.set_id(id) in the body. The CSStudent::get_name() method delegates to stu_.get_name(). Why might factoring out a Student class this way be advantageous? Can we decompose further?
notes_text: This is composition in action: CSStudent has-a Student. The memory layout shows the Student's members nested inside CSStudent (stu_.name_, stu_.id_, stu_.major_, stu_.gpa_, stu_.grades_) followed by hoursInSAL_. The delegation pattern requires CSStudent to explicitly wrap each Student method it wants to expose.

images.description: Side-by-side class definitions showing the Student class (with name_, id_, major_, gpa_, grades_) and the CSStudent class containing a Student stu_ member. A memory layout diagram on the right shows the nested structure of CSStudent.

title: Student (De-)composition [2]
summary: Shows further decomposition by extracting a Person class from Student, creating a deeper composition hierarchy.
main_text: Further decomposition extracts a Person class with just name_ and id_ from Student. Now Student contains a Person p_ data member plus its own major_, gpa_, and grades_ members. Student::get_name() delegates to p_.get_name(). CSStudent still contains a Student stu_ member and delegates through it. The CSStudent constructor calls stu_.set_name(n) and stu_.set_id(id) in the body. The memory layout now shows the deeply nested structure: stu_.p_.name_, stu_.p_.id_, stu_.major_, stu_.gpa_, stu_.grades_, and hoursInSAL_. This demonstrates multi-level composition where CSStudent has-a Student which has-a Person.
notes_text: The deeper nesting shows both the power and the cost of composition. Access chains become longer (stu_.p_.get_name()) and wrapper methods multiply. This motivates inheritance as an alternative that avoids the explicit delegation burden.

images.description: Three-level class hierarchy using composition: Person class (name_, id_) contained in Student class (with Person p_, major_, gpa_, grades_), contained in CSStudent. Memory layout diagram shows the deeply nested member structure.

title: Student (De-)composition [3]
summary: Shows how factoring common aspects into general objects enables reuse across CSStudent, BuadStudent, Faculty, and Staff.
main_text: By factoring common aspects of objects into appropriate, more general objects, it makes reuse easier (it would be hard to reuse CSStudent to create a Faculty object) and makes it easier to write these smaller, more focused objects. The diagram shows nested ellipses representing how different objects share common components: CSStudent contains Student which contains Person. BuadStudent also contains Student which contains Person. Faculty contains Person directly. Staff contains Person directly. All four object types share the Person core, but specialize differently.
notes_text: This slide is the conceptual bridge to inheritance. The concentric ellipse diagram visually shows the is-a relationship that inheritance will formalize. CSStudent is-a Student is-a Person. This same hierarchy will be expressed more cleanly with inheritance syntax rather than composition.

images.description: Four concentric ellipse diagrams showing object hierarchies: CSStudent (Person > Student > CSStudent), BuadStudent (Person > Student > BuadStudent), Faculty (Person > Faculty), and Staff (Person > Staff). Each shows how the Person core is shared across all types.

title: Another Composition: Queue [1]
summary: Introduces building a Queue class via composition using an existing Linked List class, identifying needed operations.
main_text: Suppose you are given a (Linked) List class with functions to insert a new value at any logical index (i.e. 0 = front, size() = back), get a value from a logical index, and erase a value at a logical index. The List class has public methods: List(), void insert(int idx, int val), int size() const, int get(int idx) const, void erase(int idx), with private member Item* head_. Now we want to write a Queue class. What operations does a Queue support? Can a linked list accomplish those operations (so we don't have to recreate the wheel)? The Queue class uses composition with a private List mylist member.
notes_text: This example demonstrates composition applied to data structures. The Queue wraps a List and restricts its interface to queue operations only. This is a classic example of the Adapter pattern, where composition is used to change an object's interface.

images.description: A linked list diagram showing three nodes connected by arrows. Each node has a val and next field. The nodes are labeled with logical indices 0, 1, and 2. A head_ pointer points to the first node, and the last node's next points to NULL.

title: Another Composition: Queue [2]
summary: Implements Queue operations using List composition: push_back, front, pop_front, and size, each delegating to the List.
main_text: Queue class operations implemented via composition with a List: push_back(int val) inserts to end of the list at index size(): mylist.insert(size(), val). front() returns the front item at index 0: return mylist.get(0). pop_front() removes the front item at index 0: mylist.erase(0). size() returns the number of items in the queue: return mylist.size(). The Queue class restricts the full List interface to only the operations a queue needs. Users of the Queue cannot access arbitrary indices or insert at arbitrary positions, even though the underlying List supports those operations.
notes_text: This is a clean example of composition providing encapsulation. The Queue exposes only FIFO operations while hiding the full power of the underlying List. This is exactly how composition should be used: to create a restricted, purpose-specific interface over a more general implementation.

images.description: A linked list diagram showing three nodes with logical indices 0, 1, 2, alongside the Queue class implementation code showing each method delegating to the List member.

title: Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing inheritance as a way to create hierarchies of objects and reuse objects.
main_text: Inheritance: A way to create hierarchies of objects (and also reuse objects). This section transitions from composition to inheritance as the primary mechanism for defining relationships between classes.
notes_text: This divider marks the shift from composition (has-a) to inheritance (is-a). The parenthetical note about reuse hints that inheritance and composition share the goal of code reuse but achieve it differently.

title: Inheritance
summary: Defines inheritance as inheriting all data members and member functions from a base class, establishing is-a relationships in a class hierarchy.
main_text: Inheritance is a way of defining interfaces and relationships between objects, reusing classes, and extending original functionality. Inheritance allows a new class to inherit all the data members and member functions from a previously defined class. It works from more general objects to more specific objects. It defines an 'is-a' relationship. A Square is-a Rectangle is-a Shape. Square inherits from Rectangle which inherits from Shape. This is similar to classification of organisms: Animal -> Vertebrate -> Mammals -> Primates. More general classes sit at the base (top of the hierarchy) as the Parent/Base class. More specific classes are the Child/Derived classes, and even more specific are Grandchild classes.
notes_text: The is-a relationship is the defining characteristic of inheritance. Unlike composition's has-a, inheritance means the derived class IS the base class plus additional specialization. The biology analogy helps: just as a Primate IS a Mammal IS a Vertebrate, a Square IS a Rectangle IS a Shape.

images.description: Concentric ellipse diagram showing inheritance hierarchy with three levels: outer ellipse labeled Parent/Base (most general), middle ellipse labeled Child/Derived, and inner ellipse labeled Grandchild (most specific). Annotations indicate more general at the top and more specific as you go deeper.

title: Base and Derived Classes [1]
summary: Shows the C++ syntax for inheritance with Person as base class and Student as derived class, inheriting all members and functions.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. The Student class inherits get_name() and get_id() functions, as well as name_ and id_ member variables from Person. Syntax: class Person has public methods Person(string n, int ident), string get_name(), int get_id(), and private members string name_ and int id_. The derived class is declared as: class Student : public Person, which means Student publicly inherits from Person. Student adds its own public methods: Student(string n, int ident, int mjr), int get_major(), double get_gpa(), void set_gpa(double new_gpa), and private members int major_ and double gpa_. The memory layout of a Student object contains name_, id_ (inherited from Person), plus major_ and gpa_ (Student's own).
notes_text: The colon syntax 'class Student : public Person' is the key C++ syntax for inheritance. The 'public' keyword here means public members of Person remain public in Student. The memory layout diagram shows that inherited members physically exist in the derived class object.

images.description: Two code boxes showing Person and Student class declarations connected by an arrow indicating inheritance. A memory layout diagram on the right shows class Student containing name_, id_, major_, gpa_ stacked vertically, with name_ and id_ highlighted as inherited from Person.

title: Base and Derived Classes [2]
summary: Poses the question of whether calling get_name() on a Student object is legal, since Student does not define it directly.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. In the code example, we call get_name() on the Student s1 object: Student s1("Tommy", 1, 9); cout << s1.get_name() << endl;. Is this legal? Does the Student class have a get_name() function? The Student class itself does not define get_name(), but the question is whether it can still use it. The memory layout shows class Person with name_ and id_, and class Student with those same members plus major_ and gpa_.
notes_text: This slide is intentionally posed as a question to engage students. The answer comes on the next slide. The point is to make students think about what it means to inherit functionality before revealing that yes, inherited public methods are callable on derived objects.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations with inheritance, plus a main function creating a Student and calling get_name(). Two memory layout boxes side by side compare Person and Student member layouts.

title: Base and Derived Classes [2 Solution]
summary: Confirms that Student can call get_name() because it INHERITED the function from Person, making it accessible to third parties.
main_text: Derived classes inherit all data members and functions of the base class. In the code, we call get_name() on the Student s1 object. Is this legal? Does the Student class have a get_name() function? YES. Though the Student class does NOT have a get_name() function defined directly, it INHERITED it via the Person class and other code can call and use it. The comment in the code reads: 'Student has Person functionality and is accessible to 3rd parties.' So cout << s1.get_name() << endl; is perfectly valid and will output the student's name.
notes_text: This is a fundamental concept: public inheritance means all public members of the base class become public members of the derived class. External code can call inherited methods on derived objects exactly as if they were defined in the derived class itself. This is what makes inheritance powerful for code reuse.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations with public inheritance, plus main() calling s1.get_name() with a comment confirming Student has Person functionality. The word INHERITED is highlighted.

title: Access And Inheritance [1]
summary: Uses a family analogy to explain private member access: children inherit resources but cannot access them directly, only through parents' public interface.
main_text: Consider a family analogy. The parents might have resources (money) they do NOT let their children access; the resources are PRIVATE. However, the children may access those resources by asking the parents (i.e. going through the parent's PUBLIC interface). So, the children technically have the resources but just cannot access them directly. This analogy maps directly to inheritance: derived classes inherit private members but cannot access them directly.
notes_text: The family analogy is a helpful mnemonic. Just as children in a family have indirect access to family resources through their parents, derived classes have indirect access to inherited private members through the base class's public (or protected) methods. The key takeaway: inheritance does not break encapsulation.

title: Access And Inheritance [2]
summary: Demonstrates that if the parent class makes members PRIVATE, they remain private to the derived class, which must use the public interface.
main_text: The base class access levels still apply when inheritance is used. Important: If the parent (base) class makes one of their members PRIVATE, it is PRIVATE to the child (derived) class! It cannot access it directly but must go through the parent's PUBLIC interface. In the code example, Person has private members string name_ and int id_. Student inherits from Person publicly but cannot access Person's private members directly. The comment reads: 'Cannot access Person's private members directly, but must go through Person's public methods.' Student must go through Person's public interface (like get_name() and get_id()) to access inherited private data members.
notes_text: This is a critical rule that students often get wrong. Even though Student inherits name_ and id_, Student's own code cannot write 'name_ = n;' because name_ is private to Person. Student must call Person's public setters/getters. The lock icon in the memory layout diagram reinforces that inherited private members are locked away from the derived class.

images.description: Code showing Person class with private members and Student inheriting from it. A memory layout diagram on the right shows Student's members with a lock icon on the inherited private members (p_.name_, p_.id_) and dashed lines indicating Student must use Person's public interface.

title: Constructors and Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing how constructors work with inheritance.
main_text: Constructors and Inheritance. This section covers how constructors are called and initialized when using inheritance, including initialization lists for base class constructors.
notes_text: Constructor initialization is one of the trickiest parts of inheritance. The following slides will explain why you cannot directly assign inherited private members and how to use the initialization list to call the base class constructor.

title: Constructors and Inheritance
summary: Shows that the derived class constructor cannot directly assign inherited private members, since Person's name_ and id_ are private.
main_text: How do we initialize base class data members? Given what we just learned about access control, can we write the highlighted code in the Student constructor? Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) { name_ = n; id_ = ident; major_ = mjr; }. No! The Person members name_ and id_ are private. The Student constructor cannot directly access or assign them. This is because private means private, even to derived classes. The derived class must find another way to initialize the base class members.
notes_text: This slide poses the problem that the next slide solves. Students often try to directly set inherited private members in the derived constructor, which is a compilation error. The solution is to use the initialization list to call the base class constructor.

images.description: Code showing Person and Student class declarations, with the Student constructor body attempting to assign name_ = n and id_ = ident, which are highlighted in orange to indicate this is incorrect because those members are private to Person.

title: Constructors and Inheritance - Solution
summary: Shows the correct approach: using the initialization list to call the base class constructor, since constructors cannot be called directly.
main_text: Constructors are ONLY called when a variable is created and CANNOT be called directly from another constructor. How to deal with base constructors? Also, we want or need base class or other members to be initialized before we perform this object's constructor code. Use the initializer format instead. Incorrect approach: Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) { Person(n, ident); } - No! You CANNOT call a constructor like a member function to initialize data. Correct approach: Student::Student(string n, int ident, int mjr) : Person(n, ident) { cout << "Constructing student: " << name_ << endl; major_ = mjr; gpa_ = 0.0; }. The initialization list syntax ': Person(n, ident)' calls Person's constructor before Student's constructor body executes.
notes_text: This is the essential mechanism for inheritance constructors. The initialization list is not just a best practice here - it is the ONLY way to invoke a specific base class constructor. Without it, the base class's default constructor would be called (if it exists), which may not initialize members correctly.

images.description: Two code examples: the top one shows the incorrect approach of calling Person(n, ident) inside the constructor body (highlighted in orange as wrong), and the bottom shows the correct approach using the initialization list : Person(n, ident) (highlighted in green as correct).

title: Constructors and Destructors
summary: Explains constructor and destructor ordering in inheritance: constructors run base-to-derived (inside out), destructors run derived-to-base (outside in).
main_text: Constructors: A Derived class will automatically call its Base class constructor BEFORE its own constructor executes, either by explicitly calling a specified base class constructor in the initialization list, or by implicitly calling the default base class constructor if no base class constructor is called in the initialization list. Destructors: The derived class will call the Base class destructor automatically AFTER its own destructor executes. General idea: Constructors get called from base outward to derived (inside out). Destructors get called from derived inward to base (outside in). In a three-level hierarchy (base, child, grandchild), construction order is base(1), child(2), grandchild(3), and destruction order is grandchild(1), child(2), base(3).
notes_text: The inside-out / outside-in pattern is fundamental. Think of it as building a house: you lay the foundation (base) first, then build up. When demolishing, you tear down the top floor (derived) first. This ensures base class invariants are established before derived class code runs, and derived class cleanup happens before base class resources are released.

images.description: Two concentric circle diagrams showing constructor and destructor ordering. The constructor diagram has arrows pointing outward from base(1) to child(2) to grandchild(3). The destructor diagram has arrows pointing inward from grandchild(1) to child(2) to base(3).

title: Constructor and Destructor Ordering Example
summary: Full worked example with classes A, B, C showing exact constructor and destructor call order with output tracing.
main_text: Three classes form an inheritance chain: class A (base) with int a, class B : public A with int b, and class C : public B with int c. Each constructor and destructor prints a message. A() sets a=0 and prints 'A:0'. A(int mya) sets a=mya and prints the value. B() sets b=0 and prints 'B:0'. B(int myb) sets b=myb and prints. C() sets c=0 and prints 'C:0'. C(int myb, int myc) uses B(myb) in init list and sets c=myc. The test program: Allocating a B object (B b1) prints A:0 then B:0. Allocating 1st C object (C* c1 = new C) prints A:0, B:0, C:0. Allocating 2nd C object (C c2(4,5)) prints A:0, B:4, C:5. Deleting c1 object prints ~C ~B ~A. Quitting triggers c2 then b1 destruction: ~C ~B ~A then ~B ~A.
notes_text: This is the most important tracing exercise in the unit. Pay close attention to: (1) B b1 calls A() then B() in that order, (2) new C calls A(), B(), C() in that order, (3) C c2(4,5) calls A() default, B(4), then C body sets c=5, (4) delete c1 calls ~C, ~B, ~A, (5) at program end, c2 is destroyed first (later created, earlier destroyed in stack), then b1.

images.description: Two concentric circle diagrams on the right showing constructor ordering (A->B->C outward) and destructor ordering (C->B->A inward) with colored arrows.

title: Odds and Ends of Inheritance - Section Divider
summary: Section divider for miscellaneous inheritance topics including overloading, scoping, and composition comparison.
main_text: Odds and Ends of Inheritance. This section covers additional inheritance topics including overloading base functions, scoping base functions, and comparing inheritance versus composition.
notes_text: The remaining slides cover practical details of working with inheritance: how to override base class behavior, how to still access the base version, and when to choose inheritance over composition.

title: Overloading Base Functions
summary: Shows how a derived class can redefine a base class member function, with base objects using the base version and derived objects using the derived version.
main_text: A derived class may want to redefine the behavior of a member function of the base class. A base member function can be overloaded in the derived class. When base objects call that function, the base version will be executed. When derived objects call that function, the derived version will be executed. Example: class Car has double compute_mpg() that returns 30.0 if speed > 55, else 20.0. class Hybrid : public Car adds drive_w_battery() and its own double compute_mpg() that returns 45 if speed <= 15 (hybrid mode), 30.0 if speed > 55, else 20.0. A Car object calls Car::compute_mpg(), while a Hybrid object calls Hybrid::compute_mpg().
notes_text: The term 'overloading' here refers to the derived class providing its own version of a base class function with the same name and signature. This is sometimes called 'hiding' the base class function. It is distinct from polymorphic overriding with virtual functions, which is covered in the next unit.

images.description: Two class box diagrams showing Car (with model and speed) and Hybrid (with model, speed, and battery) side by side, illustrating the inheritance relationship and the overloaded compute_mpg function.

title: Scoping Base Functions
summary: Shows how to call the base class version of an overloaded function using the scope operator (::) from within the derived class.
main_text: We can still call the base function version by using the scope operator (::). Syntax: base_class_name::function_name(). In the Hybrid example, Hybrid::compute_mpg() can call Car::compute_mpg() for the non-hybrid speed ranges: double Hybrid::compute_mpg() { if(speed <= 15) return 45; // hybrid mode else return Car::compute_mpg(); }. This allows the derived class to reuse the base class logic for cases that haven't changed, only adding new behavior for the hybrid-specific case (low speed).
notes_text: The scope operator :: is essential for code reuse within overloaded functions. Without it, calling compute_mpg() inside Hybrid would recursively call itself. Using Car::compute_mpg() explicitly calls the base version, avoiding infinite recursion and duplicated logic.

title: Now With Composition
summary: Reimplements the Car/Hybrid relationship using composition instead of inheritance, showing the has-a alternative.
main_text: Rather than a Hybrid 'is-a' Car we might say Hybrid 'has-a' car in it, plus other stuff. While it might not make complete sense verbally, we could re-factor our code the following way. The Hybrid class now has a private Car c_ member (has-a relationship) instead of inheriting from Car. Hybrid::compute_mpg() calls c_.compute_mpg() for the non-hybrid case instead of Car::compute_mpg(). The class structure: class Hybrid { public: double compute_mpg(); private: Car c_; string batteryType; };. And: double Hybrid::compute_mpg() { if(speed <= 15) return 45; else return c_.compute_mpg(); }.
notes_text: This slide demonstrates the same functionality achieved through composition rather than inheritance. The key difference is that Hybrid no longer IS a Car, so it would not be substitutable where a Car is expected. This is a trade-off: composition gives more flexibility but loses the is-a relationship.

images.description: Class box diagrams showing Car (with model and speed) as a standalone class and Hybrid (with model, speed, battery) containing a Car object via composition, with the inheritance arrow replaced by containment.

title: Inheritance vs. Composition
summary: Compares when to use inheritance (is-a) versus composition (has-a), noting the common advice to prefer composition for code reuse.
main_text: Code reuse is a common need in (object-oriented) programming. Use one class to help define another. We can use composition which defines a 'has-a' relationship. A Student has-a Person 'inside' of it. Or we can use public inheritance which defines an 'is-a' relationship. A Student is-a Person (and inherits its members). Private inheritance could be used but is not a universal approach supported by other languages. Often programmers say 'prefer composition rather than inheritance' when the goal is code reuse. Software engineers debate about using inheritance vs. composition. So, when should we definitely use inheritance?
notes_text: The 'prefer composition over inheritance' principle is a well-known design guideline. Inheritance should be reserved for true is-a relationships and when polymorphism is needed. Composition provides more flexibility because it does not create tight coupling between classes. The slide leaves the question open for the final slide.

images.description: Two code boxes side by side: the left shows composition (class Hybrid containing Car c_ member) and the right shows inheritance (class Hybrid : public Car). Both achieve code reuse differently.

title: Inheritance / Composition Comparison
summary: Side-by-side code comparison showing the same Person/Student relationship implemented with inheritance versus composition.
main_text: Inheritance approach: class Student : public Person inherits get_name() and get_id() directly. In main(), Student s1("Tommy", 1, 9); cout << s1.get_name(); calls Person's get_name() which was inherited. Composition approach: class Student contains a Person p_ as a private data member. Student must explicitly define wrapper methods: string get_name() const { return p_.get_name(); } and int get_id() { return p_.get_id(); }. In main(), s1.get_name() calls Student's get_name() which delegates to p_.get_name(). The memory layouts are similar: both have name_, id_, major_, gpa_, but composition prefixes inherited members with p_.
notes_text: This side-by-side comparison clearly shows the trade-off. Inheritance: less boilerplate, automatic interface exposure, but tighter coupling. Composition: more boilerplate (wrapper methods), explicit interface control, but looser coupling and more flexibility. The memory layouts are essentially equivalent.

images.description: Two complete code examples side by side: left shows inheritance (class Student : public Person) with direct method inheritance, right shows composition (Student with Person p_) with explicit wrapper methods. Memory layout diagrams below each show equivalent structures.

title: Understanding Inheritance vs. Composition
summary: Explains the key difference: public inheritance exposes base methods automatically, while composition requires explicit wrapper functions.
main_text: With public inheritance, any public method you inherit from the base is visible to 3rd parties without extra code. With composition, you must rewrite a wrapper function in the derived class that calls the base class version. The derived class must explicitly recreate the desired interface. The diagrams show inheritance as a simpler connection where external access flows directly through to inherited methods, while composition requires explicit forwarding through wrapper methods that the derived class must define.
notes_text: This is the practical summary of the entire inheritance vs. composition debate. Inheritance wins when you want the full base interface exposed. Composition wins when you want to selectively expose only certain methods or when the is-a relationship does not hold.

images.description: Two abstract diagrams: the left shows inheritance with direct connections from external code through the derived class to base methods (simple, automatic). The right shows composition with the derived class needing explicit wrapper methods to forward calls to the contained object (more complex, explicit).

title: So, When Should We Use Inheritance
summary: Identifies two key reasons to use inheritance: extending base functionality and enabling polymorphic behavior in object hierarchies.
main_text: Reason 1: When you want the full interface of the base class but just add or extend functionality. Example: class ReversibleString : public std::string. You get all the other string functions 'for free' and can write only the extended functionality, such as a void reverse() method. In main(), a ReversibleString s1("Hello") can use s1.size() (returns 5), s1[0] (returns 'H'), s1.substr(3) (returns "lo"), and the new s1.reverse() followed by cout << s1 outputs "olleH". You would have to provide constructors which are not inherited, but then you get all string functions for free. Reason 2: When you have a hierarchy of related objects, want to enforce common interfaces, and/or use POLYMORPHIC behavior. More on this in the next unit.
notes_text: These two reasons are the definitive guide for when inheritance is appropriate. Reason 1 is about convenience and code reuse. Reason 2 is about design and polymorphism, which is the more compelling reason and the subject of Unit 5e. The ReversibleString example is elegant: inheriting from std::string gives you dozens of methods for free.

images.description: Code example showing ReversibleString class inheriting from std::string, adding only a reverse() method. Main function demonstrates using inherited string methods (size, operator[], substr) alongside the new reverse method.

title: Unit 5e - Polymorphism
summary: Title slide introducing the Polymorphism unit for CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: Unit 5e - Polymorphism. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. Opening title slide for the polymorphism unit in CS103.
notes_text: This unit builds directly on Unit 5d (Inheritance) and introduces the concept of polymorphism, virtual functions, and abstract classes.

title: So, When Should We Use Inheritance
summary: Reviews two reasons to use inheritance: extending base class functionality and enabling polymorphic behavior in hierarchies.
main_text: Reason 1: When you want the full interface of the base class but just add or extend functionality. Example: class ReversibleString : public std::string. You get all the other string functions 'for free' and can write only the extended functionality, such as a void reverse() method. In main(), a ReversibleString s1("Hello") can use s1.size() (returns 5), s1[0] (returns 'H'), s1.substr(3) (returns "lo"), and the new s1.reverse() followed by cout << s1 outputs "olleH". Reason 2: When you have a hierarchy of related objects, want to enforce common interfaces, and/or use POLYMORPHIC behavior. More on this in this unit.
notes_text: This slide is repeated from Unit 5d to bridge into polymorphism. Reason 2 is the focus of this entire unit. Polymorphism is arguably the most important reason to use inheritance in practice.

images.description: Code example showing ReversibleString class inheriting from std::string, adding only a reverse() method, with main function demonstrating inherited string methods alongside the new reverse method.

title: Coupling
summary: Defines coupling as dependency between components, contrasting low coupling (good) with tight coupling (bad), and how OO design reduces it.
main_text: Coupling refers to how much components depend on each other's implementation details (i.e. how much work it is to remove one component and drop in a new implementation of it). Low coupling (good) vs. Tight coupling (not so good): Replacing a new battery in your car (low coupling) vs. Replacing a new engine in your car (tight coupling). Adding a USB device to your laptop (low coupling) vs. Replacing the CPU in your laptop (tight coupling). OO Design seeks to reduce coupling as much as possible by creating well-defined interfaces to update (write) or access (read) the state of an object, and allowing alternate implementations that do NOT require interface changes.
notes_text: Coupling is a fundamental software engineering concept that motivates both encapsulation and polymorphism. Low coupling means you can swap implementations without changing the code that uses them. This is exactly what virtual functions and abstract classes achieve.

title: Polymorphism - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the polymorphism topic.
main_text: Polymorphism. This section introduces the core concept of polymorphism: using the same expression to operate on different types with different behavior for each type.
notes_text: Polymorphism literally means 'many forms.' In C++, it is achieved through virtual functions and inheritance, allowing a single interface to operate on objects of different derived types.

title: Base and Derived Type Compatibility
summary: Explains that a derived object can be assigned to a base object (slicing), but not vice versa, using animal classification analogy.
main_text: Are base and derived objects type compatible? Can we assign a derived object into a base object? Can we assign a base object into a derived? Consider: p = s (Base = Derived) and s = p (Derived = Base). Think hierarchy and animal classification: Can any dog be (assigned as) a mammal? Yes. Can any mammal be (assigned as) a dog? No. We can only assign a derived into a base (since the derived has EVERYTHING the base does). p = s is valid (Base = Derived is Good). s = p is invalid (Derived = Base is Bad). The memory layout shows Person has name_ and id_, while Student has name_, id_, major_, and gpa_. Assigning Student to Person copies only name_ and id_ (object slicing).
notes_text: This is the foundation for understanding pointer/reference compatibility. The key principle: a derived IS a base, so you can always treat a derived as a base. But a base is NOT necessarily a derived, so the reverse is unsafe. Object slicing occurs when assigning a derived to a base by value - the derived-specific members are lost.

images.description: Memory layout diagrams for Class Person (name_, id_) and Class Student (name_, id_, major_, gpa_) with arrows showing valid assignment direction from Student to Person and a prohibition symbol on the reverse direction.

title: Pointer and Reference Compatibility
summary: Establishes that base-type pointers/references CAN point to derived objects, but derived pointers CANNOT point to base or sibling objects.
main_text: Important fact: A base-type pointer (or reference) CAN point at (reference) a derived object. The compiler will see a pointer or reference to a derived class object is type-compatible with (can be assigned to) a base-class type pointer/reference. Example: Derived d; Base* b = &d; is valid. But not vice versa. A derived class pointer or reference CANNOT point to or reference a Base object. Base b; Derived* d = &b; is invalid. And clearly a derived pointer or reference is NOT type compatible with a different derived type pointer/reference. In the code: Person *q; q = &p (ok), q = &s (ok), q = &f (ok). But Student *t = &p (not ok), Faculty *g = &s (not ok). Base pointer CAN point at any publicly derived object. Derived pointer CANNOT point at base or sibling objects.
notes_text: This is the mechanism that makes polymorphism possible. Because a base pointer can point to any derived object, we can write code that uses base pointers and have it work with any derived type. This is the key enabler for virtual function dispatch.

images.description: Diagram showing a Person* q pointer with arrows to three objects: P (Person), S (Student with P inside), and F (Faculty with P inside). Green checkmarks show valid pointer assignments, red X marks show invalid ones. A separate Student* t pointer shows it cannot point to P or F objects.
labels: Base pointer CAN point at any publicly derived object
Derived pointer CANNOT point at base or sibling objects

title: Think About Ability
summary: Explains why base pointers can safely point to derived objects: derived objects guarantee they can do everything a base can do.
main_text: Is it a guarantee that a Student or Faculty object can do anything a Person object can? Yes, because each inherited the Person class. So, we can treat any Student or Faculty as we would a Person. Is it a guarantee that a Person can do anything Student or Faculty can do? No! Inheritance enforces and provides guarantees on what certain objects can do. This is why base pointers can safely reference derived objects: the derived object is guaranteed to support all base operations.
notes_text: This slide provides the logical justification for pointer compatibility. The guarantee flows downward: derived classes inherit all base capabilities. But it does not flow upward: base classes do not have derived-specific capabilities. This guarantee is what makes polymorphism type-safe.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q pointer pointing to three nested objects (P, S containing P, F containing P), each with a print_info() method. Dashed lines show the pointer can reach any of these objects.

title: Which Function Gets Called?
summary: Poses the question of which overloaded function version is called when using a base pointer to a derived object, introducing static binding.
main_text: Since a Student or Faculty can do ANYTHING a Person can do, we can point a base class pointer at the Derived object and call Person member functions on a Student and/or Faculty. But what happens if both base and derived overload a function? Which version gets called? The default approach is to always apply the function from the class corresponding to the pointer type being used. In the code: Person *q; q = &p; q->print_info() prints Name=Bill, ID=1. q = &s; q->print_info() prints Name=Joe, ID=2. q = &f; q->print_info() prints Name=Ken, ID=3. All three calls use Person::print_info() because the pointer type is Person*.
notes_text: This slide sets up the problem that virtual functions solve. Without virtual, the compiler uses static binding based on the pointer type, not the object type. So even though q points to a Student, Person::print_info() is called because q is a Person*. This is not the desired behavior when we want derived-specific output.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q pointer with dashed arrows to P, S, and F objects, each with their own print_info() method. The question mark indicates uncertainty about which version is called.

title: Non-Virtual Functions: Base Pointer => Base Functions (Static Binding)
summary: Explains static binding: without virtual, a base pointer always calls the base class version of an overloaded function.
main_text: For the second and third calls to print_info() we might like to have Student::print_info() and Faculty::print_info() executed since the actual object pointed to is a Student/Faculty. BUT it will call Person::print_info(). This is called 'static binding' (i.e. the version of the function called is based on the static type of the pointer being used). With no VIRTUAL declaration in the base class, only the base version from the POINTER TYPE can be called. Output for all three calls is just Name and ID, even when pointing to Student or Faculty objects: Name=Bill, ID=1; Name=Joe, ID=2; Name=Ken, ID=3.
notes_text: Static binding is the default in C++. The compiler determines which function to call at compile time based on the declared type of the pointer/reference. This is efficient but does not support polymorphic behavior. The next slide introduces the virtual keyword that enables dynamic binding.

images.description: Diagram showing Person* q with arrows to P, S, and F objects. Annotations show (1) No VIRTUAL declaration and (2) only the base version from the POINTER TYPE can be called. Output shows all calls produce Person-level output only.

title: Virtual Functions: Dynamic Binding
summary: Introduces the virtual keyword enabling dynamic binding, where the function called is determined by the actual object type, not the pointer type.
